title: NFL predictions: 3 keys to victory for Bills over Vikings in Week 9
summary: Week 9 of Monday Night Football is setting up to be a great game between two of the NFL’s hottest teams in 2026. The 6-1 Buffalo Bills are in Minneapolis, MN this evening looking to take down the 6-1 Minnesota Vikings on their home turf in front of a national audience. It’s a matchup featuring […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 13: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills signals for a first down during the first quarter against the Minnesota Vikings at Highmark Stadium on November 13, 2022 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images Week 9 of Monday Night Football is setting up to be a great game between two of the NFL’s hottest teams in 2026. The 6-1 Buffalo Bills are in Minneapolis, MN this evening looking to take down the 6-1 Minnesota Vikings on their home turf in front of a national audience. It’s a matchup featuring Super Bowl-starved franchises with championship DNA all over their rosters. The Bills boast a top-ranked scoring offense (33.3 ppg) led by an all-world quarterback in Josh Allen. However, their defense is among the worst in the NFL when it comes to holding opponents out of the end zone. Buffalo heads into U.S. Bank Stadium as a slight favorite (-3) with FanDuel Sportsbook , but the Vikings and their top-ranked scoring defense (13.3 ppg) will provide the toughest test yet for Allen and the Bills. Quarterback Carson Wentz is set to reprise his role as backup-turned-starter due to a hamstring injury that has quarterback Kyler Murray listed as week-to-week. That roster change may actually benefit Minnesota. Despite what Murray brings to the field as a dual-threat quarterback, the Vikings’ offense has found more success this season with Wentz at the helm. Wide receivers Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison could feast this evening if Buffalo’s defensive backs let their guard down on even one play. It’s strength versus strength between the Bills’ offense and the Vikings’ defense, but something has to give. Will that marquee matchup decide who wins, or will it instead be the game within the game featuring Buffalo’s defense against Minnesota’s offense? Beyond the obvious need for ball security and points, here’s what I predict happens for the Bills on offense, defense, and special teams if they improve to 7-1. There are plenty of ideas to consider, so be sure to sound off in the comments with your best plan to see Buffalo take down Minnesota in primetime! Bills lean heavily on RBs, WRs w/screens There’s a segment of analysis that believes the best way to attack the Vikings’ defense and the exotic blitz packages is by leveraging running backs in the screen game. That, and getting wide receivers involved in quick bubble screens could help Buffalo take down Minnesota. The Bills have one of the game’s best third-down running backs in Ty Johnson, who is a true weapon as a receiver out of the backfield. Buffalo also features wide receiver Khalil Shakir, a bona fide pinball wizard after the catch and between the down and distance. If the Bills want to stress defensive coordinator Brian Flores’ blitz-heavy scheme, they have plenty of options to send Vikings defenders scrambling back from where they came. Since his return from Injured Reserve to begin the season, Johnson has been lethal catching passes from Allen. In five games played, Johnson has 15 catches (15 targets) for 174 yards — averaging 34.8 yards per game. I expect a heavier workload for Johnson in Week 9, perhaps doubling his per-game averages in catches and yards. If true, that looks like a six-catch, 70-yard day. Shakir is the Bills’ second-leading wide receiver, having caught 27 passes (37 targets) for 354 yards and one touchdown. Look for Allen and Shakir to cook up a modern throwback that see No. 10 darting through traffic early and often. Head coach Joe Brady and Allen would be wise to throw more than a cursory pass or two to running back James Cook III. We’ve yet to see Cook really highlighted as a receiver, which is interesting given his pre-draft status as that class’ best dual-threat back. Cook has just 12 catches (18 targets) for 109 yards in seven games. I say he gets at least three receptions tonight, and he takes one of them to the house. Jim Leonhard rolls out blitz-heavy game plan Carson Wentz is a grizzled vet whose scrambling game scares no one. He much prefers passing from a clean pocket, allowing his receivers to do the leg work. Lucky for Wentz, he has two of the best in Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison. The Bills can’t allow Wentz to sit back and get into rhythm. Bringing disguised blitzes could be the move to speed up and fluster Wentz, forcing him to try and escape the pocket. Even better, confusing Wentz with blitzes might just stop him in his tracks, or send the football the other way with Buffalo. In his first season as a 3-4 outside linebacker, Greg Rousseau has played the most dominating football of his career. Rousseau has seven sacks, nine tackles for loss, seven pass defenses, three forced fumbles, and one epic blocked field goal. Minnesota will have to figure out how to handle Rousseau, but it may cost them a couple sacks in the process. That’s because the Vikings are likely going to do all they can to try and limit the damage done by defensive tackle Deone Walker. The second-year interior D-lineman has been a wrecking ball each week, and teams have begun focusing on stopping him on every down. Remember, Ed Oliver is back now, and he’s likely to get in on the sack party. Then there’s also Bradley Chubb at outside linebacker. Can Minnesota stop Rousseau, Walker, Oliver, and Chubb the entire game? Don’t bet on it. All the focus on Buffalo’s primary pass rushers could lead to good things for the interior linebackers and safeties. We saw safety Cole Bishop used as a blitzer against the Baltimore Ravens, and it’s likely his number is called when Wentz least expects it. With safety Damar Hamlin now installed as a field general in the defensive backfield, Bishop appears to be playing more free, and instinctual in key moments. The goal on defense: Make life miserable for Wentz and Minnesota’s offensive line. Force him into mistakes while locked-in on Jefferson and Addison, sending the Vikings’ offense back to the sideline without points. Tyler Bass makes game-winning FG Bass-o-matic is back! Through seven games, Bass is a perfect 16-of-16 on field goals in 2026. He’s 4-of-4 between 40 and 49 yards, and 2-of-2 from 50 yards and beyond. For a team that struggles holding opponents out of the end zone, having a reliable kicker in crunch time is a must. That’s been Bass to a T so far this season. While it’s unlikely he remains perfect all season, Bass has rebounded better than anyone could have predicted. His play is one of the key reasons Buffalo is 6-1, and I have a feeling his number’s called late tonight to try and send the Bills home winners. As we know, anything can happen when the Bills hit the field. What do you see happening during Monday Night Football ? Think you’ve got what it takes to make a play with the Buffalo Bills in 2026? (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s finally Monday, which means the Buffalo Bills and Minnesota Vikings finally square off under the brightest football lights of Monday Night Football to close out Week 9 of NFL action. Bills Mafia and the SKOL Family hope this season is different with both teams entering tonight’s game at 6-1. Yet, the circumstances in both getting to this point are far different. That 33-30 overtime loss for Buffalo came in Orchard Park, NY back in November 2022. Josh Allen is 1-1 against the Vikings since entering the NFL, with his first professional win coming in a 27-6 victory back in September of his rookie season in 2018. title: The Buffalo Bills who must keep rolling in Monday Night Football showdown with Vikings
summary: The Buffalo Bills (6-1) travel to Minneapolis on Monday Night Football to take on a Minnesota Vikings team that is also 6-1 and coming off its first loss of the season, 19-15 at Detroit. The Bills beat the Baltimore Ravens 36-10 last Sunday, but Baltimore lost both quarterbacks in the first half, and I’m careful […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills (6-1) travel to Minneapolis on Monday Night Football to take on a Minnesota Vikings team that is also 6-1 and coming off its first loss of the season, 19-15 at Detroit. The Bills beat the Baltimore Ravens 36-10 last Sunday, but Baltimore lost both quarterbacks in the first half, and I’m careful about using that game as a measuring stick for this one. Minnesota is a different kind of test. Brian Flores is the main reason. His defense leads the NFL in scoring (13.3 points per game) and blitzes on roughly 70 percent of dropbacks. Carolina is next at 42.6 percent (the Bills themselves blitzed on 64.5 percent of dropbacks last Sunday, second only to Minnesota in Week 8, per Next Gen Stats). Josh Allen completes 65.7 percent of his passes against five or more rushers at 8.4 yards per attempt, so, on paper it’s a great matchup but the reality is that nobody is better than Flores sending 5 or more after opposing QBs. Buffalo has the league’s best offense (33.3 points per game) and the best EPA per play (0.175), and Minnesota has the best defensive mark (-0.189). The Vikings’ offense is their problem on the other side. It ranks 30th in EPA per play (-0.099), Carson Wentz starts with Kyler Murray out with a hamstring injury, and Justin Jefferson has 335 yards heading into Week 9, a lower pace than his career-low 2025, per Pro Football Talk. I think the game comes down to whether Buffalo’s offense can stay on schedule against the blitz while the defense tries to not give Wentz and Jefferson easy completions. With all of this in mind, here are the Bills who need to keep rolling and those who must step up Monday night. KEEP ROLLING Christian Benford, CB: Jefferson is the assignment Zay Flowers entered Week 8 second in the NFL in receiving yards per game (101.3) and first in yards after the catch (331). He caught none of his five targets, and four came from rookie Joe Fagnano. Jim Leonhard also changed the plan: the Bills ran man coverage on 54.8 percent of dropbacks, up from 19.5 percent, per Next Gen Stats. Benford was a big part of that. His coverage EPA of -5.8 was sixth in the NFL in Week 8, he was eighth in catch rate allowed over expected, and his tight-window percentage (50) tied Damar Hamlin for sixth. He played 45 of 51 snaps. He has found his rhythm after a slow start — Pro Football Reference has him allowing a 106.6 passer rating through his first five games (22-of-36, three touchdowns). PFF had him 72nd of 102 corners (55.4) through Week 8. Monday needs the last two games version. Jefferson has 28 catches for 335 yards and four touchdowns. In games Wentz has played, he gets 31.5 percent of targets and 45.2 percent of air yards, and averages 2.52 yards per route run, per Sharp Football Analysis. Against Detroit, he caught five of nine targets for 33 yards and a touchdown. With the offense 30th in EPA, stopping him goes a long way toward stopping Minnesota. DJ Moore, WR: Flores’ blitz leaves someone alone outside In his three full games, Moore has a 28.7 percent target share and 42.3 percent air yards share, which Next Gen Stats ranks sixth and fourth in the league. Against Baltimore he caught four of seven targets for 82 yards and a touchdown. Downfield, he caught three of four for 78 yards and a score, including a 43-air-yard completion that was Allen’s longest of the game by air yards. PFF had him on the field for 37 of Allen’s 42 pass plays (54 snaps). As stated above, Allen has been successful against five or more rushers. That kind of defense leaves a receiver one-on-one, and Moore is the one the offense looks to first. His AC joint sprain is the variable. He’s always one bad fall over his shoulder away from leaving the game and making Josh’s life tougher. Keon Colrman has stepped up when it happened and could be another key in this matchup. Tylan Grable, OT: Left or right, the start of something special? Grable allowed two pressures on 42 pass-blocking snaps against Baltimore, per charting-based metrics cited by Buffalo Rumblings. Both came in true pass sets, and he had 12 of those. He played all 82 snaps, and Allen was sacked once. The numbers aren’t clean, though: PFF had him at 38.8 in Week 5 after he replaced Spencer Brown, and 55.8 for the season over 133 snaps. His negatively graded run-block play rate was 13.2 percent, against 5.3 percent for Dion Dawkins. The veteran is questionable with a rib injury and hasn’t practiced, though Joe Brady said he could play anyway. If he sits, which I expect, Grable likely moves to left tackle with Brown at right. Minnesota’s rush is led by Andrew Van Ginkel (6.5 sacks) and Dallas Turner (six sacks, 19 quarterback hits), per ESPN. The Bills line has allowed the third-fewest pressures (74) and seventh-fewest sacks (13). Grable helps decide whether that holds. STEP UP James Cook, RB: The answer to the blitz might be on the ground Cook has rushed for at least 75 yards and a touchdown in six straight games, but he got 80 yards on 21 carries (3.8 per carry) against the Ravens. On the season he has 707 yards and seven touchdowns on 138 carries. The Bills rank third in rush EPA (0.013) and second in rush success rate (49.7 percent). Excluding Week 8, Buffalo led the NFL in rush DVOA (16.1 percent). The Vikings are beatable on the ground. They rank 17th in rush yards allowed (116.7 per game) and gave Jahmyr Gibbs 153 yards and a touchdown on 23 carries last week. Screens have produced +0.39 EPA per play on 12 attempts against Minnesota, per SIS. Cook played 44 snaps (54 percent) against Baltimore and had three targets. He needs to be both the draw and the screen outlet against the blitz. We know very well Joe Brady loves a screen opportunity. Dee Alford, NCB: Is the veteran really the best option? PFF has him at a 42.6 overall grade, 96th among 103 cornerbacks. His coverage grade is 41.8 (94th), with a 100.8 passer rating allowed on 13 receptions, in addition to five missed tackles, through Week 6. An ankle injury kept him out of the game against the Ravens, and he has no designation on the final injury report for Monday. Te’Cory Couch started at nickel last week: 36 snaps (71 percent), one reception allowed for zero yards, and one of the team’s highest PFF grades (79.9). Jim Leonhard said he executed at a very high level. Jordan Hancock, who plays nickel and safety, is questionable and needs to be activated from IR. Maxwell Hairston also has snaps in three-cornerback packages, with Benford sometimes following receivers inside. If the Bills maintain the 54.8 percent man coverage from last week (Next Gen Stats), the slot is where the Vikings will test them. I think his spot is at risk, and Monday is his chance to hold onto it. HONORABLE MENTIONS Also Rolling Josh Allen, QB: PFF graded him 82.3 last week. He went 6-of-10 for 157 yards and two touchdowns on throws of 10+ air yards. For the season he is fourth in EPA per play (0.22), 10th against the blitz (0.11) and third against pressure (-0.03), per ESPN. On bootlegs he has 12.15 total EPA, second among quarterbacks, per SIS. Greg Rousseau, OLB: six of the team’s 30 pressures and a 27.3 percent pressure rate, fifth among players with 10+ rushes, per Next Gen Stats. Wentz has less mobility than Murray, and Rousseau is the Bills’ best answer. Davison Igbinosun, CB: coverage EPA of -4.7 (10th) and a -74.6 percent catch rate allowed over expected, second-best among qualified defensive backs. He played 41 of 51 snaps (80 percent), PFF graded him 73.4, and he had his first career interception. Jordan Addison is his target. Also Stepping Up Jackson Hawes, TE: 29.3 from PFF, the lowest on offense. His bobbled pass became Broderick Washington’s interception and set up the Ravens’ only touchdown. With the need for the run game to get going, he should see a lot of snaps on offense. Michael Hoecht, OLB: 32.5 from PFF against the Ravens, second-lowest on the defense, and 47.9 through Week 6 (110th of 115 edge defenders). Buffalo’s pressure rate was the…

title: Discussion: Was the Panthers loss to the Broncos a moral victory?
summary: There’s no such thing as a moral victory, right? That’s what people like to say, but I think that mindset misses a lot of nuance that can be useful when assessing the state of the team and what could be expected going forward. The Carolina Panthers lost at home to the Denver Broncos on Sunday. […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 08: Tommy Tremble #82 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates after scoring a touchdown with Chuba Hubbard #30 during the second quarter against the Denver Broncos at Bank of America Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Grant Halverson/Getty Images) | Getty Images There’s no such thing as a moral victory, right? That’s what people like to say, but I think that mindset misses a lot of nuance that can be useful when assessing the state of the team and what could be expected going forward. The Carolina Panthers lost at home to the Denver Broncos on Sunday. They didn’t put up as many points, but they outgained the Broncos and averaged more yards per play. The run defense that had been embarrassingly bad at times this season limited Denver to 3.0 yards per carry and got in the backfield on a number of plays. Bryce Young through for 276 and Chuba Hubbard averaged nearly five yards per carry. On a play to play basis, the team played well enough to win. However, untimely penalties and the flukiest of interceptions massively swung the momentum of the game in the Broncos favor, and the Panthers ultimately couldn’t overcome that. That brings us to our question… Was Sunday’s loss to the Broncos a moral victory? MY TAKE: I think so. The Panthers needed to show some life after disastrous outings in their last two games. The beginning of the game looked like another disaster was incoming, but the team righted the ship in the second quarter and more than held their own. The Broncos have had a weird season, but they are 6-2 and in contention for the top seed in the AFC. They’ve also got some rabbit’s foot black magic voodoo going on where they keep snatching victory from the jaws of defeat. The Panthers seemed to be victimized by that in a way yesterday. The interception was one of the flukiest I’ve ever seen, to the point where the player that intercepted the pass didn’t even realize he had an interception. There also should have been a pass interference on the play, but the officiating crew that was spamming pass interference calls all day somehow missed that one. Otherwise, the Panthers’ undoing was a result of penalties largely from the practice squad players that are currently occupying the starting cornerback spots. And even then, I thought at least a couple of them were questionable flags. The parts of the defense that you’d want to look improved under a new defensive coordinator did look better. The offense had a good day against a very good Broncos defense. Bryce Young looked like the version of himself we saw earlier in the season and posted a season high 86.5 QBR. The schedule lightens up significantly in the next month or so. If the Panthers play like they did today minus the penalties, they can post a good record in that stretch of games. So while the result of yesterday’s game was bitterly disappointing, I think there were enough positives to take away that we can feel good about what this team is capable of going forward.
author: Jonathan DeLong

title: The Optimist: Not even half-way done yet
summary: Bryce Young was right yesterday, insofar as the team’s perspective goes, that they need to win games by margins that can’t be overturned by a single, atrocious officiating error. “We should never be relying on Refs, or calls, or anything like that. It’s on us to go leave no doubt.,” he said during his postgame […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 08: Nik Bonitto #15 of the Denver Broncos blocks pass by Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers during the fourth quarter at Bank of America Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Grant Halverson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Bryce Young was right yesterday, insofar as the team’s perspective goes, that they need to win games by margins that can’t be overturned by a single, atrocious officiating error. “We should never be relying on Refs, or calls, or anything like that. It’s on us to go leave no doubt.,” he said during his postgame press conference. Unfortunately, doubt was about the only thing the Carolina Panthers left on the field in their 21-26 loss to the Denver Broncos yesterday. 13 penalties for 119 yards (a 69-yard differential) against the Panthers and a controversial, replay-assisted turnover in the end zone held one of the most injured teams in the league back from beating one of the most charmed teams in existence. The Broncos have now won an NFL record 16 consecutive one-score games. They established that record yesterday by playing against a roster that, at several important positions, has been assembled over just the past couple of weeks. If I were a Broncos fan, I wouldn’t be excited about my team after beating the Panthers yesterday. If I were a Panthers fan, I wouldn’t be too down on my team. Folks in the comments have spent a lot of time pointing out that the Panthers only wins come against the Cooper Rush Falcons, the Tanner McKee Eagles, and the Detroit Lions (who are actually a good team). I’ll counter that with the fact that the Panthers have been the most injured team on any field they have played this season. If the most important ability is availability then the Panthers have been far from the most able team on their own schedule. Let’s dig into that. Bryce Young vs his offensive line Panthers quarterback Bryce Young and his offensive line are having career years. For Young, he remains, statistically, a top ten passer in the NFL. He is fourth in yards per game and tied seventh for touchdown passes. He has also taken the fourth most sacks in the league and often shows up as the most pressured quarterback in the league in weekly advanced metrics. That’s because his offensive line has been awful in pass protection this season. Left tackle Rasheed Walker and center Luke Fortner have been free agency busts, with both leading the league at various points this season with most pressures allowed at their respective positions. Right guard Robert Hunt, who has also made those lists, has clearly not returned to form after a torn bicep last season. Their disappointing seasons have combined with the nagging injuries for left guard Damien Lewis, the effectively total absences of right tackle Taylor Moton, left tackle Ikem Ekwonu, and do-it-all lineman Brady Christensen, and the rookie learning curve for tackle Monroe Freeling to make “the most expensive offensive line in the league” a strength that barely ever existed on paper. Add in the occasional injuries for back-up guards Torricelli Simpkins and Corey Bullock and it is clear that Young and running back Chuba Hubbard haven’t been playing from positions of strength. Hubbard has been earning what I call “Jonathan Stewart yards” where he ends a game with more yards after contact than total yards. Young has been harrassed from the snap more often than he has had a clean pocket. Yet both show up in the top ten at their positions. Complain all you want about the lack of offensive success, but let’s point fingers where they are due. Everything begins in the trenches in the NFL and the Carolina Panthers aren’t winning many battles there. Hope arrives next week, possibly, in the form of a returning Christensen. He’s unlikely to magically elevate everyone’s level of play, but sometimes all it takes is change at one position to settle the whole line in. Short yardage situations Yesterday’s goal-line fiasco (I’m trying to be polite) would never have happened if head coach Dave Canales and offensive coordinator hadn’t tried to get cute with a pass to Tommy Tremble. They had first and goal at the one yard line. They should have just run it in, right? I’m not so sure. The Panthers have struggled in short yardage situations all season. Most of their success has come either with passes or Hubbard bouncing a run to the outside when his intended gap has been congested by Panthers linemen not winning their blocks. This is going to be an ongoing area of concern and the biggest part of their current identity that will keep them back from making or succeeding in the playoffs. As for the goal line yesterday, Carolina had two choices: they could play to their strengths or they could try to impose their will with players who had proven they were not up to the task. I’m not mad at the call they made. That play I am mad at the decision to review the first down play after second down had been run and the ball was being spotted for third down. I think the NFL got it wrong, but I’m going to dive deeper into that later today. For now, suffice it to say that the interception, as far as the actual catch goes, was legit. Hilarious, even. I love plays like that. I also think that pass interference should be able to be assessed on review and that the challenge flag was late. The Panthers were failed by multiple layers of the officiating and review process yesterday and that is the biggest thing that stood between them and beating a team that has a better record and a healthier roster. Now is not the time for a team that is still sitting at first in its division to talk about firing coaches and drafting new quarterbacks. It may be time to talk about their field, training staff, and anything else that concerns the health and rehabilitation of their players. Can the defense catch a break? The Broncos 14-play, 80 yard drive for a touchdown probably doesn’t happen if even one of Jaelan Phillips, Nic Scourton, Bobby Okereke, Jaycee Horn, or Mike Jackson were on the field. The Panthers defense is hurt, trying to evolve under changing leadership, and playing a roster that looks straight out of the preseason. Marco Wilson was signed to the practice squad during the Week 5 bye. That means he had two weeks of practice with the practice squad before starting two games in a row in Weeks 8 and 9 that featured his defensive coordinator and passing game coordinator being dismissed from their roles in between. Corey Thornton and Chau Smith-Wade have been with the team for a couple of years now, but have had vanishingly little game experience this season as outside corners. In Thornton’s case, this was his first game active this season. I truly do not mind the penalties here. Nor do I point to them as coaching errors. These are young, inexperienced, and rusty players being thrown straight into the game against opponents in midseason form. They will either calm down and play smarter or prove why they were fringe roster/practice squad players in the first place. Improvement on defense will come, similarly to the offensive line, when they can field players who can reasonably be expected to compete in an NFL game. What’s next? Well, the Panthers are favored for their first game against the New Orleans Saints this season. That would put them on track to hold onto the first place position in the NFC South that they have held since beating the Atlanta Falcons in Week 2. Why are they favored, you ask, when they are on a three game losing streak and the Saints just beat the Browns? Probably because the NFL just watched a beaten up Panthers team almost beat the “fearsome” 7-2 Broncos. Carolina had to contend with outrageous officiating, poor health, poor protection, and a missed field goal. They lost by five points in a game that was ended by an excellent defensive play by the Broncos. The Panthers are also due to receive reinforcements in the way of Damien Lewis, Will Lee III,…

Week 10 Spread : -2.5 (-118) Panthers: -1.5 (-105) Saints: +1.5 (-115) O/U 47.5 (-115/-105) Moneyline Panthers: -118 Saints: +100 The Saints beat the Browns in over time, albeit a Shedeur Sanders-led Browns, and the Panthers lost to the Broncos in regulation. summary: The Carolina Panthers battled, but some bad penalties and bad luck resulted in a loss to the Denver Broncos, 26-20. First Quarter The Broncos got the ball first and immediately marched it down the field. They ran the kickoff out past the 40 then took two deep shots. Neither connected, but the second drew a […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 08: Devon Key #26 of the Denver Broncos intercepts a pass during the third quarter against the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Grant Halverson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers battled, but some bad penalties and bad luck resulted in a loss to the Denver Broncos, 26-20. First Quarter The Broncos got the ball first and immediately marched it down the field. They ran the kickoff out past the 40 then took two deep shots. Neither connected, but the second drew a rather ticky tack pass interference call. Jonah Coleman broke off a few nice runs to quickly put the Broncos in goal to go. The defense stepped up there. They stopped a first down run then got pressure on Bo Nix on second and third down to force incompletions and a fourth down field goal. The Panthers offense did nothing outside of a first play completion to Mitchell Evans. The Broncos moved the ball quickly once again. A couple of chunk plays got them into Panthers territory. Lee Hunter had a couple of nice plays, but another pass interference extended the drive. A few plays later, Bo Nix hit Courtland Sutton on a quick slant for a touchdown. The Panthers went three and out after a near miss to Tetairoa McMillan and a bad route by Darren Waller. After the punt, Marco Wilson got called for a taunting penalty for standing over Jaylen Waddle after an incomplete pass. The quarter ended after Bobby Brown led a group of Panthers in the backfield for a tackle for loss. Second Quarter The defense got off the field on third and long to get the ball back. The offense finally moved into Denver territory with a completion to McMillan and a couple of good runs by Chuba Hubbard, the second of which drew a late hit at the end. The drive fell apart after that. Young was nearly picked by Riley Moss, then three players jumped early for a false start. They ultimately settled for a 43 yard field goal, which Ryan Fitzgerald pretty much shanked out to the right. The Broncos moved the ball into Panthers territory, aided by a pass interference by Marco Wilson, his fourth penalty of the game. He was bailed out this time though. A couple plays later, Corey Thornton skied to undercut a receiver for an interception. The momentum shifted a little bit from that point. Bryce Young picked up a 3rd and 15 with a deep comeback to McMillan. He found Darren Waller a few times over the middle to continue the march into Broncos territory. The offense was faced with a 4th and 1, and Chuba Hubbard broke free off the left side for a big game. A few plays later, Young found Tommy Tremble in the backfield corner of the end zone for a toe tapping touchdown. Ryan Fitzgerald actually made the extra point this time, but he followed that by kicking the ensuing kickoff out of bounds. That gave the Broncos a short field to manage a quick two minute drill into field goal range to make it 13-7 heading into the half. Third Quarter The Panthers got the ball first out of the half and carried their momentum from the end of the first half. Young found Waller out of the gate for a big gain. A nine yard run from Hubbard and a nine yard catch by Evans put the Panthers on the edge of the red zone. After a couple of ineffective plays, Young found Waller deep over the middle for a touchdown to put the Panthers up 14-13. The defense kept the good vibes rolling. They stuffed a couple of early down runs to force the Broncos into an obvious passing situation. They got quick pressure, which forced Nix to step up into the waiting arms of Pat Jones. Young continued to pick apart the Broncos defense with more help from Darren Waller. He also had a 15 yard scramble to help the drive along. The Panthers got inside the five. Young tried to find Tremble in the end zone, but the ball was batted away. It somehow landed on Tremble’s arm on the way to the ground and was caught by a Broncos defender for the unlikeliest of interceptions. And it probably should have been a defensive pass interference as well. Fourth Quarter The Panthers committed a couple of penalties to help the Broncos start their drive, and they were followed by a series of easy short to intermediate completions from Bo Nix. It was a 14 play drive and was capped off by Jonah Coleman running to the outside and stiff arming Corey Thornton to the ground on his way to a go ahead touchdown. The offense couldn’t muster a response. A run went nowhere, a pass was incomplete, then Monroe Freeling was blown by for a rapid sack to end the drive with haste. The defense looked like they got off the field after a few plays, but Corey Thornton was called for a pass interference on third down, and it was another pretty soft call. A few plays later, Nix found Pat Bryant completely uncovered for an easy 26 yard touchdown. Bryce Young led a march down the field. He connected with Chuba Hubbard on a fourth down slant for a clutch conversion to keep the drive alive. Things got bogged down from there, and the Panthers ended up in a 4th and 15 spot. Young found space, stepped up, and hit John Metchie down the field to pick up the first down. Young was hit in the head in the process, which added a few extra yards to put the Panthers inside the ten. On the next play, Young found McMillan open on a slant for a touchdown to make it a one score game. The defense needed a quick stop. They stopped Jonah Coleman on first down. On second, Coleman dropped a pitch and the ball went bouncing back towards the goal line. Coleman eventually fell on it, but it was a loss of 18 yards. The Panthers made the tackle on third and long and forced the Broncos to punt coming out of the two minute warning. Young hit McMillan on a slant for a 21 yard gain on the first play of the drive to move into the Broncos side of the field. There was an offsides Bronco, and penalty would have stopped the clock even if it was declined. Instead, the Panthers had to hurry to the line, and on the next play, Young was hit in the arm trying to throw the ball. He fumbled, and the Broncos recovered. They were able to pick up a first down to run out the clock. Overview The Panthers actually outplayed the Broncos on a play to play basis. They averaged 5.7 to the Broncos 4.8 yards per play. Penalties and mistakes were the difference. In the defense of the Panthers, some of the drive extending pass interference calls were very questionable. Also, the interception probably could have been a pass interference on Denver, and it was a complete fluke that the ball ended up in the hands of a Bronco. It’s a disappointing loss, but it was an admirable performance for such a banged up Panthers team against a 6-2 Broncos team. The Broncos are just a charmed team right now, and the Panthers couldn’t overcome whatever black magic voodoo Sean Payton has done to earn his team some good fortune. The Panthers travel to New Orleans to take on the Saints in a key divisional matchup.
author: Jonathan DeLong

title: The Bears needed an ugly win like this. Now, never do it again.
summary: Sometimes, it’s good to win ugly. After all, what do you learn from steamrolling everyone and making things look easy all the time? That’s the silver lining I’m trying to take from the Chicago Bears’ messy 27-24 walk-off win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday Night Football.  I, like many, scoffed at the idea […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 08: Rome Odunze #15 of the Chicago Bears reacts after a first down reception against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the second quarter at Soldier Field on November 08, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sometimes, it’s good to win ugly. After all, what do you learn from steamrolling everyone and making things look easy all the time? That’s the silver lining I’m trying to take from the Chicago Bears’ messy 27-24 walk-off win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday Night Football. I, like many, scoffed at the idea that the then-3-5 Bucs would “humble” the Bears the way several analysts had suggested Tampa would. And for the first quarter or so of action, it looked like we’d be right. Unfortunately, we weren’t. It was terrible football from there on out. Five turnovers (four interceptions, varying in their degrees of bad, and an unfortunate fumble by Luther Burden III while he was concussed). The Bucs willed their way back into the game and eventually tied it up. The 2025 Bears played and won some rough games, but nothing quite that bad. But a win is a win, especially on a short week, and sometimes complementary football requires you to pick up your guys when they’re struggling. The offense did it in Week 1 as the defense couldn’t stop a nosebleed, scoring 59 points. This time, it was the defense’s turn to work their magic. We even got a Jaylon Johnson pick-six, for crying out loud! And in the end, the offense did just enough—thanks to some busted coverages by the Bucs—to seal the deal with Cairo Santos’ 38-yard field goal. The most important thing: the Bears will go into their bye week at a strong 7-2, with their opportunity to seize the division lead still intact when they return. Get healthy. Learn from the failures of this game. Get back on the horse in Week 11 against the New Orleans Saints. Also…let’s not do this again. In the same way as the Bears didn’t need to continually prove their mettle in the clutch the way they did last year, they certainly don’t need to demonstrate they can give the ball away five times and still win every week. That’s not going to cut it. Get that out of your system, and get back to being locked in and executing at a high level. The 3-5 Saints might not look like much, but they fight. People are already suggesting the Bucs gave the league the blueprint for how to deal with Chicago’s offense, that this won’t be the last time we see Williams and Ben Johnson struggle like this. For their sake, the Bears need to make sure it is. Because there’s a reason the 2006 Bears are the only other team in NFL history to win a game that brutal: it simply isn’t a winning formula. The good news is that, as easy as it would’ve been for them to lose, they made the choice not to mail it in. And that counts for something. Specifically, it’s another positive number in the win column.
author: Khari Thompson

title: 10 Bears Takes: An Unlikely Win and Some Trade Deadline Thoughts
summary: It’s been yet another impressive week for the NFC North as they continue to prove that they are the best division in football. For the first time in NFL history, there’s a 6-3 team in last place heading into Week 10. If the season ended today, all four teams in the division would be in […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 8: Jeffery Simmons #99 of the Chicago Bears in action during the second quarter against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Soldier Field on November 8, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s been yet another impressive week for the NFC North as they continue to prove that they are the best division in football. For the first time in NFL history, there’s a 6-3 team in last place heading into Week 10. If the season ended today, all four teams in the division would be in the playoffs, but with a Vikings loss on Monday Night Football, the Bears will be in sole possession of first place heading into their Week 10 bye. Sunday night’s game was quite the rollercoaster that featured a dominant start, followed by three quarters of flirting with disaster. Despite blowing a 14-point lead, the Bears’ offense was able to march down the field in the final three minutes of the game to set up Cairo Santos’ game-winning field goal to give Chicago a 27-24 victory. More importantly, despite five turnovers, the Bears moved to 7-2 and put themselves in a great position over the final eight games of the season once they return from the bye week. We’ll cover that, some trade deadline thoughts, and much more in a loaded Week 9 installment of 10 Bears Takes. 1. After an unbelievably impressive first quarter, quarterback Caleb Williams set a career-high for interceptions in an NFL game with three in the second quarter alone. The first two-and-a-half drives started like a dream for head coach Ben Johnson and the Bears offense. They marched down the field on back-to-back drives with impressive passing touchdowns from Williams. On the third drive, Williams once again made unbelievable throws, and the NFL world was in awe. Then came a 15-yard personal foul on Zavion Thomas that set the offense back to the 21 on a second-and-goal. On the next play, Williams fired one into double coverage for his second interception of the year. It was clear he was feeling himself, but he got caught trying to do too much, forcing a ball into the end zone for Rome Odunze. A few plays earlier, he hit Odunze in the chest for what should have been an easy walk-in touchdown. In a few plays, what should have been a 21-3 lead remained 14-3. Following a failed fourth-down attempt from Baker Mayfield and the Buccaneers, Chicago had the ball back at the 35-yard line with a chance to build an 18-point lead. Instead, Williams threw off his back foot, couldn’t get the ball out of bounds, and threw back-to-back interceptions on consecutive passes. A few drives later, following a big Cam Lewis interception, Williams threw his third interception of the night off his back foot, once again. Simply put, Sunday night’s second-quarter performance was as uncharacteristic as we’ve seen from Williams throughout his two and a half years in the league. Every quarterback in the league has bad games, but the way it happened felt unbelievable. A few observations: On his second interception, he had D’Andre Swift wide open in the flat as a checkdown option, which would have resulted in a first down, if not more. Despite the interceptions, Johnson did not shy away from calling a pass-heavy attack in the first half. Two of Williams’ three interceptions came off back-foot throws. With the bye week ahead, fans can rest assured knowing that Williams will obsess over his disastrous second-quarter decision-making. As we’ve learned with this offense, things only become a concern when they repeat themselves. Considering his history, this feels like a one-off that we might not see again for multiple seasons. Regardless, those mistakes let the Buccaneers stay in the game going into the half, which I’m sure will be a big talking point as they start prepping for New Orleans after the bye week. 2. In many ways, Sunday night’s game was a complete disaster. Not very often do teams win games when they turn the ball over five times and lose the turnover margin by three. Yet, they found a way to do it when everything was failing them. Following the first quarter, it felt like everything was going wrong for the Bears. Williams threw three interceptions in the second quarter, the Buccaneers scored right before the half, and the offense went completely silent for most of the second half. Most teams would have completely fallen apart, and to a certain extent, the Bears did. This was a very uncharacteristic game for this team under Ben Johnson, and there’s just no real other way to put it. The offense failed to score 30-plus for the first time since Williams’ return, and for the first time in the same time frame, they relinquished a lead. The good news is they still haven’t trailed in those four games, but that was a game where most of this team is probably going to want to flush it and move on. Sometimes these games just happen, and even when everything was going wrong, somehow, some way, the Bears held onto the lead for all but about three minutes. A big reason why the game stayed so close was their five turnovers, but while they lost the turnover margin by three, they allowed just 10 points off those five turnovers, which is pretty remarkable. Ultimately, Chicago is a well-coached team, and the Buccaneers, despite a slow start, were on a bit of a roll and had a chance to take over first place in the NFC South. This was a motivated team with plenty to play for, and even if they don’t have that one game-breaker at receiver, there’s still plenty of talent on both sides of the ball. In fact, heading into Sunday night, Tampa Bay’s defense was leading Seattle’s in many statistical categories. While you never want to see an offense go completely dark and turn it over that many times, when it counted most, Williams found 38 yards to get them into field goal range and eventually win the game. There will be plenty to take away and clean up from this game, but the bye week is coming at the right time. More importantly, their 7-2 start could be good enough to get them into first place by the end of Monday night. For now, we’ll turn our attention to the trade deadline on Tuesday, but as long as this one bad game stays just one bad game, the Bears are right on schedule as Super Bowl contenders. 3. Even with the late touchdown they gave up, the defense played a helluva game and was the reason they found a way to get to 7-2. The impact that Jeffery Simmons has had on this defense cannot be overstated. Despite a sackless first half, they came away with four in the second half, plus a pick-six from the much-maligned Jaylon Johnson. For the most part, they did a good job of bottling up the league’s most dangerous rushing attack. Before Tampa Bay’s final drive of the night, when they scored the game-tying touchdown, Irving had 80 yards and averaged 4.44 yards per carry. While that’s not great for the defense, it was much more manageable than most defenses have been against him this season. In the passing game, they had just one big coverage bust: Kyler Gordon was burned down the field by Tez Johnson for 58 yards. Outside of that, quarterback Baker Mayfield was uncomfortable in the pocket and didn’t consistently hit receivers past 10 yards. On the night, Mayfield finished with 243 passing yards, but had no touchdowns and two interceptions. The defense also defended five passes, despite being on the field for almost six more minutes than the offense. Simply put, without the defensive effort they received, the Bears don’t win on Sunday night. The box score might show 24 points and 352 yards, but they allowed just 10 points off those five turnovers and had four sacks and an additional tackle for loss on the night. This group will be a work in progress until they can get healthier. Honestly, they probably need at least another addition on that side of the ball, but all things considered, they are playing at a much higher level than anyone had expected coming into the season. With any luck, they’ll get…
author: Aaron Leming

title: Bears vs. Buccaneers: Inside the Snap Counts, Stats, and a Familiar Win
summary: If you’re a long-time fan of the Chicago Bears, then this 27 to 24 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers must have felt familiar. The offense kept shooting itself in the foot, so the defense had to bail them out, and then the special teams won it in the end. The Bears looked unstoppable early, […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 8: Jeffery Simmons #99 reacts after Jaylon Johnson #1 of the Chicago Bears runs the ball into the endzone for a touchdown after an interception during the third quarter against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Soldier Field on November 8, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images If you’re a long-time fan of the Chicago Bears, then this 27 to 24 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers must have felt familiar. The offense kept shooting itself in the foot, so the defense had to bail them out, and then the special teams won it in the end. The Bears looked unstoppable early, but after jumping out to a 14-point lead, everything that could go wrong did go wrong. But this team found a way to win, and if it felt like “the Bears are who we thought they were” type of game, you’d be right. The Bears became just the second team in NFL history to win a primetime game despite throwing at least four interceptions and rushing for fewer than 75 yards. The first team to do it was the 2006 Chicago Bears against the Cardinals in the “the Bears are who we thought they were” game. Last night the Bucs had more total yards (352 to 349), more first downs (18 to 15), ran more plays (64 to 60), and had the time-of-possession edge (32:52 to 27:08). They also had fewer penalties, with 8 for 45 yards to 9 for 74 for Chicago. The Bears did get the better of the Bucs on third downs as Tampa Bay was just 2-12 (16.7%) to Chicago’s 7-13 (53.8%). Tampa Bay’s record may not look it, but that’s a good football team that just happened to run into a better one on Sunday night. This nugget from CBS Sports’ Doug Clawson shows just how good the Bucs have been playing. “The Bucs are the 1st team with 1,000+ rush yards and 17+ takeaways in a 5-game span since the 1985 Bears.” And this nugget from OptaSTATS shows how much the Bears had to overcome to get the victory, as they are the only team in NFL history to have 5+ turnovers, 9+ penalties, have no 10+ yard rushes, blow a 14+ point lead, and yet still win the game. Let’s look at the Bears’ playing-time breakdown and a few individual stats from the game. OFFENSE This was one of the worst games of Caleb Williams’ career, and the first time he ever threw four interceptions in a game. After the game, he immediately recalled that he threw three picks once in high school and threw three in one game in college. Considering he’s one of the least-intercepted quarterbacks in league history, I’ll view this stinker as an anomaly. He’ll learn from it and come out after the bye focused, playing like the same Caleb we’ve gotten used to. Despite the poor performance, he did lead the offense down the field on a game-winning drive, which was his first this year after a league-leading 6 a season ago. DEFENSE Statistically, Jeffery Simmons had a “quieter” game than his debut, but he still filled the stat sheet, and his presence allowed his teammates to make plays. Simmons plays with a high motor (and he only missed 2 snaps), and that’s infectious to the entire unit. If Simmons can chase wide receiver Emeka Egbuka 20 yards downfield to make a tackle, then every other defender can play with that same kind of effort. Devin Bush had a season-high in tackles and passes defended. Grady Jarrett and Shemar Turner picked up their first sacks of the year. Turner’s was his first career sack. Montez Sweat had his most tackles in a game since he had 7 on October 26, 2025. Jeffery Simmons on seeing Caleb in “2-minute mode”: “I didn’t panic because Caleb is a baller.” Adds “once we put a complete game together, good luck.”😈 pic.twitter.com/H4iilULr9g — CHGO Bears (@CHGO_Bears) November 9, 2026 SPECIAL TEAMS* *The above image has players who only played in the third phase. Cairo Santos was 3 for 3 on extra points and made both field goals, including the 38-yard game-winner. Tory Taylor punted 4 times for a 40.3-yard average, and he had 1 blocked for a second straight game. Zavion Thomas had a 29.3-yard average of the 3 kickoffs that counted. Kalif Raymond had 6 punt returns for 48 yards and 1 fumble that he recovered. Roschon Johnson had 2 special teams tackles. To check out the complete Bears vs. Bucs box score, I find ESPN’s site is easy to navigate. All statistics and snap counts, as well as the accompanying pictures, are taken directly from the NFL’s Game Statistic and Information System.

title: Bears prove that good teams find a way to win
summary: It was one of the ugliest Chicago Bears victories in recent memory. And yet, it was still a Bears victory. Cairo Santos hit a last-second 38-yard field goal to give Chicago the 27-24 victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday night, improving their record to 7-2 in the process. Caleb Williams threw a whopping […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 8: Jeffery Simmons #99 of the Chicago Bears reacts during the fourth quarter against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Soldier Field on November 8, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images It was one of the ugliest Chicago Bears victories in recent memory. And yet, it was still a Bears victory. Cairo Santos hit a last-second 38-yard field goal to give Chicago the 27-24 victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday night, improving their record to 7-2 in the process. Caleb Williams threw a whopping four interceptions against Tampa Bay, which he confirmed is the most he’s ever thrown in a single game dating back to his youth football days. After a red-hot start to the game with a stellar first quarter, he appeared to falter against a Buccaneers defense that has been one of the best in the NFL this season. Still, a pick-six by Jaylon Johnson and an overall strong defensive outing from the Bears gave them the win. The Bears have their bye week coming up in Week 10, and it couldn’t have come at a better time after such a sloppy performance. Still, they found a way to win, and that says a lot about this team. Here are some of my takeaways’ from Chicago’s win on Sunday night. Caleb reverts to his rookie self The stat sheet isn’t kind to Caleb Williams this week. His four interceptions buried any opportunity at sustained drives that the Bears could have hoped for. Two of them came on passes that he tried to throw away but simply didn’t have enough distance behind, and a Buccaneers defender got under it and made the play. One was a forced through into a tight window, but one that was bobbled and ended up into the arms of a Tampa Bay defender. The first one was simply a missed read of a nearby safety in zone coverage. I’m not as worried about some of the interceptions as I am what followed. Williams looked inaccurate and rattled on a handful of passes. He found the open man, but he simply put the ball in the wrong place to where the receiver couldn’t make the catch. He’s done a much better job of playing on time within Ben Johnson’s offense this year, but after the second or third interception, his progressions felt rushed. Caleb has been fantastic overall in 2026, but this was one to forget. The bye week will be beneficial for him to get his confidence back. The resilience of Chicago’s defense As much as it felt like the Bears’ offense kept finding new ways to let the Buccaneers back into the game, Tampa Bay’s offense also struggled throughout the course of the game. Some of that comes down to that team’s own offensive issues, but some of it comes down to the strong coaching of defensive coordinator Dennis Allen and the resilience of the defensive personnel. Jaylon Johnson, who has struggled this year to the tune of the No. 105 overall grade among NFL cornerbacks in PFN CB Impact grading , came through in the clutch with a pick-six. Cam Lewis, who had to move from safety to the nickel after Kyler Gordon got hurt, had an interception of his own. Jeffery Simmons had another sack and made some incredible effort plays in pursuit. Austin Booker and Shemar Turner each had sacks, and Grady Jarrett split a sack with Daniel Hardy while also making multiple big plays along the defensive interior. The Bears’ defense stepped up when it mattered most. Good teams still find a way to win Make no mistake about it: this was a bad performance by this version of the Chicago Bears. Having seen what this team is capable of, this was an incredible disappointment. And yet, they still came out on top, extending their winning streak to four games. If your worst game is still a win, you’re doing something right. Chicago now has the bye week to rest, recover from injuries, and regroup. This team fought hard in the face of adversity, and even after making boneheaded mistake after boneheaded mistake, these guys managed to pull it off in a primetime setting. Many inferior teams around the NFL would’ve collapsed when faced with the downturn of momentum the Bears faced on Sunday. This game served as a reality check that the job isn’t finished. There’s still a lot of work that needs to be done. It’s too early to crown the Bears as a Super Bowl-caliber team, but it’s much better to get that wake-up call in Week 9 instead of in the postseason.

title: Chicago Bears Fans Waiting All Night for Good, Better, Best
summary: For the third time in three weeks, I find myself in a familiar spot. Fired up after a Chicago Bears primetime victory, I sit waiting to hear seventeen sweet words before I go to bed. “Good, better, best. Never let it rest. Until your good gets better, and your better gets best.” Carrie Underwood may […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 08: Jeffery Simmons #99 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after a sack against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the fourth quarter at Soldier Field on November 08, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images For the third time in three weeks, I find myself in a familiar spot. Fired up after a Chicago Bears primetime victory, I sit waiting to hear seventeen sweet words before I go to bed. “Good, better, best. Never let it rest. Until your good gets better, and your better gets best.” Carrie Underwood may have been waiting all day for Sunday night, but I’ve been waiting all night for Good, Better, Best. Doctors may frown upon screen time before bed, but I can’t sleep until I see it. For those of you Bears fans who prioritize a good night’s sleep over watching Ben Johnson give out game balls and shouting out his triumphant message, you might not realize that it takes a minute for the Chicago Bears social media team to edit these up and post for our viewing pleasure. Last week’s Monday Night win in Seattle dropped at 11:53 pm Central Time: Building something special pic.twitter.com/TrvCBNakX1 — Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) November 3, 2026 The week before, a Thursday Night Football win against the Patriots dropped at 11:27 p.m. Central Time: Good luck falling asleep after this one pic.twitter.com/YWvaOMGQIr — Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) October 23, 2026 That one was a bit earlier and, let’s be honest, victory Fridays are easy to get through – you can catch up on sleep on the weekend. So here we sit again, waiting for the social media team to drop another Good, Better, Best video after the Bears complete the Primetime Trifecta. This has been a great stretch as the Bears go into the bye week at 7-2, winners of 4 straight, even if this one was… weird. Even better for our sleep schedules, the next four games are noon kickoffs. Sure, one of them is on Thanksgiving, and you might be distracted during family dinner, but if your family loves you, they’ll understand. Honestly, the whole family should be waiting to serve dinner until that video drops, but that’s a discussion for another day. The beauty of the Good, Better, Best videos is more than a peek inside the locker room. For many of us, a Bears game is an all-consuming experience, and the videos provide a chance to cap the experience. It’s like a nice bourbon at the end of a big day to help us relax. We get to compare notes with Coach Johnson on who we think should get a game ball and, best of all, we get to see the men we cheer for every week celebrate their hard-earned victory. It’s a brilliant piece of fan service by the Bears social media team. Okay, it’s now past 11 pm and I’m going to cheat. The Sunday Night Football crew did us a favor and showed it at the end of the broadcast, and it is honestly what you might expect after that weird game. Jaylon Johnson gets the game ball, and they move into Good, Better, Best immediately. They’re thankful for the win, as we all are, but frustrated by the path it took to get there. I think we can all agree. Understandably the least enthusiastic good, better, best to date. pic.twitter.com/BMgTMjLNrE — ✶Ⓜ️𝕒𝕣𝕔𝕦𝕤 ▶️✶ (@_MarcusD3_) November 9, 2026 The prayer hands at the end really sums it up for me. Drop a note in the comments on what time you watched this Good, Better, Best. Hit me with your honest timestamp. Are you a wait all night until it drops person, wait until morning, or did you just learn that these exist? EDITOR: I’m an up-all-night person, so here’s the official version! "Our best football is yet to come" pic.twitter.com/c3XpbnREtS — Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) November 9, 2026

title: Bears v Buccaneers: Bears Cruise Early, but Bucs Rock the Boat Late
summary: Bears 27, Buccaneers 24 – Bears go to 7-2 Soldier Field, Sunday Night Football – The 6-2 Chicago Bears hosted a 3-5 Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and Chicago jumped out to a 14-0 lead, then spent most of the night handing Tampa Bay free possessions as the wheels came completely off. Caleb Williams threw four interceptions […]
full_text: Bears 27, Buccaneers 24 – Bears go to 7-2 Soldier Field, Sunday Night Football – The 6-2 Chicago Bears hosted a 3-5 Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and Chicago jumped out to a 14-0 lead, then spent most of the night handing Tampa Bay free possessions as the wheels came completely off. Caleb Williams threw four interceptions – at least three of them were his fault. The Bucs erased a double-digit deficit in the fourth, as we turned the ball over yet again in our own territory. But, somehow, Chicago still found a way to win when Cairo Santos hit a 38-yard field goal as time expired. It was ugly, self-inflicted, and ultimately enough. Who cares – we are 7-2 going into the Bye. But let’s talk the specifics, and no, I won’t be accepting any “parlay” requests. First Quarter: The Bears Look Like the Team We Thought They Were Chicago opened with two touchdown drives. Williams hit Rome Odunze for a 9-yard score on the opening possession, then found Luther Burden on a short throw that turned into a 56-yard touchdown after Burden broke multiple tackles. It was 14-0 before the Bucs had done much of anything. Observation: The offense was efficient and explosive when it was clean. Burden’s after-the-catch ability turned a routine completion into a backbreaker. Gooch Hot Take: This is the version of the Bears that made people talk about January. We were cruising to an easy victory…until… Second Quarter: The Interception Tour Begins Williams threw three interceptions in the period. Tykee Smith and Zyon McCollum (twice) took turns collecting them. Tampa Bay turned the opportunities into two Chase McLaughlin field goals. Chicago managed a Cairo Santos field goal of its own. Halftime: 17-6. Observation: The Bucs’ defense created multiple short fields and still only managed six points. Chicago’s offense stopped itself repeatedly in Bucs territory. Gooch Hot Take: It all started with what seemed like an innocuous hand-fighting situation that went a bit too long – but Zavion Thomas was flagged for it, and suddenly the Bears were back at the 20 instead of on the doorstep of taking a 3-touchdown lead. A cascade of bad things happened, almost as if we had been given a gold coin from the Black Pearl’s treasure, and befell the Bears. Three picks in one quarter after going most of the season without multiple interceptions in a game, and suddenly a game that seemed quite in hand was suddenly looking very much in question. The Bucs’ inability to turn those gifts into more than field goals is almost as impressive in the wrong direction – this Bears defense is for real. Gooch looking at Todd Bowles: “That may be the best pirate I’ve ever seen.” Third Quarter: Pick-Six and a Temporary Reprieve Tampa Bay opened the half with a drive capped by Bucky Irving’s 2-yard touchdown run, set up by a long completion to Tez Johnson, cutting the lead to 17-13. And suddenly the quiet jaunt out to sea turned into a fricking hurricane. No problem. We have Zavion Thomas and the weather eye. Chase McLaughlin kicked off after Bucky Irving’s touchdown run, cutting the Bears’ lead to 17-13. Zavion Thomas took the kick at the Chicago 8 and returned it 91 yards (listed as ~92 in some reports), nearly reaching the end zone before being pushed out at the Tampa Bay 1 (replay might have made it a touchdown). But then the scurvy pirates used their dark magic, and the play was nullified by an “offensive holding penalty” on Bears linebacker D’Marco Jackson. The penalty was enforced from the Chicago 30, wiping out the return. Terry on the broadcast said it was clearly not a hold. So, Chicago started its next possession deep in its own territory instead of near the goal line. The sequence came right after the Bucs had scored to open the second half, so the nullified return kept the game tighter than it would have been. We had to punt, and it seemed that the seas were broiling in favor of the Bucs. But then, the sky parted, and Jaylon Johnson intercepted Mayfield and returned it 67 yards for a touchdown. The Bears led 24-13 heading into the fourth. Observation: The defense bailed out the offense again. Johnson’s return was Chicago’s cleanest play of the night. Gooch Hot Take: A pick-six is nice. It does not erase the fact that the quarterback who was supposed to be the difference-maker had already thrown four interceptions by this point. One of them was tipped; the rest were simply available. Fourth Quarter: The Collapse Arrives, Then the Kick Saves It McLaughlin kicked a 35-yard field goal to make it 24-16. But still, the Bears had it all in hand. Calm seas were ahead – all we needed was to tack once or twice, and the race would end. But then lightning struck once again, as Burden was struck in the helmet and he lost the ball deep in Chicago territory. After yet another Chicago turnover, Irving scored again from short range. Mayfield scrambled up the middle for the two-point conversion to tie the game at 24-24. All seemed lost. But then – the clouds parted, the sun shone down, and Colston Loveland was open like a dolphin in clear blue seas. Chicago then drove into field-goal range, and Santos connected from 38 yards as time expired for the 27-24 win. Observation: The Bucs’ ground game stayed consistent. Irving finished with 97 yards and two touchdowns. Williams finished 22-of-37 for 279 yards, two touchdowns, and four interceptions. Mayfield threw two of his own but avoided the volume Williams produced. The Bears’ defense and special teams ultimately outlasted the self-inflicted wounds. Gooch Hot Take: This is what happens when you dominate a quarter and think it is the whole game. You can’t take defensive coordinators as savvy as Todd Bowles for granted. Four interceptions against a 3-5 team on Sunday night is not the profile of a locked-in contender – but hey, a win is a win. The Bucs deserve credit for hanging around and finishing drives late; Chicago deserves credit for making it possible—and for Santos still being able to end the night with the ball going through the uprights. Final takeaway: Chicago looked sharp for one quarter, then spent the rest of the night donating possessions. The defense kept them in it long enough for the offense to keep shooting itself in the foot, and the kicker finished what the quarterback could not. I will say it again: a win is a win, and 7-2 is better than the alternative. It was still a messy night for a team with January ambitions, especially against Tampa Bay. The next few weeks will show whether this was an outlier or a warning. At least we have the bye. Let’s put into harbor and get a good fortnight’s rest before the next encounter. But what do you think about the Bears’ thrilling victory after the Bucs’ amazing comeback? Tell us in the comments below.

title: 3 things we learned from the Bengals’ fun game against the Falcons
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals are cruising right now, thanks in large part to an offense that is just too much for defenses to handle for four quarters. Here are three things we learned from Cincinnati’s 34-17 win over the Atlanta Falcons in Madrid. This is the best offense in the NFL It’s settled. The Bengals are […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - OCTOBER 15: Ja'Marr Chase #1 of the Cincinnati Bengals runs with the ball while being chased by Devon Witherspoon #21 of the Seattle Seahawks in the first quarter at Paycor Stadium on October 15, 2023 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Dylan Buell/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals are cruising right now, thanks in large part to an offense that is just too much for defenses to handle for four quarters. Here are three things we learned from Cincinnati’s 34-17 win over the Atlanta Falcons in Madrid. This is the best offense in the NFL It’s settled. The Bengals are better than the Buffalo Bills, the Dallas Cowboys, the Green Bay Packers or any other high-flying offense, simply because their three elite players outmatch every single defense in the league. Cincinnati is now averaging 30 points per game and has 30 points or more in four straight games. Against the Falcons, they didn’t turn it over, and Joe Burrow didn’t get sacked. Oh, and he threw for another three touchdowns and ran for one. He now leads the league in passing touchdowns and passing yards per game. The best part is that, while the Bengals tend to start slow, we’re now at the point in the season where Burrow, Chase Brown, and the offensive line all get hot, which means (barring injury) this train isn’t slowing down. Ja’Marr Chase is happy again Though a superstar, Chase is truly a team player. So he bit his tongue while the Bengals played around with the under center stuff that saw his numbers take a hit. But the Ravens game seemed to help the offense gain clarity about who they are. Now, after not getting 100 yards receiving his first six games, Chase has gone over 140 in back-to-back games. Cincinnati is back to being the Burrow-Chase-Higgins show, and Uno’s energy and body language show that he’s ready to regularly torch teams again. The defense need a drive or two to get going That’s the third straight game where the opponent surprised the Bengals by taking a lead (though not as big as the leads the Ravens or Titans took). And in all three games, the Bengals’ defense slowed down opposing offenses, especially their running backs, after those early bursts. On Sunday, it was Bijan Robinson who was held to just 58 yards on 16 carries following a huge opening drive, in which he had 42 yards on just three carries. It’s not perfect, but it does show you that the defense is capable of stepping up once Burrow and company put on their fireworks every game.

title: Bengals vs. Steelers opening odds for massive Week 10 showdown
summary: This is as big of a home game as it gets for the Cincinnati Bengals. It’s mid-November, against the Pittsburgh Steelers, and first place in the AFC North is on the line. Both the Bengals and Steelers are 6-2 and have both won four straight games. Not to mention, these two teams have already played […]
full_text: This is as big of a home game as it gets for the Cincinnati Bengals . It’s mid-November, against the Pittsburgh Steelers, and first place in the AFC North is on the line. Both the Bengals and Steelers are 6-2 and have both won four straight games. Not to mention, these two teams have already played this season. It was in Week 3, with the Steelers winning 30-27 in Pittsburgh. Right now on FanDuel , the Bengals are 3.5-point favorites next Sunday night. The Bengals’ moneyline is -200, while the Steelers’ is at +168. The over/under is at 47.5. Sunday night could be an extremely physical game. It’s an AFC North rivalry with sole possession of first place in the division at stake. Also, it’s the Bengals and Steelers. That’s all you need to know for the potential level of physicality. Pittsburgh stole the first game against the Bengals, aided by two Bengals turnovers in the fourth quarter that included Joe Burrow getting strip-sacked with the Bengals on the edge of field goal range in the final minute. The Bengals never ran an offensive play with the lead in that game, but there were some great performances from their star players. Joe Burrow was 28/37 for 282 yards and three touchdowns, Ja’Marr Chase caught nine passes for 98 yards and a touchdown, and Tee Higgins hauled in six passes for 90 yards and a touchdown. Mike Gesicki also caught a 25-yard touchdown on 4th&2 early in the fourth quarter. For the Steelers, Aaron Rodgers completed 19 of 34 passes for 292 yards and three touchdowns, while Jaylen Warren rushed for 127 yards on 17 carries. Eight different players caught a pass for the Steelers, with Darnell Washington leading the way with 67 receiving yards on three receptions. Roman Wilson, D.K. Metcalf, and Ben Skowronek each caught a touchdown for the Steelers. Rodgers currently has 1,871 passing yards and 13 touchdowns on the season, but he’s also thrown six interceptions and is completing just 60.8 percent of his passes. Warren has 704 rushing yards and two touchdowns, while Washington and fellow tight end Pat Friermuth lead the Steelers with three and four touchdowns, respectively. T.J. Watt, as of Sunday night, leads the NFL with 7.5 sacks, and he also has nine tackles for loss. Cornerback Jamel Dean also has three forced fumbles. Bengals right tackle Amarius Mims held T.J. Watt off the stat sheet in that game, which bodes well going into Sunday night. The Bengals’ offense scored on five of their eight drives in the first meeting in Week 3, gaining 352 yards of offense and rushing for 83 yards on 18 carries. Chase Brown rushed for 61 yards on 13 carries.
author: Alex Frank

title: Dexter Lawrence has a message for Joe Burrow: “Be Legendary”
summary: When the Cincinnati Bengals surrendered the 10th overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft to acquire Dexter Lawrence from the New York Giants, they were looking for a dominant defensive tackle who could transform their defense. But the three-time Pro Bowler is bringing something else to Cincinnati: A voice of encouragement for quarterback Joe Burrow. […]
full_text: When the Cincinnati Bengals surrendered the 10th overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft to acquire Dexter Lawrence from the New York Giants, they were looking for a dominant defensive tackle who could transform their defense. But the three-time Pro Bowler is bringing something else to Cincinnati: A voice of encouragement for quarterback Joe Burrow. Lawrence recently revealed the message he regularly delivers to his superstar teammate, and it speaks volumes about the respect he has for the Bengals’ quarterback. “I always whisper in his ear and say, ‘Be legendary, be a legend,” Lawrence admitted. “That’s who you are, and you don’t have to go outside yourself. Just be you, and that’s what he does.’” Dexter Lawrence has a message for Joe Burrow before every game: “Be a Legend.” The Bengals beat the Falcons 34-17 on Sunday day to improve to 6-2 on the season pic.twitter.com/ke8GPtMtAg — James Rapien (@JamesRapien) November 8, 2026 Those words carry considerable weight coming from a player who spent seven seasons establishing himself as one of the NFL’s premier interior defensive linemen before joining Cincinnati in April. And Burrow certainly has been living up to that billing. After throwing five touchdown passes and running for the game-winner in overtime against Tennessee, Burrow followed with three more touchdowns through the air and another one rushing in Sunday’s 34-17 victory over Atlanta in Madrid, extending Cincinnati’s winning streak to four games. Based on his eight games to date, Burrow is on a near-historic pace of roughly 5,070 passing yards and 49 touchdown passes over a full 17-game season. Only two quarterbacks in NFL history have passed for over 5,000 yards and 50 touchdowns: Peyton Manning in 2013 and Patrick Mahomes in 2018. Lawrence was brought to Cincinnati to help the Bengals win games by strengthening their defense. But his words suggest he also understands something important about the quarterback on the other side of the ball. Burrow doesn’t need to reinvent himself to become a legend. He simply needs to keep being Joe Burrow.

title: Joe Burrow shares best part of Bengals’ Madrid trip; wants to play in NFL’s first Tokyo game
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals are now 6-2 on the season after taking care of business against the Atlanta Falcons this morning in Madrid, Spain. Joe Burrow has been adamant about getting the Bengals an international game, and the NFL granted his request this season. Ja’Marr Chase, Tee Higgins, and Burrow put on an absolute show for […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals are now 6-2 on the season after taking care of business against the Atlanta Falcons this morning in Madrid, Spain. Joe Burrow has been adamant about getting the Bengals an international game, and the NFL granted his request this season. Ja’Marr Chase, Tee Higgins, and Burrow put on an absolute show for the international fans and Bengals fans that traveled to Madrid with the team. After the Bengals 4th win in a row, Burrow was asked about the best part of the trip to Spain, and he had a perfect answer as the leader of this team. “Just being around the guys all week, and I really think it was a huge bonding experience for us. To see the excitement of the city with us being here was a little surprising for me and in a pleasant surprise at that,” Burrow stated. Burrow on what was most meaningful this week: "Just being around the guys all week and I really think it was a huge bonding experience for us. To see the excitement of the city with us being here was a little surprising for me and in a pleasant surprise at that." — Paul Dehner Jr. (@pauldehnerjr) November 8, 2026 The excitement grew more and more throughout the week, and it was incredibly cool to see fans on the other side of the world excited to watch the Cincinnati Bengals play football. The NFL can’t help but tip their cap to the Bengals after the show Burrow, Chase, and Higgins put on display for the world to see. So, when can we expect to see the Bengals take another overseas trip? The NFL is looking to potentially have a regular-season game played in Tokyo for the first time . That’s something Burrow would love to be a part of. Joe Burrow says — down the road — says he to play a small part in the NFL’s goal of an international franchise. Says he would “love” to be on the field for the league’s first game in Tokyo. pic.twitter.com/brNlajPF02 — Charlie Clifford (@char_cliff) November 8, 2026 The Bengals will now fly home to Cincinnati and prepare for the biggest game of the season vs. the Steelers.
