title: The loss to the Chiefs shows the Jets are falling apart
summary: Over the last several weeks, we have seen the classic unraveling of a Jets season. The faces change, but the results always seem to stay the same. Entering Week 7, the Jets faced a two game homestand against beatable opponents. Victories against both the Dolphins and the Raiders would get the team to .500 through […]
full_text: Nov 8, 2026; Kansas City, Missouri, USA; Kansas City Chiefs running back Emmett Johnson (10) scores a touchdown during the fourth quarter against the New York Jets at Arrowhead Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Denny Medley-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Over the last several weeks, we have seen the classic unraveling of a Jets season. The faces change, but the results always seem to stay the same. Entering Week 7, the Jets faced a two game homestand against beatable opponents. Victories against both the Dolphins and the Raiders would get the team to .500 through eight games and give this team real momentum heading into a tough stretch facing the Chiefs and Bills back-to-back. Of course, the Jets handed the previously winless Dolphins their first victory and then lost to the Raiders, dropping their record to 2-6. Not even at the halfway point, the season was over. It is normal for the competitive portion of the season to end early for Jets fans. It feels like an annual tradition in November to be discussing NFL Draft position above all else. The only thing the Jets still had going for them is it felt like the team was still united. Players were fighting for each other. Things changed in the Week 9 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs. The Jets looked like an imploding team. Fans could see it in obvious ways like Minkah Fitzpatrick making a couple of business decisions when he had opportunities to make plays. Armand Membou threw his helmet in frustration in an emotional outburst after allow a second half sack. Geno Smith was demonstrative in his frustration frequently as the game slipped away. These are symptoms of a season that is slipping away and a team that is in a spiral. Through each offseason NFL fans of all 32 teams convince themselves that their team has made all of the right moves, and their roster is improved. That’s part of being a fan. At this time of year, Jets fans frequently are forced to confront the reality that the team made bad moves in the previous offseason, and that has a lot to do with the team’s struggles. The Jets might not have gotten everything wrong in the 2026 offseason. David Bailey increasingly looks like a budding star. If the two pass catchers the Jets took in the first round of the NFL Draft after Bailey aren’t dominating, they at least look promising. Still, at this point I think the obvious is staring Jets fans in the face. This remains a bottom tier roster, and many of the offseason moves that provided hope in March were poor decisions in hindsight, particularly on the defensive side of the ball. And on offense, the internal improvements fans hoped for just haven’t been as big as fans wanted. Adonai Mitchell has grown into a starting receiver capable of throwing up a big game now and then, but he consistently leaves plays on the field and leaves fans wanting more. Armand Membou and Olu Fashanu remain competent starting tackles, but at this point they don’t look like the elite bookends fans dream of when their team makes back-to-back first round picks at the position. Of course, no discussion on a Jets loss would be complete without discussing Aaron Glenn, Frank Reich, and the Jets coaching staff. The typical criticism this crew gets on a weekly basis mostly applies so I’d like to turn my attention elsewhere. Despite getting blown out in the second half, a strong case can be made that the Jets played better than Kansas City in the first half. The Chiefs came out flat. They were making mistakes, and the Jets forced a couple of turnovers. Despite outgaining Kansas City, the Jets still trailed at halftime. Why was this? There are no simple answers, but one thing stuck out to me about the way the Jets coaching staff approached the game. They didn’t seem to be interested in making big plays and scoring touchdowns. It felt like their objective was ball control, playing keep away, even if it came at the expense of offensive efficiency. In theory, that sounds great. With the right mix of players, it could even work. But this undermanned Jets team was not going into Arrowhead Stadium and winning the game with field goals. The defense just isn’t good enough to hold Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs down, even if they were successful in keeping the ball from them for a quarter or two. This was a game the Jets needed to play from ahead. Put some pressure on the Chiefs. Maybe they don’t react to it well. Maybe David Bailey can fire upfield and make a big play that changes the game. It felt like the conservative offensive gameplan the Jets chose was implemented to reduce the odds of being blown out, not the maximize the odds of winning the game. The Jets aren’t going to beat a team like the Chiefs playing like that. Once this team went to the locker room behind despite arguably being the strong first half team, the game was probably over. And you somewhat counterintuitively actually maximize the odds of being blown out. Add all this to the typical sloppy Jets football with no communication on defense and untimely penalty after untimely penalty, and you have a recipe for a 23 point blowout loss. Unfortunately for the Jets, there is no end in sight. Next week this team has to figure out a way to deal with Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills. If you’ve got any confidence that game will go differently, I’d love to hear why.

full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JANUARY 04: Ty Johnson #26 of the Buffalo Bills runs the ball in the second quarter against Keidron Smith #46 of the New York Jets at Highmark Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. This week the Jets visited the Kansas City Chiefs. They kept it competitve for a half. In the first half the Jets outgained the Chiefs. They won the turnover battle. The embarrassing Jets loss left the Jets with a 2-7 record to start the season, in 3rd place in the AFC East. Unsurprisingly the oddsmakers think the Bills will easily handle the Jets. The current line has the Jets home underdogs by 8.5 points. The game has an over/under of 51.5 points. On the moneyline the Jets are +400 while the Bills are -520. Any given Sunday and all that jazz, but an upset here seems like a bridge too far for the Jets. title: Jets vs Chiefs: Jets fold in second half, Chiefs cruise to easy win
summary: In the New York Jets’ ninth game of the 2026 season, on a gorgeous, warm and sunny day in Kansas City, Missouri, the Jets lost to the Kansas City Chiefs, 35 – 12. The game opened with the Jets on offense. They put together a nice drive, mixing runs and short passes effectively. Breece Hall […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - NOVEMBER 8: Kenneth Walker III #9 of the Kansas City Chiefs celebrates after scoring a touchdown during the second quarter of the NFL football game against the New York Jets at Arrowhead Stadium on November 8, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images In the New York Jets’ ninth game of the 2026 season, on a gorgeous, warm and sunny day in Kansas City, Missouri, the Jets lost to the Kansas City Chiefs, 35 – 12. The game opened with the Jets on offense. They put together a nice drive, mixing runs and short passes effectively. Breece Hall and Braelon Allen combined to do much of the heavy lifting. The Jets got the ball down to the Chiefs five yard line before they were forced to settle for a chip shot field goal and an early 3 – 0 lead. The Jets defense then stepped up. They recovered a Justin Fields fumble on a quarterback sneak and the Jets quickly had the ball back in Chiefs territory. Unfortunately the Jets did not fully take advantage of the golden opportunity. They failed to get a first down and had to settle for another field goal. The Jets were up 6 – 0 late in the first quarter, but it felt like the points left on the field as they settled for field goals rather than touchdowns would come back to bite them later. The first quarter ended with the Chiefs knocking on the door, looking to go ahead with a first and goal at the Jets 7 yard line. On the first play of the second quarter Mahomes found Kenneth Walker for a touchdown and, despite all the good things that happened for the Jets early, the Chiefs had the lead at 7 – 6. The Jets fought back. They drove the ball near the Chiefs 20 yard before three consecutive plays went backwards. The Jets settled for a 49 yard field goal to regain the lead. Midway through the second quarter the Jets had scored on all three drives to this point, yet had only nine points and a two point lead to show for it. If they didn’t start converting scoring opportunities into touchdowns it was likely going to be another long day for the Jets. It didn’t take long for the Chiefs to take the lead back. Braelon Allen failed to protect the ball with two hands and fumbled. The Chiefs recovered deep in Jets territory. A couple of plays later Patrick Mahomes hit Kenneth Walker for his second touchdown of the game. The Chiefs had a 14 – 9 lead with a little more than five minutes left in the first half. The Jets answered with yet another scoring drive. Again they were forced to settle for a field goal. With a little more than two minutes left in the first half the Jets had scored on four of five drives yet still trailed, 14 – 12. A few plays later the Jets got a strip sack of Mahomes and recovered the ball deep in Chiefs territory. The Jets were unable to take advantage of the opportunity as their drive went nowhere and Jason Sanders missed a long field goal attempt. The Chiefs returned the favor as time ran out, missing a field goal to end the half. The Jets went into the locker room trailing the Chiefs 14 – 12. They had left a lot of points on the field. They had dominated time of possession, scored four times, outgained the Chiefs, out-sacked the Chiefs, led the turnover battle, and still trailed. It would be a surprise if that didn’t cost them the game in the end. The Jets opened the third quarter on defense. It did not go well. The kickoff went out of bounds, giving the Chiefs great field position at the 40 yard line. From there the Chiefs went on a drive ending in a short touchdown pass from Mahomes to Travis Kelce. The extra point gave the Chiefs a 21 – 12 lead. The Jets offense responded with a three and out. Midway through the third quarter the Jets were in serious trouble. Towards the end of the third quarter the Chiefs put together a drive ending in a Kenneth Walker touchdown run. Walker was single handedly dismantling the Jets. The extra point made the score 28 – 12 in favor of the Chiefs as the third quarter ended. The game was all but over. On the Jets’ next drive they moved the ball quickly downfield before Geno Smith was sacked on fourth down, ending the drive. The Jets trailed by 16 points with a little over 11 minutes left. Turn out the lights, the party was over. All those points left on the field in the first half had come back to bite the Jets in the second half. Late in the fourth quarter the Chiefs tacked on another touchdown. They had now outscored the Jets 21 – 0 in the second half as they cruised to an easy victory. Final score: Chiefs 35, Jets 12. The loss brought the Jets’ record to 2-7. A 16th straight season without the playoffs is all but certain. Another November and December talking about next year and the draft looms. What fun awaits as the holiday season approaches! The Jets limp home to take on the first place Buffalo Bills next week. That should be a blast.

title: Where will this Eagles season rank among the all-time worst?
summary: There was a time when virtually every Eagles season was like this. Prior to 1988, the autumn was generally a depressing time in Philadelphia. There were very few seasons to celebrate. But since Buddy Ryan broke through with the first of his three straight playoff appearances in ‘88, the Eagles have been one of the […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 08: Joe Milton #14 of the Philadelphia Eagles scores a two-point conversion during the first quarter against the New York Giants at Lincoln Financial Field on November 08, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images There was a time when virtually every Eagles season was like this. Prior to 1988, the autumn was generally a depressing time in Philadelphia. There were very few seasons to celebrate. But since Buddy Ryan broke through with the first of his three straight playoff appearances in ‘88, the Eagles have been one of the marquee teams in the NFL. Their .575 winning percentage over the last 39 seasons is 5th-best , with only the Chiefs (.578), Patriots (.596), Packers (.602) and Steelers (.611) better. Seasons like what we’re experiencing now have been few and far between over that stretch. After another brutal offensive showing with their fourth quarterback in a 19-11 loss to the Giants at Lincoln Financial Field on Sunday, Nick Sirianni’s Birds have lost seven in a row and dropped to 2-7 on the season. This would be just the 10th losing season in the last 39 for the Eagles. They are in last place in a laughingly bad NFC East, having lost to each of their three divisional opponents in three consecutive weeks by a combined score of 84-42. And while it’s highly unlikely the team will lose their final eight games and finish 2-15 this year, it’s difficult right now to envision how they’re ever going to win again. When all is said and done, will this be the worst Eagles team of the last 40 years? There are four other squads they’ll have to contend with for that dubious honor. Let’s take a look at how this year’s Eagles, through nine games, compare with the very worst of the last four decades. View Link There are a few key terms that are helpful to know more about. Yards +/- quantifies the difference in yards gained and yards allowed and where that team ranks in the NFL. The higher the number, the worse the ranking. Strength of Schedule helps paint a picture of how difficult a schedule the Eagles had to deal with that year. Negative numbers mean an easier schedule. Margin of Victory is the average difference in score per game. SRS is a metric by Pro Football Reference called Simple Rating System that takes into account margin of victory and strength of schedule and provides a number relative to average (0.0), that can be considered a point spread. So, a -6.7 SRS means that team, on average, would have been a 6.7 point underdog. OSRS and DSRS measure offensive and defensive Simple Rating System. Based on the numbers, the 1998 season is quite clearly the worst team the franchise has fielded in the last 40 years, and it actually isn’t all that close. Ray Rhodes’ final campaign was an utter disaster. Their -183 point differential and -11.4 point margin of victory drove their -12.8 SRS that was far and away the lowest of any of the five teams we’re discussing. As painful as the 2026 offense has been to watch, Rhodes’ ‘98 team averaged 10.1 points per game against one of the easiest schedules in the NFL that season. Koy Detmer, Bobby Hoying and Rodney Peete “led” an offense that scored 20+ points just ONCE , in a Week 4 24-21 loss to the Chiefs. They didn’t score more than 17 points in any of their final 12 games, and they were shut out three times that season. Somehow Duce Staley ran for 1,065 yards, and Jeff Graham was their top receiver in yards (600). They threw 7 touchdowns as a team and tossed 18 INTs. Defensively, they had nine interceptions as a defense, with Brian Dawkins, Troy Vincent and Mike Zordich with two each. Hugh Douglas piled up 12.5 sacks, and the legendary Al Wallace was 2nd, with 6. It was a tough watch. Incredibly, the team made a highlights video for this unit, entitled “A New Beginning.” You’ll notice most titles of highlight videos of terrible teams that resulted in the firing of a head coach have similar themes. “A New Beginning.” “A New Era Begins.” “Into The Great Wide Open.” “Free Fallin’.” Sorry, those last two were just Tom Petty songs. And they got 23 whole minutes out of it, although much of the play was in slow motion, which helped take up some time. The 2012 season was just slightly worse from an SRS perspective (-8.9) compared to this year’s team (-8.8). Their -10.3 point margin of victory was 2nd-worst, with an offense that was slightly more functional than this year’s group, but a worse defense. This was Andy Reid’s final season and, coming off an 8-8 record the year before, got off to a 3-1 start thanks to several last-second victories. The team then completely fell apart, losing 10 of their last 11 in what was clearly the end of an era. Mike Vick, who led the team on a miraculous run in 2010, couldn’t duplicate that feat and made just 10 starts for the 2012 Birds. Nick Foles, the back-up, made the other six. Outside of the QB, however, there were building blocks on that offense, including LeSean McCoy, DeSean Jackson, Jeremy Maclin, Jason Avant and Brent Celek. The defense started the season with Juan Castillo, the team’s long-time offensive coordinator, leading the defense for a second season, but he was replaced by Todd Bowles midway through the year. The defense gave up 30+ points in 7 of their last 10 games, and at least 25 in 27 or more in 9 of their last 10. This was one of the few cases where the defense was the weaker link. The team’s season highlight video was titled “A Season of Change.” That’s putting a positive spin on things. With half a season in the books, the 2026 Eagles’ SRS would put them 3rd on this list of awful teams, but nipping at the ‘12 Eagles’ heels. Just below them is the pandemic Birds of 2020. The entire country was desperate for live sports during the height of COVID, but fans in Philadelphia quickly reconsidered that desire watching this team play. But with fake, cardboard cutout fans in the stands “watching,” the Eagles in Doug Pederson’s final season in Philadelphia played like fake, cardboard cutouts themselves. At least the players didn’t have to deal with fans booing inside the stadium. And for 2020 , the team didn’t even bother with a full highlights package. Instead, they put together a compilation of the best plays only from their victories. Pretty smart, if you ask me. The Eagles were three seasons removed from their first Super Bowl title but even fresher off a wild card loss to the Seahawks at home in which Carson Wentz, playing in his first playoff game, was concussed in the first half. He never recovered from his litany of injuries and led an absolutely dreadful offensive effort in which he threw an NFL-leading 15 interceptions with a QB rating of 72.8. He was also sacked a league-high 50 times, with rookie Jalen Hurts eventually taking over for the final four games of the season. Those Eagles had a point differential of -84. By comparison, this year’s Birds have a point differential of -73. So this year’s team is on pace to blow past that number. That team averaged 20.9 points per game, this year’s Eagles are averaging 16.4. And at least that squad had an interesting young quarterback to get excited about. Last, the 1999 Eagles . This season launched the Andy Reid era, one of the most successful and exciting runs in franchise history. But it was a slow build under then-QB Doug Pederson, who tried to guide a brand new offensive system while rookie first round pick Donovan McNabb got his feet wet. Once McNabb got comfortable, the team played pretty well over the final three weeks, and it was clear this was an improving roster with competent coaching. And yet, the ‘99 Eagles finished 30th in the NFL in terms of yardage differential. This year’s Eagles are 31st, 2nd-worst in the league. But I’d say, right now, the ‘26 Eagles are worse than Reid’s first year in Philadelphia. Honorable mention must be given to the 1994 Eagles, who started 7-2 in Rich Kotite’s final year with the team, only to…

title: Joe Milton doesn’t expect many Eagles players will leave town during the bye week
summary: The Eagles lost to the Giants on Sunday, but it was quarterback Joe Milton’s first NFL start, and he talked about the experience and his performance in his post-game press conference. The QB was asked is he would be staying in Philly during his extended break, and he noted he might go home for like […]
full_text: Photo by Todd Olszewski/Getty Images | Getty Images The Eagles lost to the Giants on Sunday, but it was quarterback Joe Milton’s first NFL start, and he talked about the experience and his performance in his post-game press conference. The QB was asked is he would be staying in Philly during his extended break, and he noted he might go home for like two days, but he plans to be working during the bye week — and he expects his teammates to do the same. “Probably like two days, but if that, I just want to be better. We want to be better as a team, and I don’t think too [many] people going home, too many people going home. Sorry. I think everybody should be here and will be here, just trying to get better and closer.” Here’s what else Milton had to say: On his performance “For my first game here, I feel like I did all right. There are a lot of things that I can clean up as far as protection, just helping those guys out with protection. That’s something that we’re going to get better [at] this week coming up for sure.” Milton also agreed that they need to do a better job setting protections as a whole, and collectively need to make sure they are on the same page with their communication. Despite only being with the team for three weeks, the quarterback says that work starts with him. “It all depends [on] how the protection is taught. I feel like I was taught great here for the three weeks I’ve been here, so therefore I’ve just got to fix that right there, and that’s all on me for sure.” The QB also wouldn’t put any blame on the challenges of learning new terminology. He also talked about learning more every day and enjoying the process one step at a time. Milton was asked about what there was to learn from the last play, and while he hadn’t seen the film, he had some ideas. “I haven’t seen it. But playing out that play, I’d probably just stay behind the line of scrimmage and just let them chase me because I know I’m going to be able to get the ball down the field. But just putting the team in a better situation and understanding that situation and shoot, I don’t know if I’d be able to sleep tonight for that situation, so I’d probably practice it in my living room.” On carrying the ball if needed “If it’s there, I’m trying to get it. If not, I’m trying to throw the ball. Whatever the team needs at that moment, that’s what I’m trying to do. We’ve just got to clean up a lot of stuff tonight and just move on, keep going. With my three weeks being here, it’s been amazing seeing these guys never give up. Seeing them tonight, they still had excitement on their faces, and I knew it wasn’t over. It’s great to see.” On the Giants second-half adjustments “Man, the Giants played great today. They had a great defensive cause and great players over there. What they did today was just pressure and play over top. Shout-out to them for stopping us and making plays.” On the Eagles skill players Milton talked about how he felt a closer bond with the whole offense after being with them in the huddle and hearing his teammates cheer him on. “My first time playing with those guys in a real game and that type of setting at a home game. It’s not as loud for us, but at the same time, you’ve got the Giants fans out there chirping and whatever. Those guys were great in the huddle. Makai [Lemon] and Dallas [Goedert] were also great in the huddle, but everybody overall was great in the huddle and just the push and the want to that we wanted in the huddle. It was great.” He also showed his support for Makai Lemon, who had a rough drop on Sunday, and expressed confidence in the rookie moving forward. “You’re going to have drops, you’re going to have missed throws, you’re going to fumble, you’re going to do whatever. But at the end of the day, it’s what you’re going to do the next time it shows up. When your opportunity is called, when your name is called, just show up and show out. I trust in Makai that he’ll make that catch next time for sure.” On his first NFL start “I felt blessed, more blessed. That’s about it. I felt more blessed than anything. I was able to see my family in the stands, so it was great, but it was also just great to be out there with the guys that I’ve been here training with for the past three weeks and learning and just that communication and connection that the team has and just being a part of it. I love it. It’s great. I wouldn’t ask for no better situation than this.”
author: Alexis Chassen

title: NFL Mock Draft 2027: Eagles land Jeremiah Smith
summary: The Eagles’ playoffs odds are bordering on an impossibility at this point. Barring some epic collapses from Philly’s NFC East rivals (possible) combined with the greatest turnaround you’ve ever seen from the Eagles offense (absolute fantasy), Howie Roseman should be looking ahead to the offseason. As it currently stands, the Eagles hold the fifth overall […]
full_text: LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 31: Jeremiah Smith #4 of the Ohio State Buckeyes looks on against the USC Trojans at Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum on October 31, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Eagles’ playoffs odds are bordering on an impossibility at this point. Barring some epic collapses from Philly’s NFC East rivals (possible) combined with the greatest turnaround you’ve ever seen from the Eagles offense (absolute fantasy), Howie Roseman should be looking ahead to the offseason. As it currently stands, the Eagles hold the fifth overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft. I would be shocked if they pick any later than that at this point and their chances of getting a better pick feel pretty high right now. Here is a midseason simulation of the first three rounds using Pro Football Focus’ Mock Simulator. While a ton will change between now and late April, this is a good way for us to familiarize ourselves with some prospects to get excited about. Pick 1.05: Jeremiah Smith, Wide Receiver, Ohio State The biggest question going into the Eagles offseason is what happens with the quarterback position. Can Jalen Hurts play football again? Does he want to play football again? Does he want to play football for the Eagles? If the answer to all of these questions is (miraculously) yes, then the Eagles should double down on supplying Hurts with as many weapons as possible. Jeremiah Smith is the best wide receiver prospect since Julio Jones and AJ Green came out of college in 2011. There are no holes in his game and he would immediately be one of the best receivers in the NFL as a rookie. Now imagine him as WR1 with DeVonta Smith on the other side and Makai Lemon in the slot. That is a great way to get Hurts (or any other quarterback) cooking. Pick 2.36: Greg Johnson, IOL, Minnesota The turnover at offensive line this season has been a mess. Injury luck combined with youth at key positions has led to the offensive line being a real problem. Greg Johnson has been a stellar player for the Golden Gophers over the last few years. He has great size and strength, with the ability to thrive at guard or center. He’d be an immediate upgrade for Philly on the inside at all three positions he’d be able to play. Pick 3.97: Boubacar Traore, Edge Defender, Notre Dame One of the many frustrations this season has been the Eagles lack of edge pressure. While Nolan Smith is having a solid year, the rest of the Eagles edge guys have been really mediocre, at best. Boubacar Traore is a bit of a pass rush specialist, at 6’5” and 250 pounds. He has great length and burst. Coming off a dominant game against Miami, Traore is getting some real NFL hype now. Maybe he goes a lot higher than this, but right now this would be a steal for the talented pass rusher.
author: Benjamin Natan

title: Eagles-Giants snap counts
summary: The official snap counts from the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 9 loss to the New York Giants are in. Let’s take a look and run through some analysis. OFFENSE DEFENSE SPECIAL TEAMS DID NOT PLAY ACTIVE: Tanner McKee, Cole Payton, Jake Majors INACTIVE: DeVonta Smith, Jihaad Campbell, Dontayvion Wicks, Jonathan Jones, Michael Carter II, Lane Johnson, […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 08: Jameis Winston #19 of the New York Giants is sacked by Nolan Smith #3 of the Philadelphia Eagles during the fourth quarter at Lincoln Financial Field on November 08, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images The official snap counts from the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 9 loss to the New York Giants are in. Let’s take a look and run through some analysis. OFFENSE Jordan Mailata is the only player who’s played 100% of the Eagles’ offensive snaps this season. He’s also played 11.16% of the Eagles’ special teams snaps. The Eagles’ starting offensive line configuration in each of their last four games has played 100% of the team’s snaps on offense. Darius Cooper and Makai Lemon continue to be the Eagles’ top two receivers with both DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks missing time. Saquon Barkley played his highest number of snaps in a game this season. It was his third-highest snap count percentage. Barkley’s 13 carries resulted in just 22 yards. Again, it’s admirable that he wants to play through injuries. But it doesn’t seem wise for the team to keep putting out there at far less than 100%. This should’ve been Hollywood Brown’s last game as an Eagle. Trade him for literally anything you can get in return. Elijah Mitchell had some of the lowest of football IQ plays you’ll ever see on Sunday. He was wide open just short of the marker and he failed to get a first down. Then he stayed in bounds instead of getting to the sideline late in the game with the Eagles having zero timeouts. Mitchell is out of practice squad elevations. There’s no need to keep him on the PS anymore and he clearly doesn’t deserve a spot on the roster. Time to move on. Facing 2nd-and-7 at the plus 47-yard line while trailing by eight points in the fourth quarter, the Eagles decided it was a good time to get Elijah Moore a designed touch on a screen play. It resulted in a three-yard loss. Why was that the time to get him involved? And in that capacity? Nonsensical. Moore is now down to four receptions for 17 yards this season. For the second week in a row, Johnny Mundt played his lowest snap count percentage of the season. Seems like the Eagles are phasing him out, as they should. Less Mundt and Grant Calcaterra, more Eli Stowers. Fred Johnson saw some playing time as a sixth offensive lineman. The Eagles scored their sole touchdown on one of these plays. Willie Lampkin saw some playing time as a fullback. DEFENSE Riq Woolen missed three snaps after getting banged up in the first half. Jeremiah Trotter Jr. led the Eagles in tackles once again with 11 total. Nolan Smith is quietly having a nice season in a lost year for the team; he has five sacks in eight games played. Marcus Epps was back as the Eagles’ safety next to Andrew Mukuba in nickel packages, replacing Kenny Moore II in that role. Jordan Davis logged two TFLs against the Giants, giving him two on the season. Not great that it took until Week 9 for him to show up in that category. Jonathan Greenard might be getting healthier? He logged his highest snap count percentage of the season on Sunday. He logged one sack, one TFL, and tied with Zack Baun for a team-high two quarterback hits. Pro Football Focus charted Greenard with a team-high five pressures. Baun suffered a back injury in the third quarter and did not return. Despite this, he led the Eagles with a team-high seven stops (tackles constituted as a failure for the offense). He came to play against the Giants. Jalyx Hunt continues to be on a pitch count as he plays through injuries. Smael Mondon filled for an injured Baun. Kenny Moore II saw a decreased role. With Jonathan Jones out, Kelee Ringo was the top backup corner and briefly saw snaps when Woolen missed time. SPECIAL TEAMS Cole Wisniewski exclusively played on special teams after being temporarily elevated from the practice squad. Would be good to see the rookie worked into the defense at some point. Braden Mann had a wild day with an 86-yard punt and a -2 yard punt in the same game. Rocco Underwood recovered a muffed punt. Second week in a row where A.J. Epenesa was limited to special teams duty. Jaydon Blue handled kick return duty. The Eagles really don’t want to use him on offense. DID NOT PLAY ACTIVE: Tanner McKee, Cole Payton, Jake Majors INACTIVE: DeVonta Smith, Jihaad Campbell, Dontayvion Wicks, Jonathan Jones, Michael Carter II, Lane Johnson, Britain Covey McKee was reportedly the No. 2 QB behind Joe Milton despite the fact he was ruled questionable to play with a rib injury. Payton was active instead of being the emergency third quarterback because the Eagles filled up their inactive spots with injured players. At least some of the Eagles’ injured players could be back on the field after the team’s Week 10 bye. As a reminder, Johnson is set to remain on the Eagles’ roster until June 2027 , even though he retired.
author: Brandon Lee Gowton

title: Eagles News: People in the NFL wondering about Jalen Carter’s availability
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! I don’t think the Eagles will move Jalen Carter prior to Tuesday’s NFL trade deadline. But it is interesting to see NFL insiders continuing to talk about the team’s interest in retaining Moro Ojomo. Maybe that’s just an effort from the […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 1: Jalen Carter #98 of the Philadelphia Eagles smiles after a play during an NFL football game against the Washington Commanders at Northwest Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! I don’t think the Eagles will move Jalen Carter prior to Tuesday’s NFL trade deadline. But it is interesting to see NFL insiders continuing to talk about the team’s interest in retaining Moro Ojomo. Maybe that’s just an effort from the Eagles to make it seem like they’re not going to trade Ojomo unless the price is really good. But maybe it’s genuine sentiment. We’ll see. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Week 9 NFL Takeaways: Why the Packers Are Looking Like Super Bowl Contenders – SI The Eagles’ reluctance to deal Moro Ojomo, and buzz that they want to eventually sign him long term, has people in the league wondering if they’d eventually trade Jalen Carter. At this point, it’s just speculation. But there’s good logic there, too (they’re already paying two guys, Carter and Jordan Davis, at Ojomo’s position). It was interesting, too, that Nick Sirianni didn’t shoot down the possibility out of hand that he’d make staff changes after Sunday’s loss. 10 Eagles things I think I think after the loss to the Giants – BGN 1) Someone on this coaching staff needs to be let go during the bye week. The Eagles have to make a significant move on this coaching staff, particularly on the offensive side of the ball. What this offense is doing in the second half of games is unacceptable. The Eagles had 99 total yards in the second half, scoring just three points. They had zero total yards in the third quarter, running 9 plays and going 3-and-out on all three possessions in the period. Philadelphia is the only team averaging under 2.0 points and 50 yards in the third quarter this season. Doesn’t matter who the quarterback is. The system remains the same, inefficient and ineffective. The offensive line allowed seven sacks, and had Joe Milton under duress throughout the day. They continue to have miscommunication up front, missing assignments and gaps in run blocking and allowing too many free rushers in pass protection. Roob’s Observations as Eagles crumble in ugly second half against Giants – NBCSP I don’t even know what to say anymore about the Eagles’ offensive line. They knew the Giants were going to blitz constantly and the Giants did and the Eagles just weren’t prepared for it. They couldn’t handle it. Everybody knows the Giants blitz more than anybody in the league other than the Vikings and still they weren’t ready for it. Seven sacks? They weren’t all on blitzes, but the Giants’ defensive line – which had just nine sacks all year coming into this game – nearly matched that in one game. This o-line can’t block anybody. It’s just embarrassing. The Eagles have now allowed 12 sacks in their last two games, the most ever in a two-game span under Nick Sirianni and second most in the last 25 years. They’ve allowed 30 sacks in nine games, which is insane. And they can’t run the ball, either. I don’t know if there are any answers. There’s nobody to bench, no young guy who needs to play and Jeff Stoutland isn’t walking through that door. This may be the worst offensive line in the NFL and I don’t know if there’s any way for it to get better. Handing out 10 awards from the Eagles-Giants game – PhillyVoice 2) The ‘Same Old, Same Old’ Award: The Eagles’ offense. The Eagles had just 220 yards of total offense. 13 first downs. A paltry 3.3 yards per play. And they were on the field nine and a half fewer minutes than the Giants. The offense has been awful all season, the coaching staff has no answers, etc. I feel like I can prewrite this award every week and just fill in the numbers. 7 and Counting – Iggles Blitz But we need to see some of the sloppiness go away. Teams that play dumb and make this many mistakes are not well coached. Sirianni needs to find some answers if he wants to be back in 2027. That doesn’t mean a bunch of wins. He needs the team to play with better situational awareness and show that they understand the little things. That would show that he knows how to solve problems and has the right messaging to get things fixed. If Sirianni can’t get the 2026 Eagles to play smarter, do you want him coaching the 2027 Eagles? The bye week is here. Identify problems. Find solutions. Get this team to play better. Or else. NFL Week 9: Big takeaways, questions and fantasy spin from Sunday’s games – ESPN What to make of the QB performance: Joe Milton got the start despite being with the team for only three weeks. Predictably, the operation was rough around the edges. Milton was able to push the ball downfield at times, and his mobility helped extend some plays. But second-half struggles continued despite the change from Tanner McKee to Milton — as did the leaks along the offensive front. Offensive coordinators have been dismissed in recent years having overseen far better production. Perhaps the Eagles wonder how the offense will finish when DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks return and Saquon Barkley is healthier. But it’s hard to view the problems as entirely personnel-related. The Eagles seem flummoxed by opposing defenses and lack answers. Their efficiency numbers are so alarming that a change would be merited if Sirianni wanted a new play-caller. Kuper’s offensive lines are not only struggling in the unavoidable shadow of his predecessor Jeff Stoutland, they’re struggling as merely a functional NFL group. 2026 NFL season, Week 9: What We Learned from Sunday’s games – NFL.com Milton can’t jump-start Eagles’ offense. Philly’s offense remains a slog, even with the athletic Joe Milton III under center. The QB added a few good runs, leading the Eagles with 64 yards on nine rushes. Milton completed 18 of 32 passes for 169 yards while taking seven sacks. Milton owns a whip, but the issue is his accuracy. Too often, the young QB was off the mark, leading to stalled drives. Saquon Barkley generated just 22 yards on 13 carries (1.7 yards per carry) with a TD. That’s not enough to help a young QB in his first start. title: Eagles players met with Nick Sirianni in his office after losing to the Giants
summary: The Eagles dropped their seventh game in a row on Sunday, losing to the Giants in a game that capped off a losing NFC East trifecta for the Birds in as many weeks. Reporters had to wait quite a while to talk to head coach Nick Sirianni after the game. Sirianni didn’t start his post-game […]
full_text: Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Eagles dropped their seventh game in a row on Sunday, losing to the Giants in a game that capped off a losing NFC East trifecta for the Birds in as many weeks. Reporters had to wait quite a while to talk to head coach Nick Sirianni after the game. Sirianni didn’t start his post-game press conference until about 72 minutes after the final whistle of Sunday’s game. When he was asked about it – since it’s pretty unusual for him to take that long – he explained that he was talking to players. “Talking to some guys, talking to some players. Those guys — everyone puts everything they have into this, so I want to make sure I talk to every guy first of all after the game. Then a couple of the guys stopped in the office just to talk through it. That’s not unusual. I appreciate the connection that we have there.” Here’s what else the head coach had to say: On Joe Milton’s performance “I think just like everybody, [Joe Milton] had some really good plays and then he’s going to have plays that he’s going to want back, naturally. But I thought he did a lot of good things, a lot of solid things, made some plays with his feet, gave our guys a couple chances downfield. Thought he was good in the play action world. I thought he did some really nice things. Obviously, we have to play better complimentary football to be able to have the run game coincide with the play actions that we were running, but there were some good things that he had.” On the 4th-and-1 play call Sirianni said that they had some time to think about the fourth-and-one call, and they were debating between a couple different options. Ultimately, the head coach was good with the call and with what they ended up running. “Obviously, it didn’t work. So, we’ll go back to the drawing board in there on that play. But there was a lot of time to think about that call because again, we got on the ball, it went to a two-minute warning, had a lot of time there, and obviously it didn’t work. So, we’ll go back and see what we can do differently offensively.” On the QB protection When asked about the unblocked sack-fumble, Sirianni said he wasn’t going to get into who was at fault, but did acknowledge that anytime there’s a guy that’s free in that situation, they have to look at the coaching to see what went wrong. He noted that it becomes an execution issue after they sort out the coaching issue, so it’s on everyone to get it fixed. “Obviously in that case, we’ll make those corrections in person with everybody. Whether it’s on us as coaches or whether it’s an execution thing, it’s still on us as coaches. It starts with me and it’s always on me; every product that’s on that field is my responsibility. ‘Well, there was an execution error on this play or that play.’ Well, did I put him in every position I could possibly put him into to go out and execute that?” On potential coaching changes “We’ll talk. Obviously, right now my job is to be there for our guys and to go watch the tape and go look through everything.” Sirianni went on to say that he’ll always look at himself first and go from there, but his job is to coach the players and the coaches, and do anything he can to help this team win games. “Everything can always be on the table, but I don’t think you change just to change because that’s what your record says that — you’ve got to look at what’s really real and not react to anything else. Again, I just don’t believe you just change just to change. If you have a strong reason to do things in anything, not just change, but in anything and you’re convicted on it, that’s how we’ll go about our business.” The head coach was asked if OC Sean Mannion was doing a good enough job maximizing the talent they have on offense, and said that no one offensively has done a good enough job. He was clear that it wasn’t just Mannion, and that they all need to get better and figure it out on offense. “I mean, I think our defense is playing solid. I think they’re doing really good things and it’s hard to keep the game there. I think we’ve got some things that we’re doing on special teams that have been really good, and then we can be more consistent in that particular case, but we have to figure it out on offense. That’s coaches, that’s players, that’s everybody.” He later said that he doesn’t have a certain threshold for when it’s time to make a change among the coaching staff, but right now he is looking at everything and anything they can do to help this team move forward. Still, he refused to throw any one coach under the bus, and said it was an issue collectively they need to figure out.

title: Dallas Goedert, Riq Woolen address Eagles trade rumors
summary: The Eagles lost their seventh game in a row on Sunday against the Giants, and with just a couple days until the NFL trade deadline, speculation continues to grow about moves that Howie Roseman and Co. might make. Two names among some of the rumors, including tight end Dallas Goedert and cornerback Riq Woolen. Both […]
full_text: Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images | Getty Images The Eagles lost their seventh game in a row on Sunday against the Giants, and with just a couple days until the NFL trade deadline, speculation continues to grow about moves that Howie Roseman and Co. might make. Two names among some of the rumors, including tight end Dallas Goedert and cornerback Riq Woolen. Both players spoke to reporters on Sunday evening, and gave their insight into the matter and made it known where they want to be for the remainder of the season. Dallas Goedert The tight end said that he hasn’t really thought much about the chance that he’ll be traded ahead of the deadline, but acknowledged that there’s always a chance, and there’s a right price for anyone. Goedert also revealed that Howie did have a brief conversation with him a few weeks ago about his future in Philly, and while he said it went well, he knows things like that change in this business. “I love this city. I always dreamt of retiring here, so we’ll see what happens. But, you know, anything’s [that’s] out of my control, I try not to worry about it.” Dallas Goedert on the trade deadline being in two days, a conversation he had with Howie and his preference on staying or being traded: pic.twitter.com/JxlJ0CfBCD — Eliot Shorr-Parks (@EliotShorrParks) November 8, 2026 Riq Woolen The CB said that it’s hard navigating the unknown as we approach the trade deadline, but he said he’s blessed to be on this team, with his teammates, and whatever lies ahead, will be. He did note that his heart is with the Eagles and with the teammates he’s grown so close to, and confirmed his preference would be to stay in Philly. “Most definitely. I mean, if you woke up every day with your friends, some of your close friends, and y’all worked hard as hell every day, and you just up and disappear when stuff got hard, or when you just up and disappear, then it would seem kind of weird —especially when it’s on you. If it’s up to Howie and the GM and my agent, I’ll leave it to them. But me and knowing me as a person, I’ve worked hard with these guys, and I love to be here and stay here with them.”

title: 10 Eagles things I think I think after the loss to the Giants
summary: That’s a wrap on the 2026 Philadelphia Eagles season. At least when it comes towards winning the NFC East and making a run at the playoffs. The Eagles won’t be making the postseason, not after a 19-11 loss to the New York Giants on Sunday. In this crucial three-game stretch against NFC East opponents, the […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - NOVEMBER 08: Philadelphia Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni reacts during the game between the Philadelphia Eagles and New York Giants on November 8th, 2026 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images That’s a wrap on the 2026 Philadelphia Eagles season. At least when it comes towards winning the NFC East and making a run at the playoffs. The Eagles won’t be making the postseason, not after a 19-11 loss to the New York Giants on Sunday. In this crucial three-game stretch against NFC East opponents, the Eagles went 0-3 and lost by a combined score of 84-32 against the Dallas Cowboys, Washington Commanders, and New York Giants. For those counting, that’s a -52 scoring differential against three teams with a combined record of 11-12-2 this season. Three of those wins have come against the Eagles. The Eagles are 2-7 for the first time since 1999 and lost seven straight games for the first time since 2012. This season is over. There still are eight more games to play, but this season isn’t getting turned around. Here are some thoughts following the latest loss. 1. Someone on this coaching staff needs to be let go during the bye week The Eagles have to make a significant move on this coaching staff, particularly on the offensive side of the ball. What this offense is doing in the second half of games is unacceptable. The Eagles had 99 total yards in the second half, scoring just three points. They had zero total yards in the third quarter, running 9 plays and going 3-and-out on all three possessions in the period. Philadelphia is the only team averaging under 2.0 points and 50 yards in the third quarter this season. Doesn’t matter who the quarterback is. The system remains the same, inefficient and ineffective. The offensive line allowed seven sacks, and had Joe Milton under duress throughout the day. They continue to have miscommunication up front, missing assignments and gaps in run blocking and allowing too many free rushers in pass protection. This falls on Sean Mannion or Chris Kuper if Nick Sirianni isn’t let go. One of these three coaches can not be back when they take the field again in two weeks. 2. The third quarter woes continue. The Eagles have the worst third quarter offense in the NFL, but somehow reached a new low against the Giants. Their third quarter possessions went like this: 3 plays, -2 yards — Punt 3 plays, 0 yards — Punt 3 plays, 2 yards — Punt Drew Kendall had a holding penalty, Joe Milton was sacked for a 10-yard loss, and Landon Dickerson had a holding penalty that was declined. The Eagles running backs had -3 rushing yards in the quarter while Milton averaged 2.2 yards per attempt. The Eagles dropped their scoring average in the third quarter to 1.4 points and their average yards to 39.2. the yards per play also dropped to 3.0. Somehow, they came out worse after halftime. Nick Sirianni claims adjustments are being made. They’re not working. 3. Joe Milton didn’t provide a spark This isn’t Joe Milton’s fault, but it was foolish to this this offense was going to be better due to a quarterback change. Milton finished 18-of-34 for 169 yards with 0 TD and 0 INT and a fumble lost. He was sacked seven times thanks to the offensive line and their communication issues and no run game to help him settle in. The run game was Milton, who had nine carries for 64 yards — 69.6% of the Eagles’ rushing yards. The Eagles offense might have been worse if Tanner McKee was back there with the Giants pass rush having a significant amount of wins up front. McKee might have been sacked 10+ times in this one. Milton couldn’t show off his deep ball because he didn’t have time to throw it. He was just 6-of-13 on throws traveling 10+ air yards, and the accuracy issues were on display throughout the game. Milton deserves another start, but does it really matter behind this offensive line? The Eagles also have an extremely limited Saquon Barkley and were without DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks again. Hard for Milton to have a fighting chance with the personnel he had to work with. 4. The run game is abysmal The Eagles don’t have much to work with at running back with Saquon Barkley on a pitch count and Elijah Mitchell being elevated from the practice squad to be his backup. The duo combined for 16 carries for 28 yards, 1.8 yards per carry. Barkley was so limited he had just three carries in the second half — for 0 yards. Nether Barkley nor Mitchell had a rushing yard in the second half. Mitchell’s impact — or lack thereof — in the second half is coming next. Neither Barkley nor Mitchell are getting much to work with up front, as the communication issues on the Eagles offensive line also carry over to the run game. Look at the 4th-and-1 play in the second quarter where Barkley loses a yard, due to the missed assignments in multiple gaps. The offensive line isn’t helping the run game either. Notice a pattern. 5. What was Elijah Mitchell doing? That final desperation drive by the Eagles were not Mitchell’s finest moments. Mitchell didn’t get the first down on the 3rd-and-8 possession right before the two minute warning, just falling down a yard short and not rolling over for the first down showed a lack of situational awareness. Mitchell somehow toped that moment by not getting out of bounds on a reception with under 20 seconds left, forcing the Eagles to chew even more clock in a 19-11 game. While the Eagles offense was abysmal all afternoon, they still had somewhat of a chance to score a touchdown in the final minute. Mitchell wouldn’t be on this team is Tank Bigsby or Will Shipley were healthy. Dameon Pierce was waived with an injury settlement and Carson Steele is out, so the Eagles really had to dig just to find a running back who knew the offense (which was Mitchell from his stint in the summer). Hard to see Mitchell taking any more snaps for the Eagles after that final possession, but that lack of situational awareness exists across the board. This is above Mitchell. 6. The defense allows points in the 4th quarter because of the offense There’s a lot to be said on how the Eagles defense falls apart in the second half, but look how long they were on the field in the third quarter on Sunday. The Eagles offense had the ball for just 4:55 in the third quarter, meaning the defense was on the field the other 10:05. Going 3-and-out on all three possessions took its toll on the defense, who did give up the go-ahead touchdown on the Giants’ second offensive possession in the quarter — which took up 7:56 of game time. Philadelphia didn’t have a single drive over 3:00 of game time in the second half, having a time of possession of 10:58. The defense is on the field for an average of 16:44 in the second half, which is third worst in the NFL. This isn’t absolving the defense, who have allowed 193.3 yards (31st in NFL) and 5.7 yards per play (24th) in the second half. There’s just a method toward their struggles, and that’s being on the field too much. They still allowed 13 points, but were on the field for nearly 20 minutes. This offense just can’t sustain drives. 7. Makai Lemon is still learning on the fly There was a lot to like about Lemon’s performance, as he finished with six catches for 61 yards (on nine targets). Lemon was the only reliable wideout on the Eagles Sunday, as his route running and separation was better than at any point this season. Joe Milton had an 85.9 passer rating when targeting Lemon, higher than any wideout with multiple targets on Sunday. While Lemon is showing progress over the last month, he still had two bad drops that he mentioned and took accountability for after the game. That’s four drops over the last three games, which Lemon has to improve if he’s going to become a reliable pass catcher in the league. Lemon can be a good WR3 this year, and eventually become a reliable WR2 over the next few years as a complimentary…

title: Steelers 2026 mid-season awards: Who is Pittsburgh’s MVP?
summary: We have reached the mid-season point of the 2026 NFL regular season (it always goes by too fast). The Pittsburgh Steelers have been one of the top teams in the league through nine weeks, sitting at the top of the AFC North with a 6-2 record while holding the No. 4 seed in the AFC […]
full_text: (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images We have reached the mid-season point of the 2026 NFL regular season (it always goes by too fast). The Pittsburgh Steelers have been one of the top teams in the league through nine weeks, sitting at the top of the AFC North with a 6-2 record while holding the No. 4 seed in the AFC playoff picture. Over the course of this week, our staff here at Behind the Steel Curtain will roll out our mid-season awards, which begins today with the Steelers’ 2026 mid-season MVP. Pittsburgh Steelers 2026 mid-season MVP Joey Bray – RB Jaylen Warren : This award simply cannot go to anyone else. Warren was third in the NFL in scrimmage yards through eight weeks of play, and remains in fifth after the bye week. Plus, he is doing so with incredible efficiency. On an offense that lacks weapons on the outside, Warren is the engine that has the Steelers’ offense on an upward trend heading into the second half of their season. Austin Bechtold – RB Jaylen Warren: Warren entered the bye week with more rushing yards than Derrick Henry and Jonathan Taylor. His 6.93 yards per touch this season is the highest in football and 1.31 yards higher than the next closest running back (Bijan Robinson). Warren is the best weapon in the Steelers arsenal and has been revolutionary for an offense that has been relatively stagnant for half a decade. I’d be happy with Warren receiving additional carries, as long as his body can hold up. Warren seems like the obvious answer, but I think T.J Watt and Jalen Ramsey also have case. Ryan Parish – C Zach Frazier: It was tempting to put Jaylen Warren here, but Frazier is so crucial to what Warren and the rest of the offense do, he has to get the nod. He’s also the Steeler with the best case at being the best at his position in the entire NFL. Ryland Bickley – C Zach Frazier: I’m torn between Frazier and Jaylen Warren here, but will go with the star center as he’s been arguably the best at his position in the entire league this year. And hey, when it’s a toss-up like this, why not give the offensive line some much-needed credit? Frazier has anchored the group that’s been the story of the team’s season thus far. Jason Aponte – RB Jaylen Warren: This offense has had moments when it needed an answer, and Warren has consistently been the answer. Pittsburgh is down a running back? No problem. Receivers go down with injury? No problem. Steelers fans aren’t surprised by Warren, but the NFL is quickly learning about this dynamic running back. What a season so far for Warren. Mike Nicastro – RB Jaylen Warren: This one could certainly be up for debate, but my vote goes to Jaylen Warren. Warren has been the igniter of Pittsburgh’s offense and arguably the biggest reason the Steelers are sitting at 6-2. Whether it’s creating explosive plays, keeping the offense ahead of the chains or providing a spark when the passing game struggles, Warren has consistently delivered. Through eight games, Warren has rushed for 704 yards on 119 carries, averaging an impressive 5.9 yards per attempt. He’s also added 294 receiving yards on 25 receptions, giving him 998 yards from scrimmage and three total touchdowns. Warren has become the engine of this offense. While there are other deserving candidates, it’s difficult to overlook the impact he’s had on a team that has won four consecutive games. Jarrett Bailey – RB Jaylen Warren: It looks like I’m the tie-breaker here, but I’m going with Warren. Even after the bye week, he’s fifth in the NFL in scrimmage yards and has emerged as one of the game’s three-five best running backs. Without his productivity, there is zero chance the Steelers are 6-2. full_text: We’ve reached NFL and therefore Seattle Seahawks trade deadline week, which often promises to have some interesting deals and rarely actually materializes. Minor or mid-level deals have happened more recently on deadline day itself, so it’s not like we live in a “nothing happens” world. There have admittedly been prominent in-season trades already this year, including the Quenton Nelson and Jeffery Simmons trades just a couple of weeks ago, as well as Joey Porter Jr going to the Dallas Cowboys, and Marvin Harrison Jr heading for the Houston Texans. For the second year in a row, the trade deadline is during Week 10. The Seattle Seahawks are usually active during the deadline, and this year they’ve pulled off one major trade. Will John Schneider cook up another midseason masterclass like he did for Leonard Williams, Quandre Diggs, Carlos Dunlap, and other names from previous deadline deals? Follow Field Gulls’ trade tracker coverage throughout Monday and Tuesday, and we’ll see what the Seahawks will do as they look to get back on track after a sputtering 5-4 start. Have the Seattle Seahawks made any trades during the regular season? Yes. They acquired longtime Indianapolis Colts guard Quenton Nelson for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder. Who could the Seahawks potentially put on the trade block? No one immediately springs to mind. The likes of Dante Fowler Jr have rarely played this year but likely wouldn’t fetch much on the trade market. Emanuel Wilson being an unofficial healthy scratch is worth monitoring, although similarly he’s not much of a valuable trade piece, and Seattle may not want to risk moving any capable RB given the injury concerns on the depth chart. Which positions would the Seahawks potentially be most interested in? Edge rusher and wide receiver might be two positions of need for Seattle. Rashid Shaheed’s injury and generally underwhelming receiving stats could impact what Seattle does at receiver. The edge rushing room is essentially three deep, and with only Derick Hall and Connor O’Toole under contract beyond 2027, there might be some forward thinking required. The New York Jets’ Will MCdonald IV has reportedly requested a trade and could be one to watch. When does the NFL trade deadline window close? At 4 pm ET/1 pm PT on Tuesday, Nov. 10. The New York Jets have dealt safety Andre Cisco to the Detroit Lions for a 2028 sixth-rounder. The New Orleans Saints have agreed to trade defensive tackle Davon Godchaux to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a 2028 sixth-rounder, which could become a 2027 sixth-rounder.

title: Sam Darnold ruled out, Seahawks expect Drew Lock to start vs. Raiders despite oblique injury
summary: The potential of Jalen Milroe making his first career start in Week 10 appears to have faded as quickly as it arose. On Seattle Sports 710’s Brock and Salk on Monday, Seattle Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald was asked about quarterback Drew Lock’s status, after he suffered an oblique injury in Sunday’s win over the […]
full_text: The potential of Jalen Milroe making his first career start in Week 10 appears to have faded as quickly as it arose. On Seattle Sports 710’s Brock and Salk on Monday, Seattle Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald was asked about quarterback Drew Lock’s status, after he suffered an oblique injury in Sunday’s win over the Arizona Cardinals. Macdonald provided an optimistic update, saying, “Good exam for Drew. He’s dealing with an oblique. And, I think it’s something we can manage in him playing the game,” while adding starter Sam Darnold would need another week in his return from his quad injury. Lock, who entered Week 9 with what was reported as severe tendinitis , was seen grabbing his right hip in the third quarter of Seattle’s win over the Cardinals. Though he went into the blue tent, he remained in the game and didn’t miss a snap. Macdonald told reporters post game that Lock’s status for Week 10 against the Las Vegas Raiders was up in the air , but after encouraging news on Monday, it appears the Seahawks’ backup will be good to start a third game in 2026. Across two starts and the bulk of Seattle’s Week 1 win over the New England Patriots, Lock has completed 71.1% of his passes, throwing for 597 yards and five touchdowns against zero interceptions.

title: Seahawks Droppings: Beset by injuries, Seattle grinds it out and holds serve vs. Cardinals
summary: Sometimes you need to take a step back to move forward. The Seattle Seahawks seem to have done that this week, relying on the run game and defense in a 17-3 victory over the Arizona Cardinals at Lumen Field. Now, all the injuries that Seattle was his with for this week might have had a […]
full_text: Sometimes you need to take a step back to move forward. The Seattle Seahawks seem to have done that this week, relying on the run game and defense in a 17-3 victory over the Arizona Cardinals at Lumen Field. Now, all the injuries that Seattle was his with for this week might have had a big hand in the simplification of the game. No Sam Darnold, Leo Williams, Quenton Nelson, Uchenna Nwosu, Charles Cross, or Rashid Shaheed? No problem. It certainly wasn’t the prettiest game offensively as Seattle finished with 295 yards. Drew Lock managed the offense well and didn’t put the ball in harm’s way much at all. Don’t take that to mean he was conservative, however. Lock slung a few in some very tight windows. Brian Fleury stuck with the run game, and it helped to shorten the game. Would Seattle have beaten a better squad today the way they played? No idea. They won today and that’s all that matters right now. Seahawks Droppings Drew Lock made it work, but was still clearly injured. I’m not sure he threw a tight spiral at all today which I’m hoping was just a side effect of his elbow injury. There were also a number of throws behind the receivers. Oh yeah, and Lock hurt his oblique during the game and may not be able to go next week. Will it be Jalen Milroe time in Las Vegas? Zach Charbonnet brings toughness to the offense. Look no further than the last drive of the game where Charbonnet broke multiple tackles to keep moving the chains and end the game. He’s not the fleetest of foot, but runs tough. Charbonnet is like a middle ground between Jadarian Price and Emanuel Wilson. Less explosive than Price, but more than Wilson with just as much toughness. The one-two punch of Charbonnet and Price could be pretty lethal. The offensive line played much better. No sacks given up today, and there weren’t many dropbacks I can remember where Lock was even under pressure. Maybe that’s an indictment on the Cardinals’ pass rushers or a testament to Fleury getting the ball out early. The only downside of this would be the fact that when Nelson comes back, Zabel will have to move over to RG again. Best case scenario would’ve been Zabel and Nelson getting reps against the Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders to be ready for the San Francisco 49ers after the bye week. That’s not a reality, sadly, so be ready for some rough weeks ahead. AJ Barner gets involved. I don’t know why they don’t use Barner more. The only thing he’s not great at is run after the catch since he always seems to get dropped within one or two yards of where he catches the ball. I’ll take that if it means more red zone TDs. Red zone issues improved. Both sides of the ball had better results in the red zone. The offense was 2-2 with Barner scoring both TDs. The defense held Arizona to 0-2 including that late-game fourth down stop from the two yard line. Short-handed defensive line stepped up. DeMarcus Lawrence looked like 2025 D-Law. He took accountability this week for some of the issues against the Chicago Bears. Whether or not it was really his fault, he took that personally this week and made his presence known with 1 sack, 2 TFL, and a forced fumble that was recovered by Arizona. Lawrence’s former Dallas Cowboy teammate, Dante Fowler Jr, also showed up for really the first time as a Seahawk with a sack and a forced fumble on Gardner Minshew to end the first half. With Big Cat and Nwosu out, Seattle needed others to step up and they did. The refs were pretty awful. It’s a good thing Seattle won this game or I would’ve been nearly apoplectic at the refs. Yes, the Seahawks had some very dumb self-inflicted penalties that they absolutely cannot afford to have playing against better competition. I’m looking at you, Jalen Sundell. And sure, the Cardinals made their own share of penalty mistakes to extend Seahawks drives. Yet, that defensive PI call on Josh Jobe was garbage. He barely touched Trey McBride and then turned to make the interception. Before the second Seahawks TD drive, the refs also called McBride’s forward progress stopped just prior to him fumbling which was recovered by the Seahawks. At least they didn’t overturn Barner’s TD which I was anticipating. Other pass catchers not named Jaxon Smith-Njigba made plays. I had to specify “pass catchers” instead of WRs because the leading receiver was actually RB Jadarian Price with 54 yards on 4 catches. I thought he couldn’t catch the football?? That over-the-shoulder catch early in the game was a thing of beauty! Cooper Kupp only had three catches for 32 yards, but I’m pretty sure all of those were for first downs. Tory Horton also had a key first down catch. The passing numbers overall won’t wow anyone with only 175 total yards receiving, but getting other players besides JSN involved is key. For the most part, this was Seahawks Football. If Mike Macdonald and crew can right the ship, it was a good step in the right direction. Theoretically, the running game should continue to gel and improve as Charbonnet and Price get more action. Play great defense, hold on to the ball, and make key passes when necessary to supplement…that’s how they will need to play. At least for one week, we can enjoy a victory with a whole host of backups no less.

title: Seahawks-Cardinals post-game analysis: Defense, offense both Locked in
summary: Looks like the rule against owning multiple NFL franchises doesn’t apply to Vinod Khosla. Not after the Seattle Seahawks re-demolished their rivals from the desert 17-3 in a game that could’ve been closer, I suppose, but also could’ve easily been a much wider blowout. Truthfully, only a couple main outcomes were on the table today […]
full_text: Looks like the rule against owning multiple NFL franchises doesn’t apply to Vinod Khosla. Not after the Seattle Seahawks re-demolished their rivals from the desert 17-3 in a game that could’ve been closer, I suppose, but also could’ve easily been a much wider blowout. Truthfully, only a couple main outcomes were on the table today in Seahawks-Cardinals II: Defensive Boogaloo: A) narrow Arizona victory aided by touchdown drives and various balderdash (including but not limited to officiating shenanigans), or B) return-to-form Seattle win reminiscent of Week 8 against the Chiefs and *waves at entire Mike Macdonald era*. We very nearly got A), but instead, it was indeed B), a Macdonald lab-grown triumph via timely contributions from your remaining defensive stars, excellent containment of explosives, and mistake-free offense. Watching the defense, was, as ever, a series of little climaxes leading to the sweet release of victory formation. The Seahawks had one favorable officiating decision (the Barner TD reception) outweighed by several unfavorable ones, and still prevailed by two touchdowns, undermanned, without Jaxon Smith-Njigba being the main reason, either. I’ll tell you: I came into Week 9 weirdly excited. We were going to see the Hawks win extremely shorthanded and confirm that they still have a role to play in the NFC, or they’d lose and spend at least one week at the bottom of the division, underwater at 4-5 and 1-2. They won’t be spending that week in the cellar and we won’t spend the week thinking about draft targets. In part because the red zone woes flipped; in part because Drew Lock was up to managing the game flawlessly; and as usual, in largest part because it’s so dang hard to score against them. You need a lot of things to go right in the proper sequence, and the Cardinals didn’t have the weapons beyond Trey McBride to pull off the upset. The visitors did receive more than their fair share of breaks, such as Reggie Virgil’s third-down bobble being ruled a catch on the opening possession or Josh Jobe’s interception being nullified because Trey McBride can’t run in a straight line without falling down: It feels fan-conceited to say, but the Seahawks defense is so complete (and so deep! Leonard Williams and Uchenna Nwosu didn’t even suit up!) that they could pitch a shutout every time they take the field. Remember the Super Bowl? Guessing it rings a bell. The Patriots got some garbage points in the fourth quarter and put up a big goose egg until then. There’s nobody this Seahawks defense can’t dominate. Give them another shot at the Bears in January, NFL scriptwriters, I dare you. Q1: Cardinals 3, Seahawks 0 Predator : Feels good to mention Nick Emmanwori again. Prey : Gardner Minshew, who peed his pants a little but the broadcast was too chicken to show it. How: One of the things that sets really good ball carriers apart is how quickly they get up to full speed. I really like what Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price bring to the table, especially as complements to one another, but Kenneth Walker was so good at accelerating straight from first gear to fifth. Emmanwori does that here and also finds time to maul Minshew with his whirling tentacles. Minshew was flagged for intentional grounding. When you don’t give a QB time to process, good things happen. Anytime the competition committee wants to change the grounding rule to reward the nearest defender with a sack, they should feel free, by the way. Recap : Opening the game with three JSN targets is a choice, and I don’t necessarily mind it, and it’s hard to argue it didn’t work, given the later success both Charbs and Price had on the ground. I like Brian Fleury dictating to his Arizona counterpart, or telling him, you think we’re gonna approach this game one ultra-conservative way? Think again. The plan didn’t result in points, Drew Lock was off target twice and the Seahawks went three-and out. There’s still something to be said for putting the fear of Jax into the opponent’s collective psyche right away. Pinned on the 1 by Michael Dickson’s sumptuous right foot, the Cardinals drove the length of the field, although as mentioned earlier, if the Virgil non-catch is called correctly, there are no points for them. What was most encouraging of all, was seeing the Seahawks defend the red zone blades of grass like the rest of the blades. They broke an unfortunate string of nine consecutive red zone touchdowns allowed. And the field goal Chad Ryland knocked through would be his — and his teammates’ — last of the day. Seattle’s next possession stalled at midfield when Mack Wilson was left unblocked on third down. But no matter, the E-Man would show up as advertised, Arizona punted right back. Price’s receiving chops are better than advertised. He’s shown willingness an aptitude in downfield routes. He’s explosive so just get him the ball wherever, you know? If you see a little C.J. Prosise in his game after this clip, well, who am I to stop you? Charbonnet and Price each moved the sticks afterward, the Cardinals ended the quarter with a brain fart, jumping offsides before the clock ran out, and as the quarter ended, the hosts were knock, knock, knockin’ on end zone’s door. Q2: Seahawks 7, Cardinals 6 Predator : Seahawks pass rushers, composite, as the half drew to a close. Prey : Not to pick on him again, but Minshew. Look, he plays the game voluntarily. How: On the Cardinals’ final five pass plays of the half, Minshew was sacked twice, pressured all five, and completed one pass for two yards, that McBride fumbled. Five different Seahawks got there: Byron Murphy II on third down midway through the quarter, then Lawrence, then Emmanwori, then Ernest Jones won a seven-man race, before Dante Fowler finally finished him off to send everyone to the locker room. Minshew had been 8/10 with 8.0 YPA until the full weight of the Seattle pass rush fell upon him. He was 13/20 with 3.4 after. Recap : Two yards from paydirt, the Seahawks stopped getting cute. A.J. Barner took the handoff both times and they helped him scoot his glute for loot. The second thrust was the charm, and Seattle had a lead it would never relinquish. All 58 yards on the touchdown drive were gained by running backs or rushing plays. The teams traded punts for the next four possessions, but Murphy’s sack was especially well-timed, as it blew the Cardinals out of field goal range. Seems like every week the Seahawks give up an inexplicable points-scoring drive, and with that out of the way, they set out to complete another side quest: scoring in 90 seconds or less. Under two minutes remained. Perfect timing. A couple completions and some tough Charbonnet running moved the chains. A 29-yard obvious DPI flag got the Seahawks close, and then Jax made his biggest contribution of the day: With only one timeout you needed an explosive to open up the playbook and go for six instead of three. With a crossing pattern you needed to break tackles. This is why you made the man the highest-paid WR in football. Barner doesn’t quite hold on to the ensuing touchdown pass — you can see the ball moves at he hits the ground and replay shows it slides along the turf next to his arm. It’s a lot of contact with the ground, and it wouldn’t have felt unfair to see it overturned. But here’s the thing about refereeing decisions: they tend to even out. Arizona scored three points on a catch that wasn’t and got to punt on an obvious fumble in their own territory. Let’s call it even? Q3: Seahawks 17, Cardinals 3 Predator : I just really appreciated the cool demeanor Drew Lock exuded as he calmly dropped this sidearm throw around a rushing Andrew Wingard. Prey : Fear and anxiety of getting your sh-t rocked. How : How indeed. This catch gave the Seahawks a new set of downs, which they invested in three points later to cap the day’s scoring. Arizona’s opening possession out of the break ran into the outstretched arm of Josh Jobe on another well-timed corner blitz (how…
