title: Washington’s loss to the Rams confirmed what we already knew
summary: If I told you the Washington Commanders lost a game in which they held the NFL’s No. 8-ranked third-down offense to a 21% conversion rate, limited the No. 6 red-zone offense to a 50% success rate, and forced two turnovers against the league’s No. 4 offense while surrendering just 20 points, would you believe me? […]
full_text: If I told you the Washington Commanders lost a game in which they held the NFL’s No. 8-ranked third-down offense to a 21% conversion rate, limited the No. 6 red-zone offense to a 50% success rate, and forced two turnovers against the league’s No. 4 offense while surrendering just 20 points, would you believe me? Yes? Well, I’d believe me, too. When the same mistakes and shortcomings keep plaguing a team week after week, you eventually have to accept that the team is exactly what it has shown you. For the Commanders, that reality has become increasingly difficult to ignore after their 20-13 loss to the Los Angeles Rams, dropping Washington to 2-5-1 . Dan Quinn at the podium: "We have not nailed our complimentary football, and I'll keep saying it until we do. " — Martenzie Johnson (@10zJohnson) November 8, 2026 Time is running out on Dan Quinn and the Commanders, and the urgency surrounding their season is growing with every passing week. Few expected Washington to knock off Los Angeles heading into Sunday’s matchup, but the Commanders had a legitimate opportunity to pull off the upset. More importantly, Quinn’s defense gave the offense every opportunity to make it happen. Instead, Washington wasted one of its better defensive performances of the season. After jumping out to a 10-3 lead, the Commanders’ offense completely unraveled. Over their next eight possessions, excluding the final drive, Washington averaged just 4.5 plays and 15 yards per possession while turning the ball over. An offense that had an opportunity to seize control of the game suddenly couldn’t sustain a drive long enough to give its defense a breather, much less put additional points on the board. Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford struggled with his accuracy throughout the afternoon, and multiple drops from his receivers only compounded those issues. Washington’s pass rush wasn’t particularly effective, either, ranking 27th in Week 9 pressure percentage, according to SumerSports . Yet despite its inability to consistently disrupt Stafford, the defense did enough to keep the Rams within striking distance. That’s what makes this loss particularly frustrating. The Commanders didn’t need an extraordinary offensive performance to win. They needed competence, consistency, and the ability to capitalize on the opportunities their defense created. They couldn’t deliver any of the three. The problems start with roster construction, and Sunday’s loss exposed just how significant those shortcomings have become. Nobody should reasonably expect an offensive line to completely neutralize elite defensive linemen like Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald for an entire game. Two future Hall-of-Fame players of that caliber will win their share of matchups. But, as Garrett piled up three sacks and forced a fumble, the talent disparity along the line of scrimmage became impossible to ignore. Washington simply doesn’t have the personnel to consistently compete against that level of defensive talent. And while the pressure itself was problematic, the larger issue was how Rams defensive coordinator Chris Shula manipulated matchups along the line of scrimmage to expose Washington’s weaknesses. The Commanders struggled to consistently identify, communicate and execute against the challenges Los Angeles presented. The situation only worsened when midseason center signing Lucas Patrick exited early and the entered concussion protocol. Washington turned to rookie Matt Gulbin rather than Nick Allegretti, whom general manager Adam Peters previously praised as an overlooked but capable option at center — who is now a guard again? pic.twitter.com/Dane2Y6klK — Josh Taylor (@JoshTaylorFB) November 9, 2026 That decision only confirmed what was obvious to me: Allegretti may have sustained some form of injury a few weeks ago, but he was certainly handed a “soft-benching” that paved the way for Gulbin to see the field at center. Quinn and Peters’ in-season decision-making only highlights the personnel evaluations and the disconnect between what Washington believed it had entering the season and what its coaching staff actually trusts on game day. These issues didn’t appear overnight. They are the consequences of decisions made throughout the offseason, and the Commanders are now paying for them when the margin for error is at its smallest. #Commanders GM Adam Peters says that the team is comfortable with Nick Allegretti & Matt Gulbin as “two good starting level centers” https://t.co/iUBQmzaYit — brandon (@JayDanielsMVP) September 4, 2026 Beyond the pass-protection issues, Washington’s inability to establish a competent rushing attack remains one of its most damaging offensive deficiencies. Another week passed without the Commanders consistently generating production on the ground, leaving Jayden Daniels to shoulder an increasingly unreasonable burden. When an offense cannot run the football, protect its quarterback or consistently stay ahead of the chains, everything becomes more difficult. Defenses can dictate matchups, pressure packages become more effective, and the quarterback is repeatedly forced into situations where he must manufacture something out of nothing. Daniels is talented enough to overcome some of those deficiencies. But expecting him to overcome all of them, week after week, is neither sustainable nor a legitimate offensive identity. At one point late in Sunday’s game, Rams receiver Puka Nacua had amassed 14 receptions, 150 receiving yards, and a touchdown , outproducing Washington’s entire passing attack by himself. That statistic alone illustrates just how ineffective the Commanders’ offense had become. And that’s where the accountability extends beyond the players. Quinn and his staff have had plenty of opportunities to identify what isn’t working and make the necessary adjustments. Offensive coordinator David Blough must find ways to manufacture production despite the personnel limitations, and while he is a rookie coordinator, the season is on the line as well as jobs. There’s only so much grace a coach in that position gets if the operation doesn’t look good. Still, most of the responsibility falls on Peters for assembling a roster with deficiencies that opponents keep exploiting. At some point, the conversation must shift from what Washington can become to what this team actually is. No magic adjustment, schematic wrinkle or personnel change will suddenly erase the Commanders’ problems. Their offensive struggles are too consistent, their weaknesses too apparent, and their margin for error too small to continue relying on the idea that everything will eventually click. Either Washington starts playing better, more disciplined football or its 2026 season could effectively end with a loss to the New York Giants this Thursday. If it hasn’t already. Listen to the latest Trap or Dive postgame recap , where we break down Washington’s loss to Los Angeles, the offensive issues that continue to hold this team back, and the uncomfortable reality facing the Commanders over their final nine games. title: Commanders report card: Team grades in NFL Week 9 loss vs. Rams
summary: The Commanders used to be so good in one-score games, constantly finding ways to win late. Unfortunately for Washington, the last time the team played that way was back in 2024.   In 2026, the Commanders are 1-3-1 in one-score games.   That’s the difference between Washington being competitive and their current abysmal record.   […]
full_text: The Commanders used to be so good in one-score games, constantly finding ways to win late. Unfortunately for Washington, the last time the team played that way was back in 2024. In 2026, the Commanders are 1-3-1 in one-score games. That’s the difference between Washington being competitive and their current abysmal record. They let a second-half lead (albeit a small one) slip away, and couldn’t complete a late comeback and ended up losing to the Rams 20-13 on Sunday at Northwest Stadium. Let’s dive a little deeper into this difficult loss in this Week 9 report card: Rushing offense The Commanders are normally super committed to running the football, even when the effort is relatively inefficient. That wasn’t the case on Sunday. The Commanders had 19 carries in 58 offensive plays. Not that we can fault Blough’s logic. Rushing lanes were hard to come by against the vaunted Rams defense, and Washington averaged just 3.2 yards per carry. Rachaad White averaged four yards per carry but only took seven handoffs; he also had a 15-yarder get called back. Jayden Daniels lost a fumble. The Commanders needed to control the game and the clock on the ground. They weren’t able to do that. Grade: D Passing offense Jayden Daniels started hot, with a 136.6 passer rating. It dropped a bit in the second half, but still held decent at 101.4. He completed 24-of-35 passes for 274 yards, a touchdown, and no interceptions. He still hasn’t thrown a pick all year. Daniels suffered four sacks, with three by Myles Garrett, including a critical third-down takedown in the fourth quarter that forced a Commanders punt. The pass protection also struggled against the Rams front, which was somewhat predictable against Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald. Recently signed from the practice squad Van Jefferson led the team with 58 yards and a touchdown on five catches. Stefon Diggs had three catches for 51 yards, plus a couple of drops. The screen game got an explosive and Daniels hit some shots down the field, but the passing game couldn’t develop the necessary rhythm to sustain drives and score points. Grade: C Rushing defense The Rams have relied heavily on the run game during their current three-game winning streak, including on Sunday against Washington. They ran 29 times and averaged 4.3 yards per carry. Blake Corum did most of the work, with 58 yards on 11 carries, though Washington’s defense was able to keep Kyren Williams in check. The defensive line held up relatively well (based upon watching it live) and Frankie Luvu was everywhere with 15 tackles, including two for loss. Sonny Styles was right there with him, tallying 13. It’s hard to fault the run D, or the defense in general, for Sunday’s result. There were two big runs and a touchdown allowed, but the Commanders did a relatively solid job in this phase. Grade: B Passing defense The Commanders generated a fumble and recovery following a short pass to Puka Nacua. Nick Cross also intercepted Matthew Stafford in the second half. Letting Nacua go off to the tune of 14 catches for 150 yards and two touchdowns? Not so good. Stafford got better as the game progressed, and the four-man pass rush was virtually non-existent. The coverage, however, was solid. Stafford averaged just 5.3 yards per attempt and had a 72.6 rating. Shoutouts should go to Cross, Trey Amos and Amik Robertson Grade: Coverage (B); Pass rush (D) Special teams I don’t know what Antonio Williams was thinking with a fair catch inside the 10 with less than a minute left. Return it or let it go. Not a great decision there. Tress Way punted three inside the 20-yard line – he nearly had one downed inside the 2 – and Drew Stevens was perfect when he had to be. Also, the Rams return game didn’t do much. Grade: B Coaching The Commanders are struggling with penalties. They’re struggling to perform under pressure. They’re struggling to play four quarters of football. And, try as he might, head coach Dan Quinn can’t seem to find solutions. New schemes under Blough and defensive coordinator Daronte Jones have experienced growing pains. This season is essentially done. I mean, the Commanders are 2-5-1 and can lose all hope with a loss to the Giants on Thursday. Being competitive doesn’t get you a gold star. Commanders fans should expect more from their team’s staff. Grade: F How would you grade the Commanders’ performance from Sunday’s game against the Rams? Let us know in the comments below:

title: Key takeaways from Washington Commanders loss to Rams in NFL Week 9
summary: The Commanders entered Week 9 officially in now-or-never mode. Washington had but two wins entering Sunday’s game against the Los Angeles Rams.   They were still in the mix despite an unreal rash of injuries to star players, due to poor play in the NFC East.   They needed to start stacking wins, especially with […]
full_text: The Commanders entered Week 9 officially in now-or-never mode. Washington had but two wins entering Sunday’s game against the Los Angeles Rams. They were still in the mix despite an unreal rash of injuries to star players, due to poor play in the NFC East. They needed to start stacking wins, especially with a massive upcoming clash with the New York Giants next Thursday night. That meant beating the super-talented (and also injury-plagued) Rams. Washington was not able to do that. The Commanders had a shot to win at the end but came up just short in a 20-13 loss to the Rams at Northwest Stadium. They have fallen to 2-5-1 and the New York Giants beat Philadelphia to improve to 5-2-1, putting a big dent in the conversation about Washington competing for the division title. Their season could essentially be over with a Thursday night loss to the Giants. There’s plenty of time to talk about that. Let’s examine some key takeaways from Sunday’s clash with the Rams after watching it live: Winning time doesn’t work Washington entered Sunday’s fourth quarter all tied up with the Rams. That didn’t last long. Puka Nakua – the receiver was a Commanders killer – made a leaping touchdown catch to give Los Angeles its largest lead of the day, however slim it may have been. It was a big moment for the Commanders to respond, but they didn’t, coming up short on third down, and then opting to punt rather than attempt a 58-yard field goal. The long ensuing Rams drive allowed LA to work the clock against Washington as the time dipped below six minutes. The Commanders didn’t have momentum on their side. They had scored 10 points in the first two drives of the game, but just three points over the next seven. That was not, well, great. Jayden Daniels was able to work the ball into Rams territory, but then Myles Garrett struck. The Rams edge rusher — he had three sacks — flashed past rookie center Matt Gulbin for a huge sack and a 12-yard loss. title: NFL trade deadline grades: Deals for Jessie Bates III, Davon Godchaux, more
summary: Do Jessie Bates III and Davon Godchaux lift the Jaguars' defense? Wise move for Lions to add Andre Cisco? Let's evaluate 11 trades before the deadline.
full_text:
NFL analysts Ben Solak and Seth Walder are grading deals ahead of the 2026 trade deadline , which is Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET.

 When grading trades, we evaluate them for each team based on on-field impact, cap implications, draft compensation and effects within the context of a team's overall short- and long-term outlooks. How confident are we in knowing if this is a good or bad decision? And how big is the impact of this decision? Both questions play a role in our grades, though a low-impact decision can still receive a strong or poor grade. Even with lower stakes, clear-cut wins or losses still matter.

 Here are our evaluations for 11 deals of trading season, including two quarterback moves ( Jacoby Brissett and J.J. McCarthy ) and the massive blockbuster sending  Jeffery Simmons to Chicago. Check back through the deadline for grades on the biggest moves.

 

 
 Jump to a trade: 
 Godchaux |  Cisco |  Bates |  Brissett 
 Simmons  |  Buckner |  Nelson  |  Harrison 
 Jurgens  |  Porter | McCarthy 

 
 

 

 Saints trade DT Godchaux to Jaguars 

 Jaguars get: DT Davon Godchaux 
 Saints get: 2028 sixth-round pick

 Jaguars grade: B- 
 Saints grade: B

 With DaVon Hamilton out for the season with a torn quadriceps , the Jaguars made their second deal of the day to bring in a replacement nose tackle, with Godchaux set to take over Hamilton's spot.

 

 In his 10th season in the league, Godchaux was playing just under 20 snaps per game for the Saints. His run stop win rate ranked in the 65th percentile among interior defenders this season, though he had struggled in the category the prior two years. Hamilton was just slightly better, with a 69th percentile run stop win rate at the position.

 The Jaguars' defense ranks third in EPA allowed per designed run, though they naturally felt there was risk that could drop off without replacing Hamilton externally.

 

 Godchaux has a $1.3 million salary and is in the last year of his contract. Given the Saints' situation -- 3-5 and still in the race for the NFC South but without real hopes of being an actual contender -- it makes sense for them to deal him for a draft pick while they can.

 

 

 Jets trade S Cisco to Lions 

 Lions get: S Andre Cisco 
 Jets get: 2028 sixth-round pick

 Lions grade: C 
 Jets grade: B+

 The Lions have acquired safety depth in Cisco while the team awaits  Kerby Joseph 's return. Brian Branch returned to game action in Week 7 after recovering from an Achilles injury suffered last December and has played alongside Chuck Clark . Joseph hasn't played since Week 6 last year due to a knee injury but recently returned to practice .

 In Cisco, the Lions get a veteran deep safety who could work with Clark to complement Branch until Joseph returns. But Cisco had been mostly relegated to the bench in New York, having not had double-digit defensive snaps since Week 3. That number dropped to zero on Sunday, with Malachi Moore playing ahead of him.

 Cisco is only 26 years old and costs $2 million this year between base salary and per game roster bonuses, with the Lions presumably taking over the remainder of the money owed. To me, this is pricey for a player who hasn't really been playing for the Jets and who, ideally, won't play all that much for the Lions if Joseph is able to return to his previous level of play.

 

 It makes sense for the Jets to trade him -- they are well out of contention and Cisco is on an expiring contract -- and I'm guessing they were pleased to get this kind of return. -- Walder 

 

 

 Falcons trade S Bates to Jaguars 
 Jaguars get: S Jessie Bates III 
 Falcons get: 2027 second-round pick, 2028 fifth-round pick

 Jaguars grade: B 
 Falcons grade: B+

 The Jaguars delivered the opening deal of trade deadline week, acquiring Bates to augment a defense that they hope can be part of a Super Bowl run. Bates is an impact player who delivers splash plays. Over his 3½ years in Atlanta, Bates recorded 14 interceptions and 11 forced fumbles. Yards per coverage snap is a pretty noisy stat for safeties, but over each of his seasons with the Falcons, Bates allowed 0.5 yards per coverage snap or better -- lower than the 0.6 average for the position -- per NFL Next Gen Stats.

 He'll take over the spot vacated by Eric Murray , who is out for the season with an elbow injury, and play next to Antonio Johnson . Johnson aligns as a safety only 57% of the time, as he sometimes plays from the box or on occasion even up on the line, while Bates has had more typical alignments. He is 9.5 yards from the line of scrimmage on average, spending 75% of the time at safety and 17% in the box. Despite that he has delivered big plays in the run game, too. He has 13 run stops this season -- plays where the defender makes the tackle on a successful EPA play for the defense -- tied for seventh most among safeties, per NFL Next Gen Stats. He has the best EPA on run stops among safeties (in part because two of his forced fumbles have come on run plays).

 

 I absolutely think it makes sense for the Jaguars to add talent at the deadline as they make a serious push. They currently rank second in ESPN's Football Power Index (and first in the AFC) and have a 24% chance to reach -- and 13% to win -- the Super Bowl. It is fully go time in Jacksonville. The Jags already have a good defense, ranking second in EPA allowed per play, and this will make them better.

 Bates is in the final year of his contract with a $13 million salary, and the Jaguars will take over the remaining portion of that money assuming the deal hasn't been altered. I suspect this is a pure rental because the Jaguars currently have just $4 million in 2026 cap space and negative-$15 million in 2027, per OverTheCap.com. But that is perfectly OK.

 In fact, if I were the Jaguars, I would rather this be a pure rental. Because the Jaguars are cap-strapped, they won't be active in free agency, which means they are likely to receive a compensatory pick (a fourth-rounder would be my guess) when Bates walks in free agency. If we assume this year's second-rounder is in the back-half of the round and that the Jaguars do get a 2028 fourth-round pick back, this works out to dealing a third-round pick for half a season of Bates, per ESPN's draft pick valuations.

 It's a little more than I would want; last week I proposed a Bates deal to Buffalo for a third and a fifth, though I do think now I might have been aiming too low. But ultimately I can get on board because all of the aspects of the deal (impact player, fills need, win-now window) make sense and the price ultimately isn't egregious if he is indeed a rental. So my B grade here indicates I would make this trade if I were the Jaguars, but I wouldn't have done it for more.

 

 Atlanta was somewhat boxed in to making a Bates deal because it has so much cap space -- more than $110 million in 2027, per OverTheCap.com. That means they very likely will be active in free agency and therefore would have a major risk of not getting anything back for Bates if they held him through the end of the year, as acquired free agents cancel out lost free agents in terms of compensatory picks. If the Falcons were not going to be contenders this season, then they almost had to deal Bates for the most they could get for him. And while the 3-6 Falcons are still in the race in the lowly NFC South, they had to ask themselves: Is this team really going to make a run in 2026?

 It seems they answered that question honestly. -- Walder 

 
 

 Cardinals trade QB Brissett to Ravens 
 Ravens get: QB Jacoby Brissett , 2027 fifth-round pick 
 Cardinals get: 2027 fourth-round pick, 2028 seventh-round pick

 Ravens grade: B+ 
 Cardinals grade: B

 With Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley both hurt , the Ravens are throwing a Hail Mary to save their season. Baltimore is trading for veteran Brissett, shortly after the Cardinals benched him in favor of Gardner Minshew II .

 Brissett is a respected bridge quarterback and has played…

title: As the 'Peanut Punch' takes over NFL, how do teams counter it?
summary: After Charles Tillman popularized the punch 14 years ago, it has really taken off this season.
full_text:
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. -- On Oct. 11, New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo fumbled away a win. The Giants lined up in field goal range coming out of the two-minute warning in overtime. Any points would have won the game.

 Washington Commanders defensive lineman Daron Payne had other thoughts. After Skattebo was hit in the backfield and had to use his forearms to shed a tackle, he couldn't get the ball back up to his chest. Payne threw his blocker out of the way and threw his fist at the daylight between Skattebo and the football. Ball out. The Giants' chance at a win was erased, and the game ended in a tie.

 Payne executed an increasingly popular -- and violent -- maneuver called the "Peanut Punch," wherein a would-be tackler throws a haymaker at the football in an attempt to pop it loose rather than wrapping up the ball carrier -- a technique popularized around 2012 and named after former Chicago Bears defender Charles "Peanut" Tillman.

 One day later, Buffalo Bills running back  James Cook III  fell victim to the same fate.

 

 Carrying from the Los Angeles Rams' 22-yard line early in overtime, Cook squeezed the ball low, around the left side of his abdomen. Had Cook had the ball higher, the incoming punch from linebacker Nate Landman might have left a bruise, but the ball wouldn't have had anywhere to go.

 With the ball at Cook's side, Landman found a crease between Cook's armpit and wrist and wedged the ball through. Ball out. Rams possession. Had it not been for a blocked field goal minutes later, Cook's fumble would've meant Bills defeat.

 But with fumbles come consequences.

 Though the Giants didn't explicitly call it a benching, Skattebo didn't receive any carries the week following his fumble. And despite Cook being the NFL's reigning rushing leader, Bills coach Joe Brady threatened punishments -- including decreased playing time if Cook didn't clean up his ball security.

 The NFL does not track punch attempts or their success as official statistics, and punches are almost impossible to track given the way defenders wield their arms while going for tackles, but it's clear that some of the NFL's best and most reliable ball carriers struggle with it.

 Since the start of the 2025 season, including the playoffs, Cook has fumbled 11 times to lead all running backs, a rate of once for every 44 carries. Skattebo, while not as prolific in total rushes, fumbles once every 40 carries.

 Defenders are punching at the ball nearly every drive, and being labeled a ball security risk makes you a target. The more you fumble, the more opponents try to make you fumble. As Brady puts it, every team the Bills play will have on the scouting report to punch at Cook.

 So as Cook and the fumble-prone Bills (6-1) prepare for their matchup against the Minnesota Vikings (6-1), who led the NFL in forced fumbles in 2025, let's examine the Peanut Punch's popularity, why it works, what offenses can do to counteract its effectiveness and what the state of ball security is in this ever-changing league.

 

 

 Countering the Peanut Punch 
 Offenses know how to prevent the punch. The technique exists.

 
 Carry the ball "high and tight," squeezing it across your chest diagonally at an incline. 
 One point of the ball should be in the crook of your elbow. 
 The other point needs to be somewhere between your chin and your opposite shoulder. 
 Apply pressure with your fingertips, bicep, forearm and rib cage. 
 Lower your pads. 
 Make sure your wrist is always above your elbow. 
 Make sure there's no air between the ball and your body. 
 Make sure the ball isn't visible from behind. 
 And when you sense contact coming, think "double in trouble" and brace by crossing your off-ball hand over your on-ball wrist. 
 

 

 The technique works, but ball security is a lot like darts. Darts isn't difficult because no one's cracked the mystery of how to throw a bulls-eye. It's tricky because there's a huge gap between knowing what to do and being able to do it with precise consistency every time.

 The punch has been more successful because carrying a football properly defies basic human instinct. We don't pick up speed by tucking our arms into our ribs. We don't change direction with our wrists above our elbows. And we don't fall to the ground without using our hands.

 As long as ball carriers are human, there's always going to be a sliver of daylight for defenders to punch at.

 "You've got to realize you've got the baby in your hands," former All-Pro running back Jamal Lewis told ESPN. "You've got the game in your hands. You've got the play in your hands when you're carrying the football. It's really just understanding that this is not a natural running style."

 

 'High and tight' 

 Lewis fumbled 22 times in his first three full seasons. He wasn't alone. Over the same four-year span (Lewis missed the 2001 season with a knee injury), Giants stalwart Tiki Barber fumbled 35 times.

 Reflecting on that period, Barber told ESPN he didn't think he had a ball security problem. A newspaper reporter actually tipped Barber off to just how frequently he'd been putting the ball on the ground, and it wasn't until 2004 when coach Tom Coughlin arrived in New York when Barber started to foresee consequences.

 "Coughlin comes in and he says 'Tiki, you're a great player, but if you keep fumbling you're not going to play,'" Barber said.

 So Barber and running backs coach Jerald Ingram went into the lab. "High and tight" became Barber's entire life. Anywhere he went, he had a football high and tight. On the treadmill. In the meeting room. Walking to the cafeteria.

 He instructed teammates to try to rake the ball away from him any time, anywhere.

 

 "It ultimately became second nature, so when I got in the games I wasn't even thinking about it anymore," Barber said. "You know what's interesting is I've been retired for 20 seasons now, but whenever somebody throws me a football, the first thing I do is put high and tight. It's so ingrained in my mind, I can't not do it."

 After fumbling once every 27 carries from 2000 to 2003, Barber fumbled just once every 112 carries from 2004 to 2006, making the Pro Bowl all three years and twice leading the league in scrimmage yards.

 Lewis noticed. Sometime after his 2,000-yard season in 2003 with the Baltimore Ravens , Lewis says he saw a TV special about Barber's adherence to the high-and-tight lifestyle and adopted it as his own. After fumbling once every 46 carries from 2000 to 2003, Lewis only fumbled once per 90 carries for the rest of his career.

 All these years later, Lewis is still such a believer in the importance of high and tight that he scours the internet for proof of its efficacy. Lewis says he was watching footage of current Ravens running back Derrick Henry's workouts before the 2025 season and felt Henry was pumping the ball too much when he ran. Henry fumbled in each of that season's first three games.

 This year, Lewis says he saw more of a high-and-tight ball security emphasis in Henry's offseason workout footage. Through nine weeks, Henry fumbled once only in 175 carries.

 

 Punch specialists 

 The Bears drafted Tillman in 2003, but his patented punch didn't become well-known until 14 years ago this week when Tillman forced four fumbles in the same game. What's standard practice today barely existed during Barber's and Lewis' heydays.

 Today's ball carriers have to contend with punch specialists on just about every defense. In Baltimore, there's Marlon Humphrey . In Atlanta, there's safety Jessie Bates III , who seems to jar a ball loose every weekend. In San Francisco, there's All-Pro linebacker Fred Warner , who led the league with four forced fumbles through the season's first seven games and is even more renowned for forcing fumbles in practice.

 

 "I think obviously they all understand what it requires to protect the ball anytime they're practicing against me," Warner said, "which in turn is obviously going…

title: How does Jessie Bates III help the Jaguars defense? Are Falcons still contending?
summary: The Falcons decided it was wiser to get something for Bates now rather than letting him walk in free agency.
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars addressed one of their biggest weaknesses Monday by sending a 2027 second-round draft pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick to the Atlanta Falcons for safety Jessie Bates III .

 This was the first move the team made before Tuesday's 4 p.m. ET trade deadline to try and solidify itself as a legitimate contender. The Jaguars also traded a conditional 2028 sixth-round pick for  New Orleans Saints DT Davon Godchaux , according to NFL Network's Cameron Wolfe, after losing nose tackle DaVon Hamilton for the rest of the season with a quad injury.

 At 6-2, the Jaguars are in third place in the AFC and have a three-game lead in the AFC South. These moves could suggest a win-now mentality.

 Bates, who made the Pro Bowl in 2023, can stabilize a secondary that has been hit with multiple injuries at safety and cornerback. The Jaguars made a similar move last season at the trade deadline by acquiring receiver Jakobi Meyers to help a position group that had multiple players out with injuries and that keyed an offensive surge that carried them to a division title. The hope is that Bates can do the same for the secondary because getting through the AFC means beating some of the league's top QBs -- especially Buffalo's Josh Allen .

 The Falcons, on the other hand, were able to get good draft capital for a player on an expiring contract but are still competing in the NFC South.

 What does this move mean for the Jaguars' defense and the Falcons' draft plans? ESPN NFL Nation reporters Michael DiRocco and Marc Raimondi and NFL draft analyst Jordan Reid take a look at each.

 

 
 What do the Bates and Godchaux additions mean for the Jaguars' defense? 
 The Jaguars rank second in the league in opponents points per game (15.1), yet 22nd in passing yards allowed per game (229.0).

 Starting safety Eric Murray , who went on injured reserve on Nov. 3 with a season-ending elbow injury, didn't have an interception or pass breakup this season but he was valued because he was a good communicator on the field. Bates brings that, but he also has good ball skills (28 career interceptions).

 

 Bates' durability is a huge plus, too. He has missed three games in his nine-year career while Murray has missed seven games since he signed with the Jaguars in March 2025. Murray's injury, which happened on the first play of Week 8, as well as injuries to Caleb Ransaw (placed on IR on Oct. 6 with a knee injury) and Antonio Johnson (ankle) forced the Jaguars to use special teams standout  Rayuan Lane III  and practice squad player Kaevon Merriweather more on defense. While both played well -- Lane made a game-saving fourth-down tackle against the Cincinnati Bengals and had a 92-yard interception return for a touchdown against the Colts -- this move gives the Jaguars a good safety tandem.

 This move also gives coordinator Anthony Campanile a little more versatility in how he wants to use his safeties, because he now has two players who can play closer to the line of scrimmage, whether that's in base or nickel packages. Bates also brings more as a blitzer than Murray and that should allow Campanile to be a little more creative.

 The Jaguars also needed help along the defensive line with Hamilton out for the season. Jacksonville ranks fifth in rushing yards allowed through Week 9 (89.3) -- but had their season-worst performance against the Ravens on Thursday. Godchaux will slide in as a run defender alongside Arik Armstead . Godchaux had fifteen tackles in eight games with the Saints this season.   -- DiRocco 

 

 Could the Jaguars extend Bates' contract? 

 The Jaguars traded for Meyers (who turns 30 today) last November and signed him to a three-year extension, so signing a 29-year-old safety isn't out of the question -- especially if they're unable to work out an extension for Johnson, who is in the final season of his rookie contract. But the Jaguars have some 2027 cap work to do because they're currently projected to be $15.4 million over, per OverTheCap. There's also a potential contract for receiver Parker Washington to figure into those calculations this offseason, too. -- DiRocco 

 
 

 What does trading the star safety say about the Falcons' trajectory this season? 
 The Falcons are 3-6, but still only one game out of first place in the NFC South. Atlanta still has a chance to win the division and make the playoffs, which it has not done since 2017. Bates could have helped the Falcons achieve that -- he's still playing at a very high level. But how could Atlanta turn down a second-round pick for a safety who will turn 30 years old in February?

 

 The Falcons have gone either 8-9 or 7-10 the last five seasons. At some point, they need to make the football decisions that get them to a stronger, deeper roster and not just dwell in the middle like they have been, hoping to take advantage of a weak division. Atlanta was unlikely to re-sign Bates in the offseason, so why not get something substantial in return for him now rather than wait to see if the team can somehow sneak into the playoffs?

 Second-year safety Xavier Watts , who had five interceptions as a rookie, will step into Bates' role on the Falcons defense. Bates has been a mentor to Watts, and defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich has relished that Watts has patterned his game after Bates.

 Atlanta also has young defensive backs Billy Bowman Jr . and Avieon Terrell who are ready to take on more responsibilities in the secondary, along with solid veterans DeMarcco Hellams and Sydney Brown , both of whom could start with Bates on the move. Bowman also has experience playing safety.

 Bates has also been a mentor to quarterback Michael Penix Jr . The two have had lockers next to one another since Penix was a rookie in 2024. Bates has been one of Penix's staunchest advocates. Bates will be missed on the field and off, but the Falcons decided it was an offer too good to refuse. -- Raimondi 

 

 What can Atlanta do with those incoming picks? 
 Offensive tackle and cornerback are two obvious areas of need for the Falcons. With an extra Day 2 pick, Atlanta could look to target protection for Michael Penix Jr . and Melvin Siani (Texas), Elijah Paige (USC) and Drew Azzopardi (Washington) would be names that could be available in that range and help. At cornerback, I think Audavion Collins (Penn State), Jalen Mayo (Houston) or Vicari Swain (South Carolina) could make sense, too . -- Reid

title: How to bet Bills-Vikings: Analysis, best bets and top prop plays
summary: Odds, analysis and picks to help you bet Monday night's Buffalo Bills-Minnesota Vikings game.
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings make passing difficult, allowing just 6.2 yards per attempt and four passing touchdowns all season. James Cook III gives the Buffalo Bills an answer. Minnesota allows running backs 3.8 yards per carry before halftime and 5.3 after.

 

 Buffalo already uses multiple tight ends and heavy formations, so it can keep testing that front without forcing Josh Allen into playing hero ball. Allen's legs also give the Bills another option when the pass coverage holds up.

 Minnesota's problem is getting enough offense to help its defense. Nearly 60% of its sets of downs reach third down. Buffalo allows just 3.9 yards per carry, putting more responsibility on the quarterback. With Carson Wentz starting, Justin Jefferson becomes especially interesting. Jefferson averages 87.6 receiving yards with Wentz, and Buffalo has allowed 10 of its 15 passing touchdowns after halftime. Minnesota's best opening could come late.

 

 

 

 Betting outlook 

 I lean with the Bills covering the short road spread . Minnesota's pass defense deserves respect, but Buffalo can work through Cook and Allen running the ball instead of repeatedly challenging that coverage.

 

 Buffalo's 33-point scoring average meets a defense allowing a league-low 1.18 points per drive. Something has to give, and I expect Minnesota to bring Buffalo below its usual output. The Vikings barely convert more than half their red zone possessions into touchdowns, so asking them to make up the difference on the full-game total feels optimistic, although the number has dropped.

 That's why I like the first half to go under 22.5 points . With the Vikings' defense against backs starting strong and fading late in games, Buffalo can still feed Cook, but those early carries could consume more clock without immediately producing touchdowns. Buffalo's defense has the same timing advantage, giving up more scores after the half. Both of those, combined with Minnesota's poor early-down offense, have me eyeing the first half rather than full game.

 

 Notable player props, bets 
 

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 

 James Cook III rushing attempts OVER 18.5 (-112) 

 Maldonado: This fits how Buffalo should attack. The Bills already prefer the heavier formations Minnesota encourages opponents to use, so leaning on Cook fits their normal offense. The Colts and Lions committed to their backs against this defense. Cook is already being heavily used, but the matchup is the stronger reason to expect volume. The risk is Allen taking more designed runs or Minnesota building a lead.

 Josh Allen rushing yards OVER 31.5 (-116) 

 Liz Loza: Brian Flores has built a blitz machine that has regularly befuddled opposing offenses. The Vikings' defense has allowed the eighth-fewest rushing yards to QBs, surrendering an average of 11.5 rushing yards per contest to the position. But it hasn't faced a QB with legs like Allen's. Allen is one of the position's most effective players when facing additional pass rushers. The QB1 in carries per game is averaging 38.5 rushing yards per contest, and I'm willing to wager on Allen's mobility in primetime.

title: Inside Justin Jefferson's miraculous catch for Vikings versus Bills in 2022
summary: In 2022 against the Bills, Jefferson leaped up and came down with one of "the greatest catches of all time."
full_text:
EAGAN, Minn. -- The play is commemorated everywhere. 

 It's the central ink of a tattoo that covers Justin Jefferson 's left thigh. It's depicted on a life-size Fathead wall sticker in coach Kevin O'Connell's basement and in a photograph hanging on the wall of the Minnesota Vikings ' practice facility. There is a private-issue hoodie sweatshirt that cleverly incorporates Jefferson's uniform number with what he agrees is the catch of his life: A leaping, one-handed grab to convert fourth-and-18 during a wild overtime victory over the Buffalo Bills in 2022. 

 Several Vikings staff members will be wearing that sweatshirt Monday night at U.S. Bank Stadium ( 8:15 p.m. ET, ESPN/ABC ), where the Vikings and Bills will meet for the first time since Jefferson changed the course of his career. Already a two-time Pro Bowl receiver by then, at age 23, Jefferson went on to lead the NFL in catches and receiving yards while earning his first All-Pro honor and the NFL's Offensive Player of the Year award. 

 His statistics have slipped in the past two seasons as the Vikings have transitioned through four starting quarterbacks, and players and coaches alike acknowledged his frustration during a 33-yard game Nov. 1 against the Detroit Lions . But even if he never returns to his previous production, Jefferson can rest assured that he long ago cemented himself in NFL history.

 "If you talk about the greatest catches of all time," said Vikings assistant receivers coach Derron Montgomery, "how can you leave out that one?"

 ESPN spoke with Jefferson and 13 others who were in Buffalo that day to understand the inside story behind the catch, how those who experienced it absorbed its improbability and the ways it has impacted them since. Jefferson grinned throughout his interview and ultimately offered this succinct summation: "It was just so many things going on at one time."

 "An unbelievable moment," O'Connell said. "I'll never forget it as long as I live." 

 

 

 The situation 

 The Vikings entered the game with a 7-1 record, having already won six one-score games and pulled off four fourth-quarter comebacks. On this day, the Bills held a 27-10 lead late in the third quarter before Vikings running back Dalvin Cook (brother of current Bills RB James Cook III ) ran 81 yards for a touchdown to get them within 10. 

 Blake Brandel, left tackle: That game in general was absolutely bananas. Dalvin Cook hitting that huge run kind of jump-started it for us.

 Blake Schroeder, Vikings assistant equipment manager: The entire year was kind of the same way. It was just like, "Here we go again. Let's get one, then let's get a stop, let's get another." And it kind of just went that way. And then it came down to that drive.

 O'Connell: The game was just something else.

 

 The playcall 

 

 Late in the fourth quarter, the Vikings cut the lead to 27-23, then got the ball back at their own 24-yard line with 3:26 remaining in the game. But on third-and-13 from Minnesota's own 32, Bills pass rusher Von Miller beat right tackle Brian O'Neill to sack quarterback Kirk Cousins for a 5-yard loss. That made it fourth-and-18 from the 27 at the two-minute warning. 

 O'Neill: I remember being in a slight panic because the play before, Von had caught me. And you know that fourth-and-18 is kind of a prayer.

 O'Connell: In 2022, I rarely told Kirk, "This is where the ball's going." But that happened to be one of the few where I called the play and I said, "No matter what, give Justin a chance."

 Jefferson: Kirk came up to me and said, "Hey, look, we're going to have to throw this ball up to you and you just got to go make a grab."

 Harrison Smith, safety: I mean, throwing it up to Jets [Jefferson's nickname] on fourth-and-18? That seems like the best option.

 T.J. Hockenson, tight end: I remember hoping that he wasn't going to throw it to me. On that play, I'm at, like, 6 yards past the line and so I would need 12 for the first down, and there's guys right there. So, like, throw it up to Justin Jefferson for sure. 

 O'Connell: The concept of the play, we called "Pearls." It had to do with the combination of the routes. 

 Cousins: It was somewhat of a stock play. It wasn't a designed play just for that week. It was a play that we had repped many times.

 Keenan McCardell, receivers coach: I remember the call, and I was standing there on the sideline with Jets. At the time I was like, "Jets, this ball is probably going to go up to you."

 

 The pre-snap 

 

 Jefferson lined up on the right side of the line along with Hockenson and fellow receiver Adam Thielen. K.J. Osborn was the sole receiver lined up on the left. For this play, Miller switched sides and was lined up over Brandel.  

 Brandel: That was my first time ever playing true offensive line reps in a regular-season game in the NFL. I had only played jumbo tight end to that point, but our left tackle, Christian Darrisaw , got a concussion in that game. So I came in during the second half. It was my third year. I'd only played jumbo tight end, and I'm finally getting to play. And I've got Von Miller off the edge on fourth-and-18, right after he had gotten a sack.

 Jefferson: Lining up in that whole start of it, I'm just imagining me making the play. I knew the ball was going to come to me. So it was all about getting to that spot and going up there and making that big grab.

 Schroeder: Usually I go into the locker room at the two-minute warning, just to get everything ready for coaches and players to come in so we can get out as quick as possible. But this time, I stayed to see what would happen.

 Eric Kendricks, ex-Vikings linebacker: Especially late in games when we're behind, I like to put myself above the first-down marker. Because it's a superstition of mine that if I stand above the first-down marker, we're going to get a first down.

 Cam Lewis, ex-Bills safety: We're in Cover 4 (zone defense with four defensive backs). In my head, I'm thinking I'm just about to go out here and make a play.

 

 The catch 

 The ball was snapped. Jefferson ran a deep corner route. Hockenson stopped at the 30-yard line. Thielen ran to the sticks. Cornerback Taron Johnson sat on Thielen's route as Lewis picked up Jefferson, with linebacker Tyrel Dodson in the vicinity. Osborn ran a dig over the middle.  

 O'Connell: I wouldn't classify Justin as open on the play. [Lewis] was over the top, and another defender kind of underneath playing him, a little bit more of a matchy coverage. On fourth-and-18, you're going to be hard-pressed to get any looks where you're like, "Man, this is a great look for the play."

 McCardell: The defender sat on Adam, so the read was to throw to Jets. But either way, the ball is going to him. 

 Dodson: The Mike linebacker has anything in between the hashes. So Justin broke out. I look back and the quarterback is looking that way. I knew I had Cam Lewis there. So I was like, I don't need to go full [toward Jefferson] because I know the player. If he went backside, I could get anything backside." 

 Brandel: I had a chip [from Cook], and [Miller] still got on an edge on me. I kind of ran him by the pocket, and then our left guard at the time, Ezra Cleveland , had my back. He was very aware of the situation, so came and cleaned him up even more.

 McCardell: So Kirk threw it. I'm looking at the ball, and I say to myself, "Big fella, you got to go up." And then I jumped. I jumped when I thought he needed to go up. He goes up and I'm looking at it because I'm literally seeing him right here in front of me. I'm like, all right, all right. It's going to be a tough catch.

 Montgomery: I did a little jump, too.

 

 Cousins: His attitude would always be, "Hey, just throw me the ball, I'll make it right." I look back now, and he was ready to kind of jump-ball catch it, which is probably the right approach. I was more throwing him to run underneath it. When he stopped to jump-ball catch it, the throw went too far…

title: Rasheed Walker keeps 'analyzing issue' in protecting Bryce Young's blind side
summary: The left tackle can't let Sunday's sack-fumble ignite a prolonged pass protection slump over the coming weeks.
full_text:
The Panthers were 36 yards away from pay dirt and their fourth win of the season. But with just 1:24 left in the game, left tackle Rasheed Walker was pushed into the backfield by Denver Broncos pass rusher Nik Bonitto , who smacked the ball out of quarterback Bryce Young 's right hand for a sack-fumble, which was recovered by the road team at Bank of America Stadium on Sunday.

 The play closed out a 26-21 win for the Broncos and put Walker, who has struggled mightily with pass protection over the past month, under a microscope. Following the game, Walker said he felt like Bonitto set up that final defensive play with how he rushed Walker throughout the game.

 "Bonitto is known to be a speed edge rusher -- bend the edge type of guy," Walker said. "I noticed like the whole game that he was bull-rushing me, like he doesn't really do a lot. I was sitting on the bull (rush), and then on the last play of the game, I feel like he faked the power, and then as soon as I was sitting down, he went [to the] edge and did his move and then made a play. When you're going against the best, you never know what you're going to get. Shout out to him, he's a great player and it was a good rep by him."

 

 Walker has been charged with 45 QB pressures through eight games, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. That's 19 more pressures than rookie right tackle Monroe Freeling , who has played one less game. Walker has faced one-on-one scenarios on 79.1% of his pass sets, and the free-agent addition has struggled to hold back the pressure on a consistent basis.

 The 26-year-old can't let Sunday's sack-fumble ignite a prolonged pass protection slump over the coming weeks. The Panthers are in a three-game freefall at 3-5, and while they still enter Week 10 at the top of the division race, their NFC South showdown Sunday against the New Orleans Saints (3-5) looms large.

 Every week Walker is typically going up against the opposing team's best pass rusher, and against the Broncos, he drew Bonitto. On that final play -- one that Walker wants back -- Bonitto beat Walker when it mattered the most.

 "Just a really good rush on Rasheed," Panthers coach Dave Canales said. "Got the edge [and] was hoping that there was an element of Bryce going forward to get an incomplete pass, but a really nice rush. That's a situation where we can help him right there."

 While Canales hoped the officials would signal an incomplete pass, Walker's hopes were a bit different, especially after he felt he put together a strong performance before that exclamation point for the Broncos.

 "S---, when I saw the ball come out -- we both saw the ball come out, I watched him see the ball, I tried to make sure he didn't get it -- I was hoping that we got the ball back," Walker said. "I felt comfortable playing the whole game. I knew that play didn't define who I was and I was hoping that we'd get the ball back and get another opportunity to score. But, you know, they recovered the ball and that was that."

 

 Walker spent last week studying his film to figure out what had led to his troubling performances in recent weeks. He came to the conclusion his footwork wasn't up to par, so he worked on that aspect of his game in practice and prior to the Bonitto strip-sack, he felt those adjustments paid off.

 "I've been analyzing the issue that I've been having in pass pro," Walker said. "I haven't been playing like myself, and this week, I identified the issue, and I attacked it. Honestly, I didn't get to watch the film yet, but I feel like when I watch [this] game, I'm going to see progression from weeks before up until that last play.

 "But O-line is a position where it's all about building. The three words that you should never say is, 'I got it,' cause the O-line, you've never got it. You've always gotta to keep getting better and developing."

 The Panthers need their blindside blocker to keep Young upright. And if not, the QB, his left tackle and the team will continue to sink.

 "Effort and mindset [were] never the issue," Walker said. "Honestly, it was my footwork. That's what I would say. Once I got my feet in the right footwork, which I did today, I felt like that made a huge difference. ... But sometimes people get the best of you -- it's a competitive league."

title: Is the NFC North the best division ever? Sizing up wins for Packers, Lions, Bears
summary: The Packers, Bears, Lions and Vikings are a combined 25-8 and all hold playoff spots right now. Can anyone stop the NFC North -- and who will win the division?
full_text:
Sunday, unsurprisingly, brought three more wins for the NFC North.

 During the afternoon games, the Lions comfortably beat the Dolphins 19-9 in what might have qualified as a home game given the makeup of the crowd in Miami. The Packers stomped the Patriots 45-27 with an offensive blizzard in Foxborough. And while the Bears turned the ball over five times, they had enough left in the tank to move the ball into position for a game-winning field goal and beat the Buccaneers 27-24  in primetime.

 Unquestionably the NFL's best division as we hit the midway point of the 2026 season , the NFC North can go 4-0 for the first time in a single week this season if the Vikings beat the Bills on "Monday Night Football" to cap Week 9 . But even if the Vikings fall, the NFC North can hang its hat on its first-half résumé. Regardless of Monday's result, the North will finish Week 9 with the best collective record of any division through nine weeks in the Super Bowl era. You are watching, at least by wins and losses, what so far has been the best division in NFL history .

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 Can these four teams keep it up? And if they do, what does it mean? Will the stiff competition to win the division exhaust four of the best teams in football and leave them easy pickings in January? Or does iron sharpen iron and make the North winner the favorite to win the Super Bowl? Of these four teams, which one has the best shot of actually winning the division and making that deep playoff run?

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Historically great division? 
 The Bears' case as the best 
 The Lions' case as the best 
 The Packers' case as the best 
 The Vikings' case as the best 

 
 

 Special start to 2026 
 Chicago's victory Sunday night left the NFC North at 25-8 with one game left to go in Week 9. That's a winning percentage of .757, roughly the equivalent of a 13-win team over a full season. As I mentioned, even if the Vikings lose Monday, the division's .736 winning percentage would still be the best through nine weeks since the 1970 merger. The 2022 NFC East, which went 24-9 (.727) through nine weeks, is the only other division at .700 or better.

 The list of best starts by raw wins and losses is full of teams from the 32-team era (2002 and onward) for a couple of reasons. The league's split into eight four-team divisions, and it's easier to find four very good teams in any given year than five. When NFL teams were in five- and six-team divisions, they also played more intradivision games, which naturally hurts the division's overall record since usually ( but not always ) one team has to lose each of those games.

 Of the eight losses the NFC North has incurred this season, five are to other teams in the division. The Bears, Lions, Packers and Vikings are collectively a whopping 20-3 (.870) outside of their division so far this season. The Lions have lost to the Bills and Panthers, while the Packers lost to the Falcons on a short week in September. They've collectively beaten non-North teams by just over a touchdown per game, scoring nearly 28 points per game in the process.

 

 That winning percentage is also the best mark in NFL history through nine weeks, though the Vikings could spoil it with a loss to Buffalo. In 1984, the AFC West collectively went 21-4 (.850) through nine weeks, which the 2026 NFC North would fall below (at .833) with a Vikings loss. The 2022 NFC East is the only other division to win at least 80% of its out-of-division games through nine weeks, going 20-5.

 That 1984 race in the AFC West was really between three teams, with the 8-1 Broncos just ahead of the 7-2 Seahawks and Raiders. The 5-4 Chiefs and 4-5 Chargers were very good fourth- and fifth-place teams relative to the competition, going a combined 8-2 outside of the West to start the season, but they went a combined 1-7 within the division and fell off. The AFC West sent those top three teams to the postseason.

 They combined to win exactly one playoff game, though, and that came when the Seahawks knocked off the Raiders in the wild-card round before getting comfortably dispatched by the Dolphins in the divisional round . The 13-3 Broncos, who won the division, blew a second-half lead at home against the Steelers , as a John Elway interception on a checkdown with three minutes to go set Pittsburgh up with a short field for the game-winning score.

 How often does that happen, though? Do these dominant divisions breed champions, or are they worn out by the time we get to the Super Bowl? Let's take a look at the best 12 divisions (by out-of-division record) after the 2026 NFC North and 1984 AFC West through nine weeks:

 3. 2022 NFC East 
 Out-of-division through Week 9: 20-5 (.800) 
 After Week 9: 12-7 (.632) 
 Playoff teams: Three (14-3 Eagles, 12-5 Cowboys, 9-7-1 Giants)

 Two years after the East sent a 7-9 Washington Football Team to the postseason as division champs, all four teams in 2022 went .500 or better. All three qualifying teams also won at least one playoff game. The Cowboys blew out the Bucs (in Tom Brady's final NFL game) before losing to the 49ers. Daniel Jones  and the Giants beat a 13-win Vikings team in Minnesota before getting rolled by the Eagles.

 And an excellent Eagles team easily rode its way through the NFC, dominating the Giants before beating the 49ers 31-7 in a game in which  Brock Purdy suffered a serious elbow injury early and left the 49ers with  Josh Johnson and Christian McCaffrey under center. The Eagles were slight favorites in the Super Bowl, only for the Chiefs to prevail 38-35  on a field goal at the end of regulation.

 4. 2020 AFC North 
 Out-of-division through Week 9: 15-4-1 (.775) 
 After Week 9: 11-9 (.550) 
 Playoff teams: Three (12-4 Steelers, 11-5 Ravens, 11-5 Browns)

 This division faded down the stretch, collectively failing to claim one of the top two seeds in the AFC. The Steelers lost 48-37 to the Browns in a wild-card shootout, before Cleveland  fell short against a Chiefs team that lost Patrick Mahomes to an in-game concussion. The Ravens gained a measure of revenge on the Titans after being upset by them in the prior postseason with a 20-13 victory , but they could do nothing on offense the following week in a 17-3 loss to the Bills. None of these teams even made it as far as the AFC title game.

 

 5. 2007 AFC South 
 Out-of-division through Week 9: 16-5 (.762) 
 After Week 9: 14-5 (.737) 
 Playoff teams: Three (13-3 Colts, 11-5 Jaguars, 10-6 Titans)

 This was a legitimately great division that happened to be stuck in a conference with my pick as the best team of the past 25 years, the 2007 Patriots. The Jaguars beat the Steelers on the road by two points in the wild-card round before losing to the Pats, while the AFC West champion Chargers took out the Titans and Colts in consecutive weeks, beating the latter in a game in which Philip Rivers sustained a torn ACL and turned things over to Billy Volek. Good teams, but again, they were gone before the conference championship.

 6. 1999 AFC East 
 Out-of-division through Week 9: 19-6 (.760) 
 After Week 9: 10-5 (.667) 
 Playoff teams: Three (13-3 Colts, 11-5 Bills, 9-7 Dolphins)

 This was one of the rare times when a five-team division saw each club finish at .500 or better (the Jets and Patriots both went 8-8). Bills fans remember this one well, of course, as the Titans overcame a one-point deficit from a Steve Christie field goal with 16 seconds left to win on the Music City Miracle. Tennessee then took out the Colts in the divisional round, keeping Peyton Manning out of the end zone for the first 58 minutes in a 19-16 victory. The Dolphins upset the Seahawks on the road in the wild-card round before getting shellacked 62-7 by the Jaguars in what would be the final NFL games for Jimmy Johnson and Dan Marino. Again, nobody got as far as the conference title game.

 7. 2019 NFC West 
 Out-of-division through Week 9: 19-6-1 (.750) 
 After Week 9: 7-7 (.500) 
…

title: Joe Burrow reaching new heights as Bengals face big test
summary: Burrow led the Bengals to their fourth straight win, and AFC North rival Pittsburgh is on deck.
full_text:
MADRID --  Joe Burrow talked a big game all offseason.

 He wasn't shy about the aspirations for himself or the Cincinnati Bengals , which included a potential run at a Super Bowl.

 Through eight games this season, Burrow and the team are backing all of that up. On an enormous stage, playing an international game in one of the world's most iconic venues in a standalone broadcast window, Burrow and the Bengals dazzled.

 He was nearly flawless in a 34-17 victory Sunday against the Atlanta Falcons in the historic Santiago Bernabeu, Cincinnati's fourth straight win. And with his performance, he is in the mix for an award that has eluded him -- Most Valuable Player.

 "He should have [already] won the MVP," Bengals wide receiver  Ja'Marr Chase  said. "I said this when we went to the Super Bowl [to cap the 2021 season] and he didn't get it that year. I mean, he's up for it every year."

 But this year, Burrow is working on his strongest case to date. According to ESPN Research, Burrow is the fifth player in NFL history to have at least 23 passing touchdowns and a 70% completion percentage or higher. In three of those instances, that quarterback won MVP (Tom Brady, 2007; Aaron Rodgers , 2011; Peyton Manning, 2013).

 Burrow dominated Sunday. He was 24-of-29 passing for 271 yards and four total touchdowns (three passing, one rushing). He became the fifth player in league history to have at least four passing or rushing touchdowns in four straight games. Three of those players are in the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Brady is the other one.

 But what Burrow did becomes even greater given the proper context. Sunday marked his first international game, one he has waited on for years. And he sought to match the moment.

 

 "I wanted to come out and put on a show for everybody and show what the excitement of the NFL can be," Burrow said. "And the NFL is really all about the stars and players making big-time plays."

 It wasn't just Burrow who played lights-out.  Tee Higgins  had only 32 receiving yards, but he scored two touchdowns. Chase turned in another huge game with 10 catches on 12 targets for 155 yards and a touchdown.

 And that touchdown was notable. It was a deep ball down the right sideline, a throw Burrow had missed last week against the Tennessee Titans in a very similar situation. And not only did he miss that one, but the ball was so underthrown that safety Amani Hooker picked it off for one of his three interceptions.

 That throw against the Titans prompted an extended sideline outburst from Chase. But that didn't happen Sunday as Burrow got his redemption with the 47-yard touchdown to Chase.

 "I'm not hard on Joe at all," Chase said. "He knows it. Me and him always talk all the time, but he probably did really want that touchdown."

 And his top receivers could feel that, too.

 "We were in warmups and he was throwing that pill far," Higgins said. "[Chase] was like, 'Oh, yeah, he feels good today.'

 "When we get that feeling from him, it's our job to go out there and get open for him."

 The receivers did their part as Burrow's torrid year continues. As of Sunday afternoon, Burrow led the league in QBR (79.5), which he has never done before.

 

 And it hasn't been easy. He dealt with a minor back issue at the beginning of the season. Turnovers have been costly in certain moments, especially the team's two losses. And last week, Burrow admitted with a very long pause that he is throwing the ball well -- for the most part.

 But on the international stage, he ignited the largely pro-Bengals crowd inside the home of Real Madrid, one of the biggest sports clubs in the world. The first half featured large pops of noise that swelled through the Bernabeu following big play after big play.

 And the win puts the Bengals in their best position since they drafted him with the No. 1 pick in 2020. Cincinnati has a 6-2 record with a massive matchup looming at home next Sunday night against division-leading Pittsburgh (6-2), which won the first game between the teams this season.

 At the midway point of the season, the Bengals have seemingly found their offensive identity.

 "Joe is playing at an unbelievably high level right now," Bengals coach Zac Taylor said. "It's difficult to not put the ball in his hand in every play given how everybody is playing around him as well."

 And despite how good things looked against the Falcons (3-6), there is reason to believe Burrow can be even better.

 Said Higgins: "I know he got another step in him for sure."

title: NFL Week 9: Big takeaways, questions and fantasy spin from Sunday's games
summary: Our NFL Nation reporters react to all the action, answering the biggest questions coming out of each Sunday game. Here's what we learned from Week 9.
full_text:
The Sunday slate for Week 9 of the 2026 NFL season kicked off in Madrid with the Bengals' offense erupting in a win over the Falcons. Cincinnati wide receiver Ja'Marr Chase finished with a season-high 155 yards and a touchdown on 10 receptions, and it finished with a near meltdown by  Caleb Williams  (four interceptions) and the Bears against the Bucs.

 Back in the United States, Rams edge rusher Myles Garrett  returned from injury, finishing with three sacks in a win over the Commanders. Browns quarterback  Shedeur Sanders  fell to the Saints in his first start of the 2026 season. And quarterback  Bo Nix  led the Broncos to their fifth fourth-quarter comeback this year -- tied for the most through nine games in NFL history, per the Elias Sports Bureau.

 In the late window Sunday, the 49ers forced five turnovers in a dominant win over the Raiders. Quarterback  Drew Lock  led the Seahawks to a win over the Cardinals in place of the injured  Sam Darnold . The Texans and Packers scored 40-plus points in victories over the Chargers and Patriots, respectively.

 Our NFL Nation reporters react to all the action, answering lingering questions coming out of each game -- including how teams will approach Tuesday's trade deadline . Fantasy football analysts Matt Bowen and Tristan Cockcroft also have fantasy takeaways from each matchup.

 Let's get to it with the biggest lessons from Sunday.

 
 Jump to: 
 TB-CHI | GB-NE | HOU-LAC |  ARI-SEA 
 LV-SF  |  DAL-IND  |  CLE-NO 
 NYG-PHI  |  NYJ-KC |  DEN-CAR 
 LAR-WSH  |  DET-MIA |  CIN-ATL 

 Catch up on Thursday's game: 
 JAX-BAL 

 
 

 

 Chicago 27, Tampa Bay 24 
 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap 

 

 Bears 
 What happened to the Bears after the first quarter? The Bears were primed to put the Bucs away early after building a 14-0 first-quarter lead. Then one play after Zavion Thomas was flagged for unnecessary roughness when the Bears had first-and-goal on their third possession, quarterback Caleb Williams threw his first of four interceptions. Thomas had a 91-yard kickoff return wiped off by a hold, and the Bears gained just 29 yards in the third quarter. Chicago's defense came through by holding the Bucs to 11 points off five turnovers and 2-of-12 on third down, and  Jaylon Johnson 's 67-yard pick-six was a game changer. But sloppy play from start to finish meant the Bears would need a winning drive from Williams, which set up Cairo Santos' 38-yard field goal to send Chicago into its bye week at 7-2.

 Most surprising performance: Williams accounted for one turnover in his first five games of the season, an interception in Week 2. On Sunday, he had an uncharacteristic meltdown in the second quarter when he launched three interceptions, two of which came against the blitz. He threw another late in the third quarter, joining  Michael Penix Jr . -- against the Bucs last week -- as the only players to throw four interceptions in a game this season. Prior to Week 9, Williams had four interceptions in his previous 15 games combined dating to Nov. 2, 2025. -- Courtney Cronin 

 Next game: vs. Saints (Nov. 22, 1 p.m. ET)

 
 

 Buccaneers 
 Can the Bucs turn around their fortunes with this offense? For a second straight week, the Bucs' defense had four interceptions -- adding a potentially game-saving forced fumble this time. But a blown coverage late set up the winning field goal for the Bears, and missed opportunities from the offense will be the story. The Bucs came away with only three points off the interceptions -- turnover on downs, punt, field goal and a game-changing pick-six thrown by quarterback Baker Mayfield . Tampa Bay's league-leading run game got going late to finish with 126 yards and two  Bucky Irving  touchdowns, but it was too little, too late. Mayfield finished 18-of-32 passing for 243 yards, two interceptions (both in Bears territory) and zero touchdowns, but the plays he didn't make will be the talking points heading into the bye with the Bucs sitting at 3-6.

 Key stat to know: The Buccaneers became the second team since 2000 with three or more interceptions in the first half of consecutive games, joining the 2013 Seahawks. Seattle won the Super Bowl that season. This also marks the second time in franchise history (1981) that the Bucs had four or more interceptions in consecutive games. -- ESPN staff 

 Next game: at Lions (Nov. 22, 1 p.m. ET)

 
 

 Fantasy football takeaway: Bucs running back Bucky Irving -- in a tough matchup versus a recently upgraded defense -- scored a season-high 28.5 fantasy points. Irving had 97 yards rushing and two touchdowns on 20 carries, adding four receptions for 28 yards. Irving now has 21 or more points with at least one touchdown in three straight games. The Bucs have a bye, but Irving will be a locked-in RB1 for the Week 11 game in Detroit. -- Bowen 

 
 

 

 Green Bay 45, New England 27 
 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap 

 

 Packers 
 Should Jordan Love be in the MVP conversation? If he wasn't before, he should be now -- especially considering the Packers have virtually no run game to help him. Love carved up the Patriots to the tune of 372 yards, three touchdown passes, one rushing TD and no interceptions, and he didn't even have to play the final nine minutes of the game. He was perfect against the blitz, and his deep throws were once again on target. It was his second game of the season with at least six completions on throws of 20-plus air yards. The rest of the NFL has zero, according to ESPN Research. Having receivers such as  Christian Watson (seven catches, 171 yards, one touchdown) and Matthew Golden (10 catches, 164 yards, one touchdown) certainly helps, but it's a mutually beneficial relationship.

 Trend to watch: The Packers aren't just taking the ball away this season, they're taking it early. Their 16th takeaway of the season came on the Patriots' second play from scrimmage -- an interception by safety Xavier McKinney . It was the fifth first-quarter interception by the Packers this season. They didn't have a single first-quarter interception last season. -- Rob Demovsky 

 Next game: vs. Vikings (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

 
 

 Patriots 
 How concerned should the Pats be with Drake Maye 's turnover issues resurfacing? Maye has said his commitment to owning the difference between the big play and the right play was key to overcoming his slow start, yet he lost his edge Sunday. His pick on the second offensive play reflected that, setting the tone for a day when the Pats were outclassed in every phase. Maye threw three INTs in the first half and has 11 on the season. He had eight picks all of last season. The Patriots haven't had a positive turnover differential in a game this season and are now minus-11 on the year. So there is a high level of concern, especially for a team hoping to make a deep playoff run.

 Most surprising performance: Christian Gonzalez was dominated. The NFL's highest-paid cornerback has seldom, if ever, been attacked as much as the Packers went after him. His primary assignment, Golden, had 150 receiving yards in the first half, the most in a first half by any player against the Patriots since at least 1978, according to the Elias Sports Bureau. -- Mike Reiss 

 Best quote from the locker room:  "We got our asses kicked," coach Mike Vrabel said. "There's no two ways around it."

 Next game: vs. Lions (Sunday, 9:30 a.m. ET in Munich)

 
 

 Fantasy football takeaway: Patriots WR Demario Douglas scored 15.2 points as he caught five of nine targets for 102 yards. Available in over 40% of ESPN leagues, Douglas has posted 15 or more points in four of his past five games, with at least one touchdown reception in three. He's a steady WR3 in the lineup. -- Bowen
