title: Why the Raiders are better off standing pat at the NFL trade deadline
summary: The NFL trade deadline is on Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET. Have Kubiak, Raiders given hints that they might not make moves?
full_text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- Coach Klint Kubiak said his calculations of the Las Vegas Raiders change weekly.

 In the Raiders' 38-17 loss to the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday afternoon, during which they committed five turnovers on six possessions in the second half, Kubiak saw a team that can be close to competing with the best, but doesn't have enough talent to close that gap.

 With the NFL trade deadline on Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET, the Raiders sit at 4-5 and are mathematically still in the playoff hunt. At the same time, they are not in a position to be aggressive and make a big deal for a wide receiver or interior defensive lineman -- two positions of significant need. Meanwhile, the list of players they could trade to obtain draft capital is fairly thin. Of course, there's Maxx Crosby , but the team is not expected to move him, and the star defensive end said he wants to be with the organization for a "long time." 

 

 To that end, the Raiders are better off standing pat and pushing through the remainder of the season with the roster as is.

 "I really like our team," Kubiak said. "I don't like losing games like this. We've got to have a lot more resilience when you're playing a really good team like we played today. When you start that slow, you don't put yourself in a good position, but I'm proud to coach the guys that we're coaching."

 To some degree, the Raiders might've exceeded expectations by starting 3-0 and posting a .500 record through eight weeks, the first time since 2021. Going into the season, Las Vegas wanted to be competitive, which is why they spent big during free agency. Nonetheless, the Raiders are not oblivious to the organization's current state.

 They have a first-time head coach, offensive coordinator and defensive coordinator, and No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza is in the developmental phase. Running back Ashton Jeanty is in the second year of his career, and the secondary is mostly made up of rookies (safety Treydan Stukes , cornerbacks Hezekiah Masses and Jermod McCoy ).

 Yes, the Raiders wanted to be competitive this season. But it's going to take time before Las Vegas is viewed as a serious contender. But they have cracked the door open for a playoff berth in Kubiak's first season in Las Vegas. If they somehow get five or more wins before their Week 13 bye, the Raiders have a chance to make a postseason push since they have a favorable schedule to close out the regular season.

 

 Three of the Raiders' final five games are at home, with two of those matchups against the 0-8 Los Angeles Chargers and 1-7 Tennessee Titans . Las Vegas will wrap up the season on the road against the Kansas City Chiefs , who could very well rest their starters during that game in order to prepare for the playoffs.

 With that said, there's a strong argument for the Raiders to strengthen their wide receiver room or defensive line. Two players who come to mind are  Jacksonville Jaguars ' Brian Thomas Jr . and  Indianapolis Colts ' Josh Downs .

 Thomas burst onto the scene as a rookie, totaling 1,282 receiving yards in 2024. His role has diminished ever since. Thomas has collected one catch for 12 yards on seven targets in his past four games. Downs, on the other hand, is in the final season of his rookie contract and recently requested a trade.

 Both players would be an upgrade, and they are still young in their respective careers. Indeed, Las Vegas has drafted three wide receivers in the past two years ( Jack Bech ,  Dont'e Thornton Jr . and Malik Benson ). But none of them have panned out yet, so perhaps adding more experience into the room could be the best path forward.

 As for the interior defensive line, Las Vegas desperately needs help in the trenches. They allowed the 49ers to record 190 rushing yards. It was the fifth time in six weeks that the Raiders have allowed 150-plus rushing yards.

 

 The Raiders, however, could build toward the future by parting ways with the few tradeable assets on the roster. Outside of Crosby, quarterback Kirk Cousins is the second-best trade asset, despite throwing three interceptions in the second half on Sunday. Teams such as the Minnesota Vikings could use a veteran. But the Raiders haven't received any calls about Cousins and have said that they have no intention of trading him, league sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter . The expectation is to keep Cousins past the deadline and have him start until the organization believes Mendoza is ready to play.

 Cousins said any decisions made on his future with the organization are out of his hands. He added that he loves being in Las Vegas and "feels good" about what they are building.

 When taking Crosby and Cousins out of the picture, the list of trade candidates gets thinner. Right guard Jackson Powers-Johnson could be an option. Powers-Johnson was drafted in the second round in 2024. Once viewed as a starter at interior lineman, Powers-Johnson lost his role to Caleb Rogers and rookie Trey Zuhn III , who started at right guard for the second straight week.

 Even when Zuhn exited the game in the second half due to a concussion, Rogers stepped in and finished out the game at right guard. Powers-Johnson has fallen to third on the depth chart at right guard, and there's no sign of reverting to center as long as Tyler Linderbaum is holding down the position. However, if a team needs interior support, whether it's guard or center, Powers-Johnson is a perfect candidate.

 

 "We're always talking about that with [general manager John Spytek] and looking at everything," Kubiak said.

 Las Vegas' loss to the 49ers was dreadful. It was another harsh reminder of the gap between the Raiders and the league's elite squads. The Raiders have lost 15 straight games to opponents who are five games over .500 -- the longest active streak in the NFL.

 Still, the Raiders are in a better position than they were a season ago. But their rebuild wasn't meant to be quick. As painful as afternoons such as Sunday can be to swallow, the Raiders shouldn't turn away from their long-term vision.

 "We're right in the mix," Crosby said. "...We had a tough loss, but when we're at our best, we can beat anybody. We know it's going to be a tough challenge. We have a lot of football left.

 "...We're going to keep believing and keep fighting."

title: Jordyn Tyson's Saints debut showed promise, rookie mistakes
summary: New Orleans expects to give its first-round rookie "plenty of opportunities" as the season progresses.
full_text:
NEW ORLEANS --  Saints rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson had barely processed the game ahead of him Sunday before his phone was ringing.

 It was teammate Chris Olave offering words of encouragement.

 "He was just trying to give me the confidence that I'm ready. He called me this morning. He was the first one that called me. 'Hey, you ready man?!' I was like, 'I'm ready, I'm a little nervous, but I'm ready,'" Tyson said Sunday following the Saints' 23-22 overtime win against the Cleveland Browns .

 Olave, who ranks sixth in the NFL in receiving yards (734), has been eager to see what the rookie could do once he gets on the field. Tyson was expected to be a No. 2 receiver behind Olave when the Saints selected him with the No. 8 pick in the 2026 NFL draft , but a hamstring injury in mid-August derailed those plans.

 

 Olave has had a front-row seat to Tyson's development through the first nine weeks of the season while Tyson was on injured reserve. He has been as eager as anyone for Tyson to show what he can do on the field.

 "I just like his play style, the way he attacks the game. Like everybody, everybody here has seen it, just what he's able to do. He's so talented. He's super talented. I just can't wait for the world to see that," Olave said.

 Tyson's debut was a mixed bag of rookie mistakes, but it was also a display of potential of what he can do with this skill set. He played 18 snaps, caught four passes for 30 yards and fumbled the ball after making his first catch.

 Saints quarterback Tyler Shough found Tyson on second-and-11 with 8:11 left in the second quarter. Tyson and Olave both ran shallow crossing routes and Tyson was open when he made the catch at the 11. But as he began to go to ground, a Cleveland player came in to punch the ball out, giving the Browns the ball at their 1-yard line.

 "Man, I couldn't believe it. I was like, 'god, no way I did that on my first [catch],'" Tyson said later.

 Shough talked to Tyson after the fumble and would later speak to rookie Barion Brown when Brown fumbled a punt return. The message was that it was OK to be upset, but those feelings would have to wait until postgame. The Saints needed him.

 "It happened," Shough said. "You can be pissed about it postgame ... but the rest of the game is still within your control.

 "He was able to do that. He did a really good job. It was just a realization for him that, at all times, you've got to be aware of it."

 

 The Saints not only went back to Tyson after the fumble, but they leaned on him in the most critical part of the game. The Saints were down 13-9 with 5 minutes left in the fourth quarter, needing a touchdown to regain the lead. On third-and-5 at midfield, Shough went to Tyson, who made the catch for 7 yards and a key first down.

 The Saints followed that with a 33-yard pass to Olave on the next play, setting up their touchdown. Olave said after the game that he told Tyson, "all you can do is move forward" following the fumble, and he proved that with the big catch later.

 "We're going to keep getting him the ball," Olave said. "He's one of our best players when he's on the field. You guys saw that today, especially because he made a lot of third-down catches, especially at the end of the game. But that was just a little bit that you've seen from him.

 "I know he's going to ramp up as he keeps going. He's going to be a great player for us in the future."

 The Saints put trust in Tyson late, giving him 13 snaps in the fourth quarter and overtime. While Tyson said he was on a pitch count, with the idea to keep him under 30 snaps, it's clear the expectation is to ramp up his participation moving forward.

 "He's missed a lot of time, but what he's put into this, to put himself in the position to help contribute for this team, he's going to have plenty of opportunities moving forward," Saints coach Kellen Moore said. "I was excited to see him out there playing football again."

title: The key behind 49ers' 7-1 start? Big contributions from the team's youth
summary: While the 49ers' stars have shown out, Jordan Watkins, Jaden Dugger and Kaelon Black have also led the team to its best start since 2019.
full_text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- As the San Francisco 49ers clung to an 11-point halftime lead against the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday, star linebacker Fred Warner delivered a simple message to the rest of the defense: Just get one.

 As in one takeaway. The belief, according to Warner, was that it would lead to more. And with Warner's voice still echoing in his head, rookie linebacker Jaden Dugger  delivered the knockout blow on the first play of the third quarter, intercepting Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins and returning it 37 yards for a touchdown.

 It was the first of five second-half takeaways for the Niners on their way to a 38-17 win and a 7-1 record -- their best start since 2019, when they reached Super Bowl LIV . While the play was a pivotal moment in the victory, what it represents means more for the trajectory of their season.

 Yes, the Niners will continue to lean heavily on the star-powered core that has carried them for the past seven years. But if they are going to rise to another level, the continued ascent of their youth movement will go a long way in making it happen.

 "We have a great core group of guys, guys who played the game at a very high level for a long time," tight end George Kittle said. "We have all these young guys who are playing at a really high level because they see other veteran players playing at high level and they're like, 'Hey, I want to be that good.' It's really good for the Niners and our best players will take us pretty far, but we need young guys to step up."

 

 That development has helped define the 49ers' 2026 season but gained even more steam Sunday.

 In addition to Dugger's pick-six, second-year wide receiver  Jordan Watkins led the team with 86 yards on four catches, including his first NFL touchdown. Rookie running back Kaelon Black had a team-high 70 yards on 11 carries. Nickel back Upton Stout , a 2025 third-round pick, chipped in a forced fumble at the goal line in the third quarter.

 As injuries have again ravaged the team's roster, their young players are not only logging more snaps than expected, but some have also stepped into starting roles. Through eight games, they have 16 players from the past two rookie classes who have appeared in a game. From that group, 10 have played more than 100 snaps; seven have logged more than 200.

 Rookies like Dugger, defensive tackle Gracen Halton and defensive end  Romello Height have combined to start 14 games. Second-year players, such as Watkins, Stout, guard Connor Colby , safety Marques Sigle and defensive tackle C.J. West , have started a combined 21 games.

 More importantly, there have been obvious signs of progress along the way. Watkins might offer the best example of that growth after injuries forced the Niners to dig deep into the receiver depth chart.

 After a training camp that left him on the roster bubble, injuries to Ricky Pearsall ( knee ) and Christian Kirk ( calf ) allowed Watkins to make the final roster. More injuries -- to Mike Evans , rookie De'Zhaun Stribling and others -- created opportunities for Watkins to contribute, including  against the Falcons in Week 7 .

 Watkins finished with three catches for 56 yards in Atlanta, but he also couldn't quite come down with a couple of contested passes thrown his way. For him, it stirred up thoughts of the training camp critiques he'd seen on social media of his inability to outmuscle defenders when the ball is up for grabs. Instead of wallowing on it, Watkins made it a point of emphasis to fix during the Week 8 bye.

 

 "That was just kind of a confidence thing," Watkins said about the lack of contested catches. "It was about going back in the bye week and just resetting a little bit and kind of building off the Atlanta game. It's just really a confidence thing knowing that I can do it."

 Similar confidence has seemed to overflow from the 49ers' rookie class, one that perhaps not so coincidentally seems wise beyond its years. At the time of the draft, the Niners had the third-oldest class of draftees in the league. Their eight-man draft class entered Sunday with an average age of 23.38. Dugger and Halton are the youngest at 22, while Black and Height are the oldest at 25.

 Kittle said he loved the Niners drafting the older prospects because they "understand the sense of urgency that comes with football." Indeed, the idea that the rookie class entered a locker room full of players who have been just short of the franchise's sixth Lombardi Trophy was immediately evident.

 "Ever since we got here, everybody was trying to talk about how we're like an old team or whatever, but we knew we have to contribute," Dugger said. "When I got drafted, they told me you're not just coming here to sit. Just coming in with that mentality, I feel like we knew we had to contribute early. I feel like we are just trying to do our job with the opportunities we have."

 Dugger's opportunity arrived during camp, when he won the team's "fever backer" job. Halton earned a prominent spot in the DT rotation with splash plays like his touchdown against Seattle , but he suffered a season-ending broken left ankle Sunday. Height stepped into a starting job after a series of injuries and has shown improvement as a situational pass rusher. Black will continue to get reps as the primary backup and complement to running back Christian McCaffrey . Fourth-round cornerback Ephesians Prysock has garnered snaps in each of the past two games and is now the team's primary backup at that spot.

 

 That doesn't even account for Stribling, the team's top pick in April who won a starting job before injuring his ankle in the opener against the Rams . The Niners hope to get him back at some point in December.

 Defensive end Nick Bosa has been impressed enough with the rookies that he says coach Kyle Shanahan and general manager John Lynch did "an amazing job" in the draft. But through the first half the season, Shanahan, Lynch and their respective staffs have done more than just select the talent. They, along with the team's veterans, have instilled that urgency that Kittle referenced.

 "In other locker rooms, the rookies can be the burdens," Halton said. "For us, man, we got great vets in here, great guys that's been through any type of adversity. We really just try to glue to them and that happens within the rookies ... Getting the ring, that's the goal every year. But we really want it bad just to do it for those guys, the vets."
